JAMES ABRAM GARFIELD. Roux Nova:Assn 19, 1811, DIED SEPTEMBER 19TE, 1881. T do not come to weep above thy pall, And mourn the dying out of noble powers The poet's clearer eye should see in all Earth's seeming woe the seed of Heaven's flowers. o power can die that ever wrought for truth; Thereby a law of Nature it became, And lives unvrithered in its sinewy youth, 'When he who called it forth is but a name. Therefore I cannot think thee wholly gone; The better part of thee is with us still; Thy soul its hampering clay aside has thrown. And only freer wrestles with the ill.

Such was he, our 'Martyr Chief, Whom late the Nation he had led. With ashes on her head. Wept with the passion of an angry grief; Forgive me, if from present things I turn To speak what in my heart will heat and burn, And hang my wreath on this world-honoured urn. Nature, they say, doth dote, And cannot make a man Save on some worn-out plan, Repeating us by rote: For him her Old World moulds aside she threw, And choosing sweet clay from the breast Of the unexhausted West, With stuff untainted shaped a hero new, _ - Wise, steadfast in the strength of God, and true. How beautiful to see - Once more a shepherd of mankind indeed, Who loved his charge, but never loved to lead; ' One whose meek flock the people joyed to be, Not lured by any cheat of birth, • But by his clear-grained human worth, - And brave old wisdom of sincerity! They knew that outward grace is dust; They could not choose but trust In that sure-footed mind's unfaltering skill And supple-tempered will, , That bent like perfect steel to spring again and thrust. His was no lonely mountain-peak of mind, . Thrusting to thin air o'er our cloudy bars. A sea-mark now, now lost in vapours blind Broad prairie rather, genial, level lined. Fruitful and friendly for all human kind, Tet also nigh to heaven and loved of loftiest stars. JAMES RUSSELL LOWELL. %—From the Detroit Free Press (English edition.)

THE WOODLAND SEAT. Deep in a wood—l love the spot! 'Tis fairest far in Spring, When sweet, from every bowery plot. The golden finches sing. -'- *Tls lovely in the Summer Thick set in deepest shade; When the year is in its golden prime, And verdure crowns the glade. In Autumn, too, it is a place Of glory and of gloom; And there, the last of all its race, The violet finds a tomb. In churlish Winter's cheerless days, Chill seems the lonely glen; And yet, withal. it hath a grace That lingers even then.
And long ere yet a floweret shows. Within the trim parterre, The es.rly primrose nods and blows, • The violet trembles there. —B. G. Gaznr, in Good Words for Oetobsr.

(half full). THE BEAR AN,D PAMTHER.—A hunter in North America I once witnessed az terrific "combat between a bear and a panther. He hadrthrowdhimself down by a beast lake to rest after the labours of etlee' day, when he was suddenly aroused by the most horrible howling. Presently a bear' emerged from the wood; looking for a way of escape, buti finding none. Shortly afterwards a panther appeared, which at once attacked the bear, springing upon 'its back and assailing it in the fiercest manner. The two animals fought with the utmost fury for a considerable time; bat at last the bear fell dead. As soon as the struggle was ended the panther went to the lake to quench its thirst, and, on its return, a welledirected bullet Irene the spectator of the fight - laid it low.—Little Folks Magazine. An Englishman was bragging of the spced on English railroads to a Yanked traveller seated at his side in one of the cars of a "fast train" in England. The *engine bell was rung as the train neared a station. It suggested to the Yankee an opportunity of "taking down his companion a" _,peg or two." "What's that noise 't" innocently inquired the Yankee. "We are approaching a town," said the English. E ' non "they have to commence ringing about tan piles be-1 they get to a station, or else the train would run by it " before the bell could be heard! Wonderful, isn't it? I sup- pose they haven't invented bells in America yet ?" "Why, yes," replied the Yankee "we've got bells, but can't use them on our railroads. Ate run so 'carnal fast that the train always keeps ahead of the sound. No use whatever—the sound never reaches the village till after the train gets by." "Indeed!" excleimed the Englishman. "Fact," said the Yankee; "bad to give up bells." Bow !Do Mean XOttaSELF UNIIAPPT.—In the first place, • If you want to make yourself miserable, be selfish. Think all the time of yourself and your things. Don't care about anything else: Hoe no feelings for anyone but yourself. Never think of enjoying the satisfaction of seeing others happy; bot"ratlier, if ~yett see a smiling face, be jealons lest another should enjoy what you have not. Envy every- • one who is better off than yourself; think unkindly towards them and speak lightly of them. Be constantly afraid lest someone should encroach on your rights; be watchful against it,and if anyone comes near your things snap at them' like a mad dog. Contend earnestly for everything that is your own, that may not be worth a pin. Neveryield a point. Be very sensitive, and takeeverything that is said to you in playfulness in the most serious manner. Be jealous of your friends lest they should not think enough of you; and if at any time they should seem to negitctorou, put the worst construction upon their conduct. ' WHEN IS THE Bent SAFE.—There are 'few greater lad- wirers of the bath than I myself am. I like almost every - plan of bathing—with the exception, probably, of the Russian moudjik plan of getting in neder the stove, and burying yourself in hot ashes. I hove never tried that, but doubtless it has its advantages—to a moudjik. However, I mest say there is sech a thing as over-doing even the bath. Atthough I should wish that every one in this country were like myself—amphibious, no that it thrown into the water ha would only ponder, while quietly swimming out again, where the nearest place was at which to procure dry clothes and a cup of coffee, still it must be remembered that men I are not manatees. We could not live most of our time in the water, like those interesting aquatic mammals. Feryle should neither bathe too often its the day, nor remain too long in the water at a time, else they will over-do it, they- will have too touch of a good thing. The after effects of the bath should in all cases b 3 studied, as well as the state of the rtieral health. Moreover, the temperature of the water deserves consideration ; it may.. suit some people to break the ice on their matutinal tub in winter,with a frozeo sponge for a mallet, but a dish of warm water is to be recommended when the mercury croeees the line 32deg. One bath a day in winter, and two In the heat of summer.' - I would call not over-doing the thing.—The Family Doctor' in Camell's 'Magazine. OrPosrrns IN MATRIMONY.—Theodore Parker wrote : Young people marry their opposites hi: temperament and general character, and such marriages are generally good ones. They do it instinctively. Time young man does not say, "My black eyes require to be wed with blue, and my over-vehemence requires to be a little modified with some- what of dulness and reserve." When their opposites come tor•eth tr to be wed they do not know it, but each think the other jest like himself. Old people never marry their • oppeeiree e they marry their simiiars, and from calculation. Each of these two arrangements is very proper. In their long journey these opposites will fall out by the way a great ne Inv times, an charm the other back again, and by and by they will be agreed as to the place they will go to, and the road they Will go by, and both become recenciled. The - man will be nobler and larger for being associated , with so much humanity unlike himeelle and she will be a nobler woman for havirg manhood beside her that seeks to cortect . her deficiencies and supply her with what she leeks, if the diversity be not too great, and- if there be real generosityl and love in their hearts to begin with. The old bridegroom, ' having a much shorter journey to make,must associate him- self with one like himself. A perfect and complete marri- age is, perhaps, as rare as perfect personal beauty. Men and women are married fractionally, now a smsli fraction, : eth,sn a large fraction. yery few are married totally, and 'they only, I think, after some forty or fifty years of gradual ' - aiproach and experiment. Such a large and sweet fruit is . remaplete 'marriage that it needs a very long summer to 104 o pen hi acid than a long winter to mellow and season. THE LAND QUESTION,

that in many instances under our present system, life OW the writer is not only prepared, but glad to admit satisfactorily all the duties of a good landlord. Men tenants, the nominal owners of large estates, are discharg- inglike the Duke of Bedford, the Duke of Northumberland, and many others with large estates, manage them so well that people are apt to loss sight of the seamy side of the system.uch landlords were thoroughly instructed in all the mani- fold duties of owners of property during the lifetime of their fathers, and being conscious that a large body of t dependants look to them for guidance and example,antbley enter upon the management of their estates' spirit altogether superior to commercial self interest, i en a an prepared to do for them what no mere land speculator would think of doing, and no small proprietor could afford to do. If such a landlord is a religious man he builds churches in neglected hamlets; if he is an agriculturist he sinks more in drainage and farm buildings than he Will ever receive back in rent; if he is a social reformer, he erects model cot- tages, carries out sanitary improvements, patronises schools, or devotes himself to bringing forward the most promising youths in the parishes of which he is the lord: With educa- tion enough to understand the economical and legal ques- tions which he is daily called upon to settle in practice, with leisnre enough to follow the course of affairs both at home and abroad, with refinement enough to appreciate art and literature, with energy enough to enjoy a life of con- stant activity in which "county business is relieved by field sports and a laborious summer holiday, with indepen- dence enough to smile ar official favours or displeasure, the model English country gentleman represents a species which has never been developed in any other country. There are many limited owners among our oldesifansffins who,taking; a leading part in agricultural ref orms,bring to bear (Misstate management an administrative ability scarcely to be ex- pected of the yeoman or the squire, and a reserve of ready' money drawn from ground rents of town properties, which I few owners in fee simple possess. Such is the picture drawn by a master hand of the beet of our landholders. Would that this sort were more. com- mon than they are. But there is an obverse side to the picture. What about that much greater number of land- holders who are not wealthy, who are saddled with pay- ments to widows and younger brothers and sisters and mort- gage interest, until they have a comparatively bare income on which to make the appearance in the county which is expected of them? Take, for instance, a man with £7,000 or £B,OOO a year from land, and six children. The land goes by the settlement to one son—the eldest. There is a join- ture to a widow of a former owner. There is an old mort- gage, and each of the younger children has to have a fresh slam raised out of the estate. The owner cannot save much. He has to keep up a good house, in proportion to his sta- tion. The charges for interest are heavy, and he would like, if possible, to save something more for the poor young things than the pittance provided by the settlement. Moreover, he does not like to spend money on ths land, as all money. so spent will go to increase the share of the'eldest who has already so much more of the family inherit- ance than he ought to have, according to any fair mode of division. So if cottages want rebuilding, or new farm buildings are required to meet the competitions Of the pre- sent time, or draining is badly wanted, the work cantsot be done. The 'farmers on such an estate must wait and hope. They can do no more, unless they choose to spend their own money, which is not likely when they are generally yearly tenants only, or have no legal claim to be paid fop what they have laid out, its case they leave or are turned out. • But some one may ask--Is it a common thing for these settled estates to be encumbered in this manner? Mr. Jas. Caird, CM., F.R.S., is one of the greatest living authoritiesl on agriCultural matters, and has had' innsual opportunities for studying them, and he says;—" Much of the land of England—a far greater proportion -of it than is generally believed—is in the possession of tenants for life, so heavily burthened with settlement encumbrances that they have noo the means of improving the land which they are obliged tt hold. It would be a waste of time to dilate on the public and private disadvantages thus occasioned, for they are ac- knowledged by all who have studied the subject and -are :Seriously affected by it." In another place he Writes : "The sahstantiarand capacious farmeries of Belgium, Hol- land, the North of France, and the Rhenish provinces con- trast most favourably with the farm buildings common in most" English counties ;" while again he ;says, "The one I great barrier to improvement which the present state of ' agriculture must force on the attention of the Legislature is the great extent to which _landed property is encumbered. In' every county where we found an estate more than usually neglected, the reason assigned was the inability of the proprietor to make improvements on account' of his en- cumbrances. . . . There is no capital available for the improvinrents which a landowner is called upon to, make in order to keep his property abreast of the advance in agri- cultural practices' • Other eminent and trustworthy witnesses give similar v./Menne before Parliamentary Committees. Orr. Josiah Parkes, C.E., " had not the slightest doubt as to there being a quantity of land of entailed estates which requires drain- age." Mr. Thompson of Reigate, who said he had "a good dial to dd ilth entailed estates," was of opinion that "entailed estates "generally required very great ithprove- imeitt." The well-known agriculturist, Mr. James Smith, of DeanstOn, being 'eked' if he had any observation tb make, I at once said, "Tee law of entail obstructs the sabStantial improvement of the 'mar. - But some one may say, these people have no land per- haps, or they would not talk like that." Let us see, then, what landlords themselves say. But a few years ago a Committee of the House of Lords," consisting of the Duke of Richmond, Marquis of Salisbury, Earl of Derby, and Lord Egerton of Tatton, 'presented a report-dralvn up by the Marquis of Salisbury, showing among other things that of 20,000,000 acres in this country requiring drainage, only 3,000,000 had been drained, and that; taking into account also all other necessary improvements, only one-fifth of the land had been properly. dealt with. Is not that a serious state of things ? The f armers may well complain of poor crops, especially ins wet year. In further confirmation of this defective agriculture, let no take the evidence of the late Mr. Mechi, who made high- class farming the study of his life. Writing to the Times (and there has been no change since), he said ' " There are millions of acres of exhausted grass lands, and poor stiff clays, which now bind the tenant in poverty and discontent, that would be rendered profitable by an in- vestment of from £2O to £36 per acre in the following improvements : 4 s. d. Drainage 7 0 0 subsoihng or deepened cultivation 2_o 0 Removal of hedgerows, trees, and improve- ment of roads Covered yards and good farm buildings...— 7 0 0 Suitable residence for tenant 5 0 0 Steam machinery • 2 10 0

Burnt clay, chalk, or lime 5 0 0 Guano, bones, and other manure 3 0 0 Sewage irrigation, where practicable So here is a total of landlord's and tenant's improvements which, conjointly, would certainly result in individual and national profits. lam speaking practically on the matter, and I know that it would be a happy circumstance for the generality of clay land farmers to have their present rents doubled, or even trebled, provided that the increased rental represPriled a fair interest on a sum expended in landlords' improv•ments.' But to make such suggestions to very many of our land- lords, situated as they' Amp, is simple mockery, and on of them has frankly explained the position in which many of them are placed. Lora C arring ton ,on Oot. 28th, 1879, at the Tenants' Dinner, st ited "his own case," and his remarks are so apropos they deserve to be given at length. He showed them that as tenant for life he could not charge the estate for per- minent improvements, nor could he sell a single acre of the 34 ssuare miles which he had inherited. He went on to say: —"Under these circumstances, what are the landlords to do? On all sides, we hear of reductions and returns to tenants. These are daly:cbronicled in the newspapers with a certain grim humour as Liberality of a Landlord.' It keeps some tenants going, and saves the landlord having to cultivate; bat ten per cent. reduction is no real use, and does not solve the question at all. -The time has come that the great ques- tion of Entail, should be calmly discussed. Many consider that the Land Laws .which allow a landowner by his deed or by his will to prevent his land being sold, seized, or lessened Size, either daring his own life, or for many years after his death, are necessary for the very existence of the landed interest of England. May not these laws be a positive dan- ger to the country, and one of the reasons for the present agricultural distress? In no way do I wish to introduce a principle that a living man may not do what he likes with his .oitn—buy, sell, let, or farm as much as he chooses; leave it all to his eldest son, dividtit amongst all his chil- dren,,or leave it entirely away. But though we prope-ly 'respect the rights of the living, ought we not to curtail the power of-,,,he dead ? The largest landowner in England and Scotland has a total of 1,358,548 acres. I see no harm in that, there is no reason why he should not own 2000,000 acres, but what I do think wrong is that a landowner should eitberlay, his own act or _by the deed of his pre- , decessors be saddled with an enormous tract of country of which it is impossible for him to get rid of a square yard, however necessary, however beneficial the sale of a small portion of it would be to the country, the estate, to Mel tenants, or to himself. I will try to show what the conse- quence is. In the north of the county [Bucks] I have two strong clay farms on my lands ; one I cannot get a bid for,l nobody will cultivate it at any rent. I say to my agent, What am Ito do?' He answers, 'The buildings must be rebuilt, the worst land laid down in grass, the land drained and cleansed, and in two years you may get a tenant.' Very go,d, but all this ought to have been done years ago, and the tenant would have been saved, and the land would never have got into so miserable a condition. But the same millstone is round my neck that hampered my father that I must wear till my death, my brothers as well, if they suc- ceed me, and the land is not free till after our deaths, or Oaf twenty-first birthday of an unborn heir. As tenant for life, I hoped against hop* t trusted to the good season of 1879 to put things-right; that season failed, the tenant is ruined, and the land starved. It is a small matter, one farm in hand, you will say, but look-around us. I bear of a pro- prietor ,with 4,000 acres on his hands, a Berkshire land- owner, with 13 farms, and land thrown up in all directions. People would improve their properties if they could, but the majority cannot.' Bnch is the opinion of a great landholder, who is also a or the House of Lords. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c, Reports from Ireland, where the grain crops are noW gathered, are, on the whole, highly satisfactory. Though wheat is not so plentiful as in some previous seasons, the grain is good and the straw heavy. Barley is excellent. Oats, though large in quantity, are light for want of sun-, shine. Potatoes are free from disease, the "Champion" sup- plied as seed last spring having done wonderfully well. In consequence of the rinderpest having broken out in Austria-Rungary, the "Goverament at Vienna have Opened the cattle station at Podwolsczyska on the Gailician-Russian boundary. It is said that 6,000 oxen are now waiting there' for ftnitteftransportation:. - They Wilt be transported direct to Vienna. According to the official, reports of September 12th and, 19th the rioderpest has broken. out in Rohenau (Mistelbach) and in Dialing (Sechsliatis) in Lower Austtia. SCOTCH LANDLORDS SETTING AN EXAMPLE.—The Duke of Buccleuch, and one or two other Scotch landlords, have already reduced the rents of many of their tenants with running leases to Current rates; and, in eatates where hitherto there has been no arrangement as to compensation for tenants' improvements, a satisfactory and equitable un- derstanding has been arrived at. For the sake of landlords and tenants alike, it is earnestly to be hoped that this course will be generally adopted. A METHOD OF LEADING CATTLE.—Mr. J. W. Gilman, Kearney county, Nebraska, writes of an arrangement of the halter for' the easy leading of cattle that are inclined to hang back. .He writes:—"l learned the method from a young Dane in my employ. I had two cows, neither of which would lead with any degree of:comfort ; to lead them both at once was out of the question. One day I noticed the Dane leading them with as little trouble as if they were well broken horses. This ease in leading was due to his taking a half-hitch in the halter around one ear of each cow in such a way that it would not slip off. This idea has , been worth a great deal to me." To those who have tugged , and worried over a cow that wOuld not lead at the halter, , this hint will be welcome. The rope is first put round the , base of, the horns of the animal in a noose, with the knot just under one o/ the horns; the rope is then taken round the back of the ear, up at the front and under the noose be- tween the horns. if the cow pulls the ear is at once nipped by the rope.—American Agriculturist. OCTOBER has come with bright clear skies and a second summer, causing farmers to regret that such beautiful weather did not fall to their lot in the middle of August, when their grain crops were sprouting and rotting in the fields under the influence of the oft•recurring rains. Spilt milk cannot be helped, however, and the British farmers have to consider what are the advantages of the present, rather than"dwell on the evils of the- past. The situation has become favourable for tillage operations. The land turns up well after late soakings, and can be got to work well without difficulty. The season is probably too late for much. to be done to surface cleaning where that operation cottld not be effected earlier, and it must be confessed that a wet August and damp, foggy September have caused prodigious quantities of grass and weeds in the stubbles. Where the latter are at all cleanly a better time could not possibly be chosen for sowing winter green crops, such as rye, winter barley, winter oats, and early vetches. The land is also in excellent condition for early wheat sowing, and if we had hundreds of acres to put in we should prefer, to conduct the operation now rather than later, adopting, of eourse, thin 'seeding, and a due compression of the surface where the soil e light.

M.P., speaking ,at..) a Liberal soirée at Ply- mouth on Tuesday, in refutation of the arguments of 'Fair Trade advocates, said the complaint that our imports had exceeded our exports need not alarm anyone who under- stood the subject. We must not be deluded by a cry of Fair Trade, which meant neither more nor less than that ,the food ' of the people should be taxed to subsidise a special class. Messrs. teaks and Agnew;the members for South-East Lancashire, addreseed a meet'!" Mr. Leake said that the Fair far as it promised to embarrass the Liberal Mr. Agnew spoke on the need of a reform of the stollen.% orders of the Route of , Commons. Matters had come to such a pass in Ireland as to justify active measures. He advocated an extension of the franchise to householders in counties, the abolition of the law of distress and the law of primogeniture and entail, and ridiculed the agitation for a re-imposition of import and export &Aka. Mr. W. E. Forster, speaking at a banquet giyen by the , Lord Mayor of Dublin to the Duke of Teck on Saturday night, said that, though the Government tried to keep as , cheerful of heart as they could, they were very much em- barrassed by the serious nature of affairs which occupied the House for many months and which occupied the attention of the Government still. They all knew that one great Irish measure had been the chief— almest the only—result of the session. A great and honest 1 effort had been made, and most heartily and sincerely I carried out, to do good to Ireland, and, if possible, to avoid any harm that might.come to her. He believed there was anearnest and strong determination thatthe will of the Legi- slature in carrying the Land Act should not be frustrated, and that the law passed with all this care and,detertninatien should be faithfully and honestly obeyed. ' Dr. Croke, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Cashel, re- plying to an address from a branch of the Land League, on Sunday, admitted that the Land Act far surpassed in the value of its provisions every Act relating to the tenure of land in Ireland that hail ever been passed by Parliament; but, he said, its real value was to be estimated by the actual reduction of the rental of Ireland which the Commissioners were prepared to -make. The Archbishop said the people had hitherto been paying in the shape of rent every penny they could scrape together out of the land—a statement which the curious in such matters can hardly help cm- paring with the facts which the Premier gave at Leeds respecting the enormous increase of -the agricultural savings of Ireland. The Archbishop's notions of what the landlords are entitled to will be gathered from his closing words, which caused his hearers not only to cheer but also to laugh—" When they found the labourers wholesomely fed, fairly clad, and decently housed, then, indeed, whatever re- mained after making suitable provision for their families they might give to the landlord." - Mr. Parnell, speaking at Wexford on Monday, replied to Mr. Gladstone, and said many of them would have studied the words of a great man, a great orator, who up to recently desired to impress the world with a good opinion of his philanthropy and hatred of oppression, but who stood to- day the greatest coercionist, the greatest and most unri- valled slanderer of the Irish nation that eier undertook the task. He referred to Wm. Ewart Gladstone and his unscru- pulous and dishonest speech of Friday. Not content with maligning the people, be maligned their bishops, and he maligned John Dillon. He attempted to misrepresent the Younglreland pkrty of '4B. No misrepresentation was too low for him to stoop to. It was a good sign that this mas- qaerading knight errant, this pretended champion of the liberties of every nation except Ireland, , was obliged to throw off the mask to-day, and to stand revealed as prepared to carry fire and sword into the homesteads of the Irish people, unless they humbled and abased themselves before the law and the landlords of the 'country. Mr. Gladstone accused them of preaching the gospel of "plunder," -but the land of Ireland had been confiscated three times over by the men whose descendants Mr.'Crladstone was new support- ing in the enjoyment of their plunder by bayonets and buckshot. Land League meetiress on Sunday were held in many places. A meeting which was announced at Frenchpark, near Boyle, was prohibited'. The intended chairman pro- tested against the suppression as "the most despotic act he had ever seen," and then informed the police that the meet- ing had been held earlier in the day.. At Ballymore (Kildare) Mr. Leahy, M.P., thanked the tenant farmers for the " compliment " they had paid biro by Sending him to the British House of Commons, and then proceeded to de- nounce the House and the Government with all the energy at his command. He promised Mr. Gladstone that the Parnell party would have a good deal more to say to him and his miserable Land Act." At the Wexford meeting half a dozen_ of Mr. Parnell's attaches were present, and there was the usual denunciation of British tyranny and re- ferences to the mysterious "men of 'OB '''-and the siege of Limerick. Mr. Healy, M.P., was seen in his very coarsest mood when "replying," as it was called, to Mr. Gladstone; and Mr. Redmond, M.P. who has only lately been aware that it is the duty of every patriotic ,Irishman to scorn the wages that may be earned in the service of a cruel Saxon Government in Landon, boldly advised the men of Wexford to refuse to be intimidated. At Ballyraggett,Mr. A. O'Connor,' M.P., speaking as the local champion of the League, said that they "discouraged all means which could be fairly open to the charge of lawlessness." At all' these meetings prominence was give!! to the claims of the labourers, and the tenant farmers were called upon to give then,. increased em- ployment and reduce their house rents. -- MR. GLADSTONE AT LEEDS. ; Mr. Gladstone brought his Leeds visit to a conclusion on Saturday, delivering two important addresses. The right hon, gentleman again met with the mast enthusiastic re- ceptions, the excitement culminating in the afternoon by a inagnifitent oration in 'the Cloth Hall:yaid, in which , were assembled some thirty thousand persons, mostly 1 working men of Leeds. The Premier's first sPeech on Saturday was given in reply to an hddress from the . local chamber of Commerce, and resolved itself into a splendid and overwhelming vindication of Free Trade prindiples. Touching on the subject of the French Treaty negotiations, Mr. Gladstone said it would be premature yet to anticipate what their result might be. But whether we had 'a teettty or not, be said the nation might rely upon this, taking it for all in all, that the Government would not assent to a treaty of retrogression, either small or great. On the new fangled cry for protection the utterances of the Premier were most emphatic. lie expressed the strongest and firmest conviction that no Government that could exist in this country would, either hooner or later, make itself responsible for any pro- 0 posals for restoring protective-duties. They might as well try to overthrow trial by jury, or the right of petition or of , pnblie meeting; they might as well attempt to tear-' out of our social and political system ally one of the most cherished ideas Englishmen had inherited for centuries as to overset the Free lrade legislation. At the same time, he admitted that the strange theories which had for the moment lifted their heads but of their native obscurity might become ' matter of serious conflict between parties, and might create , and propagate delusions in various quarters of the country. Mr. Gladstone proceeded to survey the state of the country, its wealth, trade, and population now as com- pared with the era of protection, showing the enormous strides thathave been made during the past forty"years. tie quoted statistics bearing irresistible evidence to the marvel- ous progress that had been made by English commerce under the auspices el "that great vampire of free trade, which was said to be insidiously sucking the life-blood of ,thiti ._ great nation." In the neutral markets of the world America's, competition WaS shown to be but puny compared with this country's, and so long as America adhered to protection Mr. Gladstone declared England's commercial supremacy to be secure. Nowhere had the competition been sharper than in the matter of shipping, and yet our tonnage had multiplied more than sixfold since 1840' and, as a sample of the pro- gress which bad been made, the speaker pointed out that when he was a ,boy living, by the mouth of the Mersey the Americans were-so superior to us with their beautiful liners that4hey monoaolieed four-fif .hs of the trade Ixtcreut Liverpool and New York, leaving English vessels the dregs, while at ' the present - day the scale was exactly reversed the British had four - fifths and the Americans had what might be called the leavings. Addressing the mass meeting in the afternoon, Mr. Glad- stone made a general survey of the Government policy abroad during the past eighteen months. - Anslwering Sir Stafford Northcote's chatge of extravagant expenditure, the Premier remarked that it was rather too much that they should be reproached for having failed, in economy, when they had been compelled to raise millions of money for the purpose ot meeting the difficulties and paying the liabilities of honour and duty which their predecessors had bequeathed to them. After referring to the settlement of the frontidf that head being of a reassgring and pacifiaescecatrohinoifadnurFsairrincdattrniteiffihere e.etc. questions in Greece and Montenegro, Mr. Gladstone alluded wthe crisis that had arisen in Egypt, his statements on twesmhoegahniuvhtittaciaiwenl which crisis iehtss ohaiibt beneficial' smhsettaeaphfhntaroeeirtrshtea enrefused eeti falliediCabinetlo, elmea tfingei believed the intervention of England and France in Egypt Treaty t roea the ty ,t capablevl ih'oi ll While r sauftobdi theaant el iConvention.owing the amendment, on the subject of the native population., Mr. Gladstone plainly intimated that the Government 'would make no concessione to the Boers. He did not know what dirwtheletto would Ttrbcoislereediagwntnhpndasoelzy endeavourtEh agtot i tahGGovernment,ntt, 01 les was to happen, but he hoped the Convention would be t con- certuplAiir teyne-signed. ~ It was a mistake to suppose that their past conces- sions were the effect of weakness or timidity, or that the Government had granted much only as an encouragement to ask for more. In eloquent terms be pointed out what Liberalism had accomplished for ' the nation at home and abroad, and added that those now in power wetild never forget what was due to the dignity of tke throne of Queen Victoria. LORD SALISBURY AND SIR STAFFORD NORTH- COTE AT NEWCASTLE. On Tuesday the Marquis of Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote attended a dinner in connection with the annual Conference of the National Union of Conservat,ive Associa- tions, at Newcastle. The noble Marquis, in replying for the House of Lords, plunged at once into an attack upon Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy. Ho profeteed to trace the present evils in Ireland to, past Liberal legietation, and quoting the Premier's statement at Leeds that Mr. Parnell's policy was one of" public plunder," he retorted by saying that such also was Mr. Gladstone's own policy as embodied in, the Compensations for Disturbances Bill of last year. With regard to the Land Act of last session be refrained from i

speaking in definite terms. To a great extent it was upon itattials. It pled enormous powers in the hands of certain judges, who let them hope, would execute the powers en- trusted to them in a judicial spirit. They had, however, been urged on many sides to do otherwise. If they did not exercise their duties in a judicial spirit—if they allowed the slighted taint of political considerationi to enter into their decisions—if they paid any regard to the political storm ttsf was raging at their doors,—" we should then know that the whole of this arrangement of judicial' machinery had been prostituted for the purpose of imposing upon Parlia- ment." He trusted that none but purely judicial considera- tions would enter into the decisions of the Land Commission- ers. Be that as it might, there was 1.10 tient:, that the_Act wal introduced it, answer to an agitation clearly calling for measures 01 nriblig plunder. If it spoke in ambiguous language, and-if sitc en interpretation was given of lie tetrns, Mr. Gladstone had no right to complain. Mr. Parnell dedinred Very strongly, to the acCusation which the Pride Minister levelled against him, but there was, he maintained, no essential difference between them. The sum Mr. Parnell I proposed to take from his victims was larger than the sum the Prime Minister proposed to take; but the principle on which they both went' waa the same. The Coercion Act, tbe Marquis added, had been a laughing stock. One hundred and, fifty people—all second-rate personages—had been locked up, but the Government had never ventured to lay hands on any, of the promoters of the disorder, Or if they had demi so in one or two cases, they had hastened with trembling bands to release them again. Sir Stafford Northcote responded to the toast of the House of Commons. —The Marquis of Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote continued their visit to Newcastle on Wednesday, and took a trip down the river as the guests of the Tyne Improve- ment" Commissioners. In the' evening the Conservative leaders attended a mass meeting at the Circus, at which about 5,000 persons were present. Several addresses were presented to Lord Salisbury' who in reply, delivered a lengthy speech. He defended the action taken by' the House of Lords on the Irish Land Bill, which, he said, they had purged of certain obnoxious principles, and otherwise greatly improved. Dealing with foreign affairs, his lordship accused the Government of appropriating to themselves whatever credit was due to those who had assisting in nego- tiating the Berlin Treaty. He disapproved of the settlement effected in ,Montenegro, and with regard to Rgypt be was glad to see that the beneficent arrangement which had been adopted by the late Government was approved of by the present Ministers, and he trusted that the interests of England in that country would not be allowed to suffer. He condemned the Government policy in Afghanistan as taking no account of Russian aggression;, While as regards the Transvaal he considered that the prestige of the nation had been permanently', injured by what had taken place there. Lord Salisbury subsequently turned his attention to fiscal matters, and explained that he did not think it possible or for the advantage of the country to return to Protection. But the hope of the promoters of Free Trade that other nations would follow our example having been disappointed, his lordship thought we might see if these could not be in- duced to lower their tariffs by taxing the luxuries which they sent us. Sir Stafford spoke chiefly on Irisheand Transvaal affairs. He expressed a hope that Parliament would deal with electoral corruption, and again dwelt on the work to be done by Conservative organisations throughout he country.

LANCASHIRE HOLIDAYS.—It is well known that the Lan- cashire operatives are very gregarious in their habits. This is seen during the fairs and wakes that take place all over the county, but more so in the annual outings to the sea- side. Daring Whit-week, Blackburn sends its 20,000 to 30,000 excursionists to the sea-side for from one day to a week, mostly averaging three days. Burnley, during its recent fair, sent away on a similar errand 12,000 to 15,000. Accrington, Darwen, and other places send proportionate ' contingents. In the southern portion of the county a like state of matters prevails. In Oldham, however, a very curious custom has arisen of late years. It is the institu- tion of "going-off clubs," as they are called. This is one of the taost singular and remarkable developments of the principle of association with which we are acquainted. We have long been familiar with its 'application to political, tocial, and commercial matters, but it seems this range did not exhaust its capability. From a writer in a local paper, referring to this matter on the occasion of the recent Old- ham wakes, we glean the following information :—" It is some ten years since 'going-off clubs' were started in Old- ham—the clubbing together of a number of people in the Ifactory or workshop for the purpose of putting their' savings together, and investing there at interest, and go supplying the means for a holiday excursion ora longer or shorter duration, just as the amount falling due to a member may allow. These clubs are peculiarly identified with the wakes. It is then that the balancing up takes place and withdrawals are made. The first of these enterprises began in 1871-2. The accumulations have every year increased from that time, and this year it is computed that there has been in the hands of private people, and in the loan accounts of limited companies, no less than £20,000. A ecribe in a London contemporary, commenting on these facts, holds them up as an example of a peculiar kind of "thrift," which, by implication, he would have his readers infer ' would be more accurately described by the addition of the Inegative affixes. It is needless to say that we do not agree with the spirit of any such remarks. We prefer to admire the intelligence which appreciates the pleasures of a few daye spent by the sea in the bracing air of Blackpool, or amongst the green hills of the Isle of Man, or, better still, amidst the grander scenery of North Wales. The prudent forethought that leads them to make early provision, either 'individually or in workshop associations, is rather to be en- couraged than despised, as it will tend to demonstrate to ' many that the means successfully taken to secure a season of pleasure Would be equally efficacious when employed to obtain a more permanent advantage. But, taken on their own merits, these "going-off clubs" are deserving of praise, because their object is to secure rational enjoyment and, healthy invigoration in the beet way possible, after which the people can return with renewed energy to their labour amongst the spindles and looms.—Textile Manufacturer. FOREIGNERS ON THE ENOLLSH POLICE.—Which country has the best police? This is a question that can only be answered when one has arrived area understanding of what constitutes a good police. To most foreigners, the ideal police is that of London. In the works of almost every foreign writer who has treated of England, one finds a tri- bute of admiration to the English ptiliceman—" the worthy representative of a free people," as M. Louis Blanc has called him. Garibaldi and the Shah of Persia have joined In expressing their praise of that blue-coated official "who Is respected by the people without being feared or hated"; andahe Shah's testimony is especially worthy of note, for In the account of his trip to Europe, In 1874, his Majesty finds not a word to say in favour of the French police. The Shah's approbation of Sir Edmund Henderson 's force was even pushed to the point of exaggeration, and let us hope that it was with no intentional purpose of hoaxing his sub- jects that his Majesty wrote, "The constable's truncheon is an emblem before which all men bow: the man who resists it is instantly put to death." The testimony of foreigners to the merits of our institutions may be allowed its proper weight; but it must not be forgotten that the majority of foreigners who have written about England have been poli- tical refugees here, and their praise of our police has- been bestowed rather on account of what it does not do than what it does. The Continental conspirator, who has fled from justice, or injustice, in his own country, and has found no rest for the sole of his foot in any other state abroad, is delighted, on landing in England, to find himself free from every sort of surveillance. He is not asked to exhibit a 'passport or papers of identity; he may lodge where he likes, land under any natne he pleases, without being required to register Igis name, profession, and previous dwelling-places, as in free Belgium, or to take out a perinis de sejour, as in free Switzerland. So long as he avoids breaking the law, he and the police need never come into contact; and the lava allows him exactly the same privileges as to a born Briton. He may form pelltical clubs; he may join inpoliti- cal demonstrations, and yell defiance at monarchs and bishops from• the pedestal of the column in Trafalgar Square; he may carry a red flag through Hyde Park; set up a Socialist newspaper in Soho; and plaster every hoard- ing in the capital with proclamations stating his views of things in general, if he can only afford the expense. Even if a foreigner gets into the custody of the Engliskpolice for a breach of the common law, he is treated with a fairness unknown in other European lands. No attempt is made to worm a confession out of him by cross-questions; he is, on the contrary, cautioned to hold his tongue. He is taken before a magistrate in a public court, within twenty-four hours after his arrest, and there the police depose against him only such things as- they know for certain, not things they suspect or have heard, said. Finally, when the foreigner has been discharged from custody he may continue to re- side in England on the, same conditiep as before, instead of being served with an arrgt d'ei,putston, as happen to all foreigners who get into trouble with the police of Con- tinental countries.—Corishill Magazines

DEATH OF SIR JOHN MOORE AT CORIINNA.—Six soldiers —42nd men and Gnardamen—bore him slowly away in a blanket; and when a waggon came up, and it was proposed to place him beside Colonel Wynch, of the 4th Regiment, who lay in it wounded, the poor fellows objected with tears in their eyes. "We will all keep step, and carry him more easily," they nage& As Moore was borne from the field of his glory, be trequently Made the bearers halt and,turn him - round, that he might behold it, sad be assured that every- where Ws:French were already failing back. In Cue town of Cornnna it was soon found that all hope was over; yet he lingered for a time, talking feebly but collectedly to those about him, and in many ways evincing the gentleness and kindliness of his heart. "Anderson," said he to the colonel so named, an old and valued friend, "you know T have al- ways wished to die in this way." After a pause: "Are the French beaten?" he asked ; and on being assured that they were so, and retiring fast, he added, with touching earnest- ness, "I hope the people of England will be satisfied; I hope my dear country will do 'me justice. ,Oh, Anderson, you will see pay friends it home ! Tell theca everything— my mother— ' Here his voice couipletely failekthian, till he inquired if all his aides-cle-carap were safe. TO One of these, the SOil Of Earl Stahharisahe,aaid, faletly—"Remem- ber me, Stanhope, to—to your sister." It was to the brilliant and famous Lady Hester Stanhope, of Djouna celebrity, who' died in Syria in 1839, he referred, and whom he is said to have loved with great tenderness. Pressing to his breast the hand of Colonel A,nderson who had saved his life at the capture of St. Lucia, he expired without a struggle, in his forty-eigth year, twin°. been born in the Trong-ate of Glas- gow in 1761.--Casyll's'lllastrated British Battles on Land and Bea. Tin FAVOURITE INDIAN GAME.—The game I am now about to describe is.par excellence the Indian game. It is played althrongh British Columbia, Vancouver Island, and Washington Territory, perhaps also in Oregon. Large • quantities of property—even women and slaves, ay, even the gambler's own liberty—are staked on it, and the din of the game resounds in every Indian village In which I had ever an opportunity of residing for any length or tithe. The .plaaers 'are generally four, two on each side; but it may be played by any number, so 'long as the number Of players is equal on either side.- The' gambling implementO, Which differ somewhat in appearance, are two round carved pieces of polished Wood, something like draught-men. These are tossed about in the hand, and from hand to hand, concealed in the blanket, and in any other manner by which the Indian can delude his opponent, the point of the game be- ing that his opponent has to guess in which hand the par- ticular disc of wood is held, and a stick (used as a counter) is lost or gained as the case may be. The game is, however, conducted without a word* be spoken, the players sitting in a circle, the only sounds being the sin-song kept up while the players are manipulating the pieces of Wood. So violent, however, are their exertions while so doing that the players are generally streaming with -Pitspitation, which might lead a stranger on first seeing them at it to'sappose them akin to the "dancing dervishes," and their employ- ment of a religious character, Instead of being the purest gambling. The betting is done by pointing to the arm of the hand id which the sought-for piece of wood is supposed I to be held. Sometimes they decline guessing and watch a little longer, to see if by any means they can be quick enough to detect the piece of wood in its passage from one hand to another. This they express by pointing their fore- finger downwards in the middle of the circle, and then the ' manipulation commences anew. A similar game is played by the Tsimpseans, on the northern coast of British Colon- Way with beautifully-polished pieces of round stick, about' the-size of the middle finger, each piece of stick having a different name. There is another modification of this game. A. number of the pieces are taken and enveloped in a quan- tity of teased-out cedar bark. They are then skilfully tossed out, and :bets are made on the guesses—whether a particularly marked one remains in the bark or not: this is played by moat tribes.—The Peoples of the World. THE EXPERIENCES OF A SAINT.—A certain pious shop- keeper felt an ardent longing to be enrolled in this venerable company, and to that end he went to a man who was uni- versally esteemed as holy, to beg him to procure him an in- terview with the Katb. After all sorts of testa this was pro- mised him, and he was commanded to the above-mentioned gate and to address himself to the first person he might see coming out of the neighbouring mosque of el Mo'ayyad. The merchant obeyed, and he was, in fact, met by the Math in the form of a dignified old man, who granted his prayer and ordered ,him to take the district south-west of the Zuweyleh Gate under his protection, with the street called Darb el -Ahmara Immediately the merchant felt that he had become a Weise, and perceived that he had insight into things hiddealrom other mortals. When he reached the district entrusted to him he saw a man selling cooked beans out of a large pot t 6 the passers-by; the newly-made saint took a stone, struck the pot over with it, and submitted with- out a murmur to a severe thrashing for the deed. When the bean-seller's rage had somewhat moderated, and he set to work to gather up the shards of his broken pot, he found a poisonous snake among the pieces; then he perceived with repentance that he had beaten a Walee who had interfered to prevent his selling food tbat would have poisoned his customers. The next day the poor saint limped round his ' district with swollen limbs, and, without thinking of the I blows had he received a few hours before he flung over a large jar of milk which was offered for sale at a stall. Again 11 he was severely beaten by the owner, but the passers-by I held the milk-seller back, remembering alhat had happened the day before. When they searched among the fragments of the milk-jar they found a dead dog at the bottom. On I the third day the Walee dragged himself again to the Darb el Ahmar, bat painfully, for he was sorely beaten. Here he mat a servant carrying a tray on his head, with delicacies and fruit-intended fora feast in a country-house. .The saint Immediately put his 'stink between the man's feet, so that he fell down and all the contents of the saucers were spilt in the street. The servant flew on him in a fury, and gave him as severe a taste of the stick as he himself expected to get from his master for his clumsiness. Meanwhile the dogs fell upon the cates that lay in the roadway, and within a few minutes of the first mouthfuls they lay dead. This proved to the bystanders that the food that had been spilt had been poisoned, and they earnestly implored the saint's fargivenessa The pious man rubbed his severely' beaten shoulders, said to himself that it was worth while to see things that were bidden from other mortals, and prayed to God and the Kutb to remove from him the burden of sane- ! iotnya tat inodn r e sot oeraev enh i nig rtaon te hisd hisformer pra yiegr and rnadnacse a asnhdo phkue empbelre, he escaped the beatings he had received as a Walee.— Egypt : Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque. The death is announced of Dr. T. H. Watts, an eminent Manchester physician. A Liverpool lad has been fined for placing combustibles or the tramway line at Edgehill. The Supreme Court of New Zealand has fined a man £350 for attempting to bribe a Government land officer. Damages to the extent of £ll,OOO were done on Tuesday by a fire at the Grove Mill, Ovenden, near Halifax. The Treasury has served notices to witnesses in the Brighten Railway murder case to attend at Maidstone On the let of November, Mr. Biight is expected at Llandudno next reolith, when it is hoped he will speak at a Liberal demonstration which it is contemplated to hold. • In an action against the Premier 61 Queensland for al- leged illegal sitting and voting in Parliament, a verdict has been returned for the defendant. A Liverpool gentleman, named Watkins, committed suicide by shooting himself in a lavatory closet in Lime- stseet Railway Station late on Monday night. Messrs. Moody and Sankey, the American evangelists, commenced their second religious campaign at Newcastle, on Sunday. The services were largely attended. ..The disappearance of Sarah Duckett from Church Stretton, in 'Shropshire, stiff remains a mystery. The men have ex- plored the old Copper Hole shaft without finding a trace-of her. A boy named Edward Downwood was shot on Monday night in Lambeth by another lad named Morgan with a toy pistol. The bullet penetrated the skull and he is in a precarious state. Lord Bute has declined to dispose of his docks at Cardiff, but has offered upon certain conditions, to make a new en- trance harbour and dock on 'the east foreshore with a lock 600 feet in length. The New North Staffordshire Coal and Iron Company who own large Collieries at Kidsgrove and Talke, have of their own accord given the miners in their employment an advance of 71 per cent. A widow lady named Ann Hutzhinson was walking on the North-Efistern line, near Binchester, on Saturday evening, when she was knocked down by a train from Ferry Hill, death being instantaneous. The ettensive premises of Messrs.. Jefferies and Son, wholesale stationers and printers Redcliffe-street, Bristol, were destroyed by fire on Sunday evening, with damage amounting to several thousands of pounds. Many of the potatoes which have been got up weigh over a pound each, and the yield of these fine samples is in many cases immense. An edifying example of the way in which jury lists are sometimes made out and jurors summoned was given at an inquest held at St Bartholomew's'Hospieal, London. When the list of jurors was called it was discovered that one of the persons summoned had been in Australia for 25 years, that another-hadbeen absent in France for six months, and that several more were also out of the country. _ Mr. Andrew, secretary-of the Mem Master Cotton Spin- ners' Association, has addressed a letter to the United States Consul in Manhcester on the subject of damp cotton. 'He states that damp, dust, and sand are evidently knowingly placed in the cotton, and suggests that the name of the planter and packer should be placed inside each bale. THE ELECTRIC LIGHT Ire PAnis.—From an official re- turn just published of the cost of lighting the streets of Paris, it appears that not only gas and the electric light are employed for the purpose, but mineral oil in certain quarters. The total cost, exclusive of the charge for the electric light, which, of course, is comparatively little used, is 4,265,000 franca, this being an increase of 148,000 francs as compared with last year. In reply to a 'request from the Stamford magistrates for the Home Secretary's advice as to the course to be pursued in reference to the street processions of the Salvation Army, a letter has been sent from the Home Office, pointing put to the local justices that while it is their duty, by every means in their power, to preserve the public peace, they must at the same time exercise their discretion, depending on all the local circumstances. Arthur Wheeler, sixteen years old, pupil teacher in the Eastbrook British Schools, Bradford, was on Tuesday coin- •mitted for trial at' the York Assizes by the Bradford magis- trates on a charge of the manslaughter of a girl named Whittaker, twelve years old, one of the scholars formerly in I his class. The allegation is that the prisoner struck the , girl on the head with a ruler, because she could not do a sum in arithmetic, and that death ensued. Itaa small agricultural village called Wrestlingworth, in the county of Bedford, an extraordinary wedding took place in the parish church on Tuesday. The bridegroom is in his seventy-seventb year, and the bride in her eigiaty-first. His Christian name is Thomas arid hers is Mary. This is the third Mary that Thomas has selected as his partner, and the third Thomas to whom Mary has been united. Both receive parish relief of 2s. and a loaf each per week. The importance of this order is I obvious. • The mining associations of Great Britain are about to convene a conference to consider the matter. The employers say that the new system will necessarily enhance the cost of production. " yah," said the smitten one, rubbing his skull dolefully, " d'yer call that Christianity ?" "Yes, Bah," replied the dusky Salvationist, as he calmly resumed `his march; "Yes, ear, fiat Zulu Christianity; how you like him ?" Bishop Fraser, delivering his inaugural address at the Manchester Diocesan Conference on Wednesday, expressed the opinion that not-much in the way of definite, tangible, practical result had be,en attained by the discussions at the Church Congress. At the same time, he admitted that several questions of great interest and moment bad been de- bated in an earnest and amiable manner. His lordship referred to the agitation in favour of freeing the Chnich from the secular courts, which he said was the revival of a contest as old as the establishment of the Church in connec- tion with the State in the days of Constantioe. To his mind the union that existed between Church and State in this country, while not free from embarrassments and difficulties, was good for the two institutions. In conclusion, the Bishop com the conduct of those legislators who, pt whiledesiring lain to see o sefe the Church liberated from State con- trol, obstructed every act of legislation which tended to make the Church stronger or more effective. THE TITHE AGITIeTION.—At a meeting of the Parishion- ers of Plumpton, held recently: it was tuihnimously agreed to carraeon the agitation against paying tithes until the Plumpton grievancs isredressed. The following resolutions were unanimously carried :—(1) "That a copy of the resolutions passed at the mass meeting, when the goods of the churchwarden and Mr. J. Simpson were distrained for tithes, be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone and the members for East Cumberland." (2) "That the offer of Mr. J. Kirkbride to refuse, in behalf of the other township of the parish, to pay tithes till the Ecclesiastical Commissioners are forced to comply with the Act of Parliament they are now in the piumpton case violating, be' thankfully accepted. A com- mittee was appointed, with the Vicar as secretary, to carry out the objects in view. These objects, as described in the resolutions refirred to, are :—"(a) To obtain a Parliament- ary ieoeiry into the Plumpton case; (b) the exclusion from the Ecclesiastical Commission of all persons pecuniarily in- terested in the allocationeof the funds under its control; (c) the abolition of extraordinary tithes, and a more equitable basis for determining the amount of ordinary tithes to be levied off land; (d) the dieendowenent of the Cathedral Establishment and the appropriation Of the funds to, relieve the berden ail Son land by applying them to the useful parts - lof the purposes' for which the endowments were ,origjdfdly intended, i.e., the aclif6tien ' and relief of the poor. o y •

div.head: ARREST OF MR. PARNELL.
div.p: ARREST OF MR. PARNELL.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Parnell, M.P., was arrested in Morrison's Hotel, Dublin. He had returned from Wiaklow the previous evening with the intention of going to Naas on--Thureday to preside at the Land League Conventiofi there, but at 9-20 Chief Superintendent Mallins, of the detqctiye force, proceeded to the hotel and entered Mr. Par- nell's bedroom. The hon. member had not risen at that hour, and was somewhat surprised at the entrance of Mr. Mailing. Tbe latter immediately announced his business, and told Mr, Parnell that resistance would only lead to tin- pleasantness, which he was sure the hon. member would not wish to create. Mr. Parnell expressed his willingness to quietly accompany Mr. Mallins wherever he pleased. Mr. Parnell then dressed, and when ready was brought round by the back of the hotel, placed on an outside car with the con- stables, and driven- direct to Kilmainham Gaol. The arrest was so quietly effected that the fact did not become gener- ally known even in the hotel until Mr. Parnell had left. The news afterwards spread through the city of Dublin and caused intense excitement. - The arrest of Mr. Parnell would surprise few people after the Primo Minister's speech last Friday, for Mr. Gladalone'a scathing condemnation of the "gospel of sheer plunder," hie statement that Mr. Parnell desired to arrest the operation of the Land Act because it would bring peace to the coun- try, and hia declaration that the Government were deter- mined that no force, no fear of force, and no fear of ruin through force, should, so far as the Government could decide the question, prevent the Irish people from having the full and free benefit of the Act indicated that a decisive blow was about to be struck at the reckless agitation of the Land League. Mr. Parnell has spoken in pablic since Mr. Gladstone's ultimatum, awl his language at Wex- ford has attracted some attention. He said he rejoiced that the country was preprred to return a fitting answer, if it should become necessary, to intimidation such as was used by an unscrupulous Government in '9B, but which would fail now as it did then. Many of them bad studied the words of a great man, a great orator, who up to recently de- sired to impress th%world with a good opinion of his philanthropy and his hatred of oppression, but who stood to- day the greatest coercionist, the greatest and most unrivalled slanderer of the Irish nation that ever lived. He referred to William Ewart Gladstone and his unscrupulous and dis- honest speech of Friday. Not content with maligning the people, he maligned their bishops, he maligned John Dillon, and he attempted to misrepresent the • Young Ireland' party of '4B. No misrepresentation was too low to stoop to. It was a good sign that this masquerading knight-errant, this pretended champion of the liberties of every nation except the Irish, was obliged to throw off the mask to-day, and to stand revealed as prepared to carry fire and sword into the home- steads of the Irish people unless they humbled and abased themselves before the law and the landlords of the country." These words ere uttered last Sunday. Mr. Parnell intended to address a meeting at Naas in Kildare on Thursday, and on Wednesday night he arrived in Dublin, and put up at Morrison's Hotel in Dawson-street. His movements were well known to the authorities, and the hotel was under sur- veillance thronghout Wednesday night. On Thursday morning, before he had left his room, he was visited by several officers of police, and informed that they held war- rants for his arrest, charging him with inciting persons to intimidate others from paying their rents and with inciting to intimidate persons from applying to the newly-created Land Court to have their rents fixed. Mr.,Parnell left the hotel in custody of the officers, and was driven to Kilmain- ham Gaol. The warrants were signed by Mr. Forster, who arrived in Dublin on Thursday, some time before the arrest was made.

LAND LEAGUERS FLEEING TO PARIS. The secretary of the Land League was interviewed shortly after the arrest. He expressed much astonishment, but exclaimed excitedly. "Let them come on; we are ready for them." Mr. Patrick Egan, Land League treasurer; Father Sheehy; and Mr. Dillon, Land League solicitor; left this morning for Paris. Mr. Parnell's position will be filled by Mr. Dillon. • _

div.head: FEELING IN LONDON.
div.p: THE FEELING IN LONDON.

The highest satisfaction is felt in official circles in London at the arrest of Mr. Parnell, and several heads of departments have expressed their gratification at this decided step on the part of the Government. An opinion is pretty generally expressed that a continued energetic course of action will have a material effect in bringing about a better state of things in Ireland. More arrests are looked for by London officials. •

div.head: PRESENTATION Of AN ADDRESS TO
div.p: PRESENTATION Of AN ADDRESS TO
fHt. GLADSTONE.

• • -- - - - - - Mr. Gladstone:was.on Thursday presentedwith an address by the London.COrporation in recognition of his,long and brilliant services in the cause of his country. The ceremony took place at the Guildhall, in the presence of a great assembly, who gave Mr. Gladstone a magnificent reception. In his reply to the address, the hon. gentleman spoke of the half -century during which he had been actively engaged in public life as a period ef years unequalled in history for their accomplishment of reforms and changes tending towards the increase of the glory and greatness of the nation. Of late years, however, the legislative and general business of the country had got lament- ably in arrear, one cause of that condition. being the conduct of people who had not been as loyal as they ought to the assembly to which they belonged. If the House of Commons was to con- tinue in that place in public confidence and esteem which it had hitherto held, it must address itself in a hold and manly spirit to consider how, either by most stringent and effective rules, by a judicious devolution of duties, or both those means, it could place itself once more in a condition of renewed capacity to pursue regularly and efficaciously the performance of its great duties to the State. Mr.,Gladstone said that there were several questions of interest at the present time, and naturally referred to the Irish question as that which most forcibly thrust itself upon their notice. He declared, in the name of the Cabinet, that they recognised they were charged in Ireland with arduous and solemn duties, which, to the best of their ability, they were determined to perform. He had received only a few moments before the news of "the first step towards the vindication of law and order and the rights of property, by the arrest of a man who, from motives with which he (Mr. Gladellbne) had nothing to do, had made himself beyond all others promient in the attempt to destroy the authority of the law." The Premier did not allude to Mr. Parnell by name, but the audience, intuitively divining the truth, testified, their ap- proval of the step taken by the Government by enthusiastic cheers. Mr. Gladstone add that the only serious apprehen- sion of the Government was that more and more of the Irish people should be forced by intimidation to abandon their just and constitutional rights And play into the hands of self-constituted dictators. The Government fully under- stood their functions, and claimed a perfect right that they should be assisted in the discharge of them by every mem- ber of every Political party, and, he added, the "leaders of every political party." Mr. Gladstone then spoke briefly on questtoo, repeating the determination of the tGh9rail :verrnmevnatatio adhere firmly to the main principles of the Convention. The Boer Triumvirate bad solemnly pledged themselves to have the Convention ratified by the Volksraad within three months, and it was therefore with some surprise that Her Majesty's Government heard of recent events in the Boer Pirliarhent, but they were resolved to abide by the terms of th2ir agreement by the burghers of the Transvaal. In conclusion, he spoke of the happy termination of the difficalty in Eastern tirope, and,congrfnlated the citizens of London on the aid they had given to 'a worthy nation in its efforts towards obtaining its liberty.

TRADE NOTES. The, new North Sta.ffardshire Coal andiron Company- , who oivn large collieries at KidagroVe anti Talke haye spontaneously agreed to give the :miners in their employ an immediate advance of 71t per cent. The employers have also promised the men another 21 per cent. as ,sosu as other colliery proprietors agree to advance wages. - The :Staffordshire chain strike ended on Monday. At a meeting of the workmen it was announced that the masters had consented to pay wages in future at 20 per cent. advance. The North Staffordshire miners have decided to give notice for an advance of 10 per cent. in wages, and have refused to consider a proposal for a sliding scale of wages.

HIGHER BROUGHTON (IST Thai..)—This match was played at Broughton, on Saturday last. Warrington journeyed with only ten men, but five substitutes were obtained on the field. Scrim- mages were very numerous and hotly contested: and when half time was called, Warripgton had scored two touchdowns, to two tonchballs and one dead ball. RUNCORN 2ND V. Dmiraa 2ND.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturdallast. Runcorn arrived on the field at 3-10, but, owing to the Dingle men not turning up, a start was not effected until 3-35, when Mason, the Runcorn captain (who had won the toss), kicked off. It is a, matter of impossibility to single out the best players, as both Runcorn ) and the Dingle met played remarkably well. The following were the teams :—Runcorn: Stubbs, full back 'i Sherlock and W. Pownall, three-quarter backs; Mason and W. Walkey, half backs; Dunbavand, Dennison, S. Walkey, Kirkham, Wainwright, Peers, Roberts, Ratcliffe, Riley, and Gittens, forwards. WARRINGTON v. Huang (IST TEAMS.)—This match was played at Vrarrington, on Saturday. Huhu° kicked off, and the ball being well returned, the play was confined to neutral I ground. A grand dribble by the home forward compelled the visitors to save," Warrington shortly afterwards scoring I a touch-in-goal. Hui= now tried their utmost to score, but the home forwards were not to be denied, and, by a good dribble passed to Warren, enabled that player to run in ; but the try was disputed. No goal resulted from the place I kick. Shortly afterwards Ilulme scored a touchdown. Scrimmages were now very frequent. On half time being called, ends changed. Turner kicked off, and the home forwards charged it down and prevented the return. A scrimmage was then formed at the Hulme 25 flag, and on the ball becoming loose Warren got hold, and rounding his opponents in fine style, grounded it over the goal-line, for which he was applauded. Turner was disputed to make the attempt at goal, which failed. Turner again put 'the leather in motion, which shorily afterwards went in touch. On the throw-out, Warren again got hold, and making good head- way was only collared on the goal-line. Some excellent tackling was then displayed by Rigby and Adamson. The visitors were than compelled to act mostly on the defensive until the end of the game. Dobson, Pemberton, and Knowles striving very hard to get in, Warrington scored a dead ball, touch-in-goal, and a touchdown in rapid succession. Just before time was called Buxton by a splendid dropkick with the left foot, scored an unmistakeable goal, for which be was deservedly cheered. For the losers Crump was the pick off the backs, and Nightingale played a very good game. For Warrington, Buxton and Warren never played to better advantage, and Knowles, Pemberton, and Dobson also played exceedingly well. In fact, each individually played a very good game. Score :—Warrington: One goal (kicked from field), one try, one disputed try, one touchdown, two touches-in-goal, one dead ball; to Hulme, two touchdowns.
ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. HEALTH commirrEE.
The monthly meeting of the Health Committee was held on Wednesday, Councillor Twyford presiding. BATHS. .
Mr. HART said they had had 330 bathers during the month, and the receipts had been £4 15s.
T-HE MANDBE DEPOT.

_ Mr. HART, in accordance with a resolution of the Council, presented his estimate of the total cost of the new Sutton Manure Depot. He said the total cost of the works would be £3,800 ; of which £1,517 10s. would be for the land °Veined ,from the railway company for site of proposed works. Remainder of the works would cost £1,730; for four railway wagons for removing manure, £280; add for contingencies, £272 10s.; making a total of £3,800. ":Ie re- marked that £353 would represent the net annual outlay when in full wprking order.—The Council having asked what would be the probable saving ly, the new yard, the Suavayou said that was impossible to say as theocalculation would have to be based upon the sale of manure which was very fluctuating. lie could not arrive at a calculation. If they told him how much manure they could sell, say two, three, or four thousand tons he would ,be able to form an estimate; but as they could not tell bow much would be Sold, he could not arrive at a figure to represent the saving, —The Cnajztatax thought it was their duty to take some action in the matter, ard it. wae. decided that the estimate and the report of the surveyor be printed and forwarded to each member of the Council.

div.head: MORTUARY.
div.p: THE MORTUARY.

Mr. Witcocit called the attention of the Council to the mortuary in Foundry-street, which be said was so little used.—Dr. Malcolm said the mortuary should be used in cases of overcrowding. When a person died of some infec- tious disease, instead of being left In the same room used by living people, the body should be removed to the mor- tuary. The authorities could enforce this.—lt was decided to call the attention of the police authorities to die matter, and to suggeSt that it be used by them for the purpose of receiving dead bodies instead of carrying them to the nearest pnblic-house.
THE STREETS ON A SUNDAY MORNING.
Mr. BELSHER called attention to the vast amount of rub- bish in the streets on a Sunday morning.—The Surveyor was instructed to cause the streets to be swept every Bundy morning.

STATE OE THE BROOK. Dr. McMtn= reported that samples of the Ecclestort branch of the brook had been taken by Inspector Williams from the usual places, namely, Sprays Bridge, Bridgewater. street, by the Timber-yard, Daglish's works, and by the Bottle Works. They were all free from acid, so also were samples from Sutton Lodge water course. Inspector Houghton had sampled the Hardshaw Brook, frcm Board- man's Bridge to Langtree-street. They contained no acid. The Inspector could obtain no sample from the drain of the St. Helen's-Chemical Werke because it was blocked up by incrustations or.sulphate of lime. The steps taken by the St. Helen's Chemical Works had 'evidently caused that blockade. Acid of the strength of over 100 grains to the gallon was found in the Parr-street sewer, by Fraser-street. Rainford Brook was full ol acid, and the canal by Merton Bank Bridge neatly en._

div.head: -HEALTH OF TEE TOWN
div.p: -HEALTH OF TEE TOWN

Dr. Maroon paid the mortality for the month had been moderate; but five deaths had been caused by fever, and eleven by diarrhcer.. .These epidemics were always present at this season of the year. The houses had been disinfected. He called "attention to the state of the atmosphere. We should have the November fogs upon us shortly, and it was very desirable that theblack smoke of the town be diminished ger much as possible. • Be had watched the chimneys of-some respectable works dering the month, and often found dense black emoke poured out for twenty minutes together. This was caused by bad stoking. If-manufacturers would not take the trouble of insisting upon their firemen doing their" work well, it would be for the dominittee to apply the Smoke Act to the whole district. Black.emoke was not only a nuisance itself, but by forming an alliance with the chemical waste in the town, produced such a state of thing, that only required a foggy 'condition* of the atmosphere to make St. Helens positively unendurable and downright un- healthy. lie hoped the committee would write to every manufacturer and insist . upon steps being taken to abate that nuisance. The more perfect ' wax would be to apply the Act at once.—lt was dedided that the Borough Enginear (Mr. Hart), report on the matter at the next meeting.,
