div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY @CTOBER.IS, 1881. ST. HELENS HELENS LITERARY AND 1 PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY @CTOBER.IS, 1881. ST. HELENS HELENS LITERARY AND 1 PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION.

PRESIDENTIAL ADDRESS. , The winter session of this association was commenced on Tuesday, whettthe members with friends assembled in the ,Council;Chamber to hear adaddreas from the president. The Council Chamber was,prettily deeorated with' plants from the conservatory of the president. Tea and coffee was prtivided in the ante-room by Mrs. Taylor, of the Fleece Hotel. There were present Mr. Richard Pilkington (paves dent of the society), Drs. McNicoll, Jamison, Hay, Read; Mr.- Sinclair, Miss Sinclair, Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Gamble, Mr. W. and Mrs. Gamble, Mr. Alderman Cook, Mr. Councillor Foster and Mrs. Foster, Mr. Councillor and Mrs. Swift, Rev. J. Moore, Rev. R. J. Ward, Mr. and Mrs. Riley, Miss Bans. ford, Mr. Thomas and the Misses Thomas, the Misses Gambles, Rev. Mr. Jagg, Rev. J. P. and Mrs. Ritchie, Mr. H. G. Bramwell, Miss Bramwell, Major Wilcocks, Mr. Coun- cillor Belsher and Mrs. Belsher, Mr. W. H. Roughsedge and the Misses Roughsedges Mr. H. J. Craik, Mr. S. Robinson and party (Crank), Mr. Sinclair, 'jun., Mr. Massey, Mi. Hart, Mr. Gaskin Dr. Gossman, Mr. Brooker, Mr. Coun- cillor T. Cook, douncillor Brook and Miss Brook, Captain McTear, Mr. R. Coop, Mr. W. J. Marrow, Mr. Dromgoole, Mr. and Mrs. C. J. Bishop, Mr. Sherlock. The PRESIDENT said : lam exceedingly sorry that we have not the presence of our Mayor.. Unfortunately he is net able to attend, his family being at Southport, and he is obliged to go. I found it exceedingly difficult to get the vice-presidents around me, and I have only been successful in getting two, Dr. McNicoll and Mr. Sinclair. There are six vice-presidents, but I suppose they are somewhat shy. You all know that this is the first meeting of the St. Helens Literary and Scientific Association for this winter, and it is customary on these occasions for your president to make a few remarks. This is the opening of the third session. On the first meeting of the first session we had a most suc- cessful meeting, but the second one, I am sorry to say, was a lamentable failure. We then met in a very cold room ; there were very few of us ; there were tiles and slates and Roman remains, and we all felt very much depressed and very low, and that the Literary and Scientfic Association of St. Helens was going to the doge, or that it was on its last legs. I think to-day we open under the most wonderful circumstances, and this large and intelligent assembly, con- stituting as It does' all that is good and excellent in- St. Helens, is of itself a guarantee that this session at any rate will be much more successful than those before. Well, I do not think the two sessions that have already passed have been failures. I think they have been very fair. For a society of this kind we have had a very fair amount of sue- CESS in the two sessions past. During the last session we had nine papers. Mr. Higgins, of Rainhill, whose papers are always never to be beaten, gave .the first on natural history in a sort of excursion; Dr. McNicoll not being so severely ecientific took us to Shakespeare's birthplace, at Stratford-on-Avon ; Mr. Sherlock gave us a paper on "Beer, some vane- ties and their effects," which had this effect that it almost made us turn teetotalers; Dr. Hay gave one on the curiosities of language; Mr. Mermargen' on cremation, which produced an animated discussion; Mr. Sherlock presented the figure 3 in a most ingenious and amusing paper; Mr. W. Gamble took us to Holland for a change. So very few of us visit that flat country, and as Mr. Gamble finds out faults in his friends, he thought he would take us to that country which nobody goes to. Mr. Higgins gave us a:paper on vitality. You will notice that all the papers we have now had have been more of a literary than a scientific character. Somehow or other up to the present time science has been to a certain extent rather a closed book. Science has been looked upon with a certain amount of suspicion, and in our educational establishments and throughout society, until very recent years, science instead of occupying the first place, occupied a very second rate place; and in some of the higher educa- tional establishments of Great Britain, it really occupied no place at all. It seems strange that science that has the key to all the wonderful secrets of nature should be so little studied. lam quite sure you will know as well as I know that 99 people out of 100 used to take the subjects that are dealt with by science in a somewhat matter-of-fact-taken- for-granted sort of way, and used to look upon all creation as divided into birds, beasts, fishes, seine tame, some domesticated, others wild, with man as lord over them all ; that this state of things had always been and always would be to the end of time. On society wakening up we found nature instead of being as we supposed a humdrum sort of the most winning book we could turn to. The secrets of nature are open to us every day, and everything in nature has not been, as we have supposed always the same, but has gradually grown and developed, and now exists in its present wonderful state in consequence of that wonderful growth. And through that growth it has become fitted to occupy the exact position it now does, and only occupies that position so long as it discharges its mission. We find on examination of nature, and all the different forms and shapes that objects have in. nature, that man is given a wonderful power over nature; a far greater power than he has had before, such as the question of meatuses now taken for the prevention and suppression Of diteise. In former times it was considered that disease came somehow, and that it had to have its run, and must do its work, and we must dO noth- log but sit still and wait. Science.has shown Us that disease consists of a number of small living germs, and it is spread about by those living germs ; and the fact that these living germs can be destroyed by disinfectants has checked to a very great extent the ravages of disease. Such a thing as the plague of London in the 17th century is almost impos- sible at the present day with our sanitary arrangements, and there is no doubt that if the present progress in medical science goes on disease will be somewhat checked and stopped ; and our power not only in this particular, but in numbers of others, will become so great over nature that we shall be able to make life amongst us better and nobler, and be able to increase the pleasures of life, and mitigate the tremendous extent of suffering which come upon men from time to time. Just consider for a moment what an effect scientific knowledge would lead to In agriculture. Just think if the agricultural class in Eng- land, farmers and land owners, were thoroughly conversant with animal and vegetable fife what a vast change would come over the spirit of the dream. The present darkness would be dispelled, and instead of English agriculture beinga by-word amongst the nations, it would take the same position as English commerce does. This it a passing illustration of what science can do, and,,l am glad to say, is doing. Of course, there are a hundred branches of science, and all useful. Some are not only eminently useful, but absorb- ingly interesting to the student. , Think of the wonders that students of geology discover in the variety of rocks, and what ' may be seen under the earth's surface, and of the pleasures it gives to the students who study it. You find in the first formation of the rocks very low types of animal and vegetable life. This goes on for ages, and then we come to the richer formations; take for instance a Belot fossils from the coal measures. There you will find luxuriant vegetable life. Then you find in the chalk higher forms of life, until at last you reach the higher formations. Then you find the forms .of animal life till you coma almost to man. Another wonderful thing is the changes in the climate. At one time ye find all over the valleys and plains of the United Kingdom great tropical forests. There is a great probability that here, where we are standing now, on Hardshaw Slopes and Cowley Hill, that in by-gone days there were tigers wandering through the jungles, hippopa- tami and alligators sporting themselves in the waters, per- haps in Sankey brook. (Laughter.) Take the history of of man himself; how you see him through almost the faded history of distant ages living in caves, sad very little removed from the level 'of the lower animals, and working himself up by the aid of implements and weapons of stone. This is called the Stdan Ago. Then as-time goes on comes the Bronze Age; and by the -discovery of the use of, iron we come to the Iron Age. Then he rapidly improved,' for we find on the monuments and tombs of the ancients their laws, customs, and religions, such as we read of in history, on the valley of the Nile, the Euphrates, and shores of the Mediter- ranean, on which our civilisation is based. The cream of the sciences is perhaps , astronomy. It is surely of anthers that which appeals most vividly to the sen,ses. There is something in the wonderful sight, and distances and size, of the heavenly bodies that has a strange fascination over the imagination. As an instance of this I ask you for a moment to consider our sun, to 'remember the fact that-the sun is a ball of fire of the very greatest heat, one million and a half times larger than the size of. this earth. The heat is so great that metals existing there existed in vapour. Now at this very moment we are pro- ceeding along our orbit at a rate round the sun of 1,700,000 miles in 24 hours, losing at the rate of 1,300 miles a minute. The sun is simply a frxedstar,and the reason why it appears so large amidst the thousands and thousands of twinkling stars we see on a splendid night, is because it is the nearest flied star. There are suns a hundred times larger than our sun. Just take these facts and look upon a sunset, or when the stars are bright lnok upon, the stars, and grasp this fact, that this extraordinary creation has gone on day and night for ages, keeping far more regular time than the most wonderful time piece that we possess, and will continue to do so for thousands and thousands of years to come. And then you Will have some idea of the wonderous secrets that science tan disclose to us. I will not occupy your time any longet think I have taxed your patience, but I think we must all agree that any time we can snatch away rightly and justly from business, and fairly and rightly take away from our home duties and given to science will be amply re- paid to us, and will not only make us better men in serving our day and generation, but will make us pleasanter tom- panions in the home we may dwell in, and pleasanter com- panions to our friends when we pay them our visit. I hope and trust our society, young as it is, may increase' year by year in the success of its sessions, and that it will have the warm and cordial support of the people of St. Helens. (Ap- plause.) Dr. JAMISON proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, I and pointed out that the president had deplored a wanted i interest in science. St. Helens as it is, was largely due to, , science, and he did not think that science gave us very' pleasant places to live in. As for seeing the sun science made it very difficult for them to see it sometimes. 'When a man was tired he really thought literature gave him more contolation than science: Mr. W. GAMBLE seconded the motion which was sup:. ported. by sDr. MeNicoll and carried with acclamations:-.Ms. Pilkington, having responded, Mr. Massey proposed, and Mr. H. V. Riley. seconded, a vote of thanks to those who read papers on the last sessions.—Mr. Sherlock responded, and also Rev J. P. Ritchie—Mr. J. C. Gamble proposed a vote ,of thanks to the ladies for their presence, which Was given. —Dr. Hay responded.—Mr. Sinclair moved, and Mr. Drom- goole seconded a vote of thanks to the Mayer and Council for lending them the use of the room.

SFORMY MEETING: EXTRAORDINARY .SCENE. An adjourned meeting of the Prescot Local Board was held on Friday evening, Mr. C. Spencely presiding, There were also present Messrs. J. Wycherley, T. Prescott, A. T. Galloway, .T.-Mawdaley, T. S. Preston, E. Beesley, and H. Fogg; with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), Dr. Hall (medical Officer) and Mr. William Goldsworth (surveyor). The meeting was called for the purpose of filling up the vacancron'the board, caused by the non-attendance of Mr. Richard Twist for six months, and also for the provision of a hospital, nurse, dm blSQrsaincArtow OF A MEMBISR A MEMBER IN A In the course of a very amusing and rather confused con- versation, Mr. MAWDSLEY asked if that was a legal meeting. —The CHAIRMAN said it was an adjourned meeting, It.was a continuation of the monthly meeting on Wednesday.—The Cratax said the first business was the appointment of a new Member to serve but the term of office of Mr. Richard Twist, who had vacated. his seat through non-attendance: Mr. Twist had pokattended themeetings since March last.—The Catantrite,quoted the Act of Parliament, which showed that any member who absented himself from the meetings of a local board for more than six months consecutively, unless in case of illness, became disqualified.—Mr. Fobet asked when Mr. Twist was elected.—Mr. Ger..Loway : I don't thing tliat has anything to do with it.—Mr. FOGG : I think it has everything to do with it, if you are going to do the thing legally.—Mr. MAWDSLEY: I don't think that the timkwhen Mr. Twist was appointed has anything whatever to do with the time he attended this Board.—Mr. FOGG : Has Mr. Twist vacated, and is his seat vacant because he has absented himself from attending the meetings for six months since the election ? —The CHAIRMAN: Oh, no. Because he has not attended for six months consecutively.—ln answer to Mr. Fogg, the CHAnzstax said Mr. Twist had not attended seven meetings consecutively. —Mr. Form said that meeting had been called for the very purpose of placing some one on the Board whom he did not know.—Mr. WYCHERLEY 06, no. I should like Mr. Cross to repeat the information he gave us on the Board night. I was given to understand the vacancy should be filled up within so many days, and that meeting was fixed to make the appointment.—Mr. Focia: Not at all.—The CLERK: It must be filled up within six weeks from the time the vacancy occurs or such further period as the Local Government Board may by order allow.—The Cirrantair : And that period would elapse before the next meeting P—The CLERK: Yes. If Mr. Twist had attended the September meeting he would have been all right.—Mr. FOGG said the appointment was in the hands of the ratepayers. If it was made by the Board, it was robbing the ratepayers of their right.—Mr. WYCHERLEY: It is not robbing the ratepayers.—The CHAIR- MAN said there was a vacancy arising out of the disqualifica- tion of some one having been away from that Board for more than six months. The question was whether that time had arrived at the last meeting or not.—Mr.FOGG (interrupt- lug): Wel), Mr. Chairman, I will tell you—The CHAIR- MAN (confirming): And whether this is the meeting at which to fill up the vacancy or at another meeting. Mr. GALLOWAY: He was away for six monthly meetings.— The CHAIRMAN: Not six monthly meetings, but more.—Mr. FOGG : Yes, far more.—Mr. MAWDSLEY: It is no use talk- ing. It's as plain as plain can be.—Mr. WYCHERLEY said he should like to show Mr. Fogg that there was no intention whatever to do things in an under-hand manner. The matter was brought up at the last Board meeting, but con- sidering that there were two or three members absent, he suggested that every member of the Board should have information direct by circular that such business was com- ing before the Board, or he believed a member would have been elected in Mr. Twist's stead at the meeting.—Mr. FOGG said no notice of such appointment appeared on his circular for the regular monthly meeting held on Wednesday. He saw it in the paper the following morning, and he had now got a circular which stated that the first business was to appoint a member in the place of Mr. Twist, who bad been absent for six months. Now, he was not at all satisfied that Mr. Twist had been absent six months, bat putting that aside, why was a special meeting called for the purpose of making the appointment ? Mr. Twist had only twelve months to • serve.—The CLERK: He has more than that. He has eighteen months.—Mr. GALLOWAY: The meeting was not adjourned to elect a member in the place of Mr. Twist —The CHAtimax: Are you going to propose that Mr. Twist's VIICARCy be filled up P—Mr. FOGG : Certainly not. I ask you, and through you I expect to get the information from the Clerk, when the vacancy became vacant—Mr. GALLOWAY (laughing): When the vacancy became vacant !—The C 112,11130,1.1.: Mr. Twist's last ap- pearance at this Board was on the 2nd March.—Mr. FoGG : The 2nd of March; that is, in this year.—The CHAIRMAN: Yes; six or seven months ago.—Mr. WYCIIERLEY: I move that Mr. Twist's seat at this Board be declared vacant. —Mr. PRESCOTT: I second it.—On being put to the meeting all the members voted in favour of the proposition with the ex- ception of Mr. Fogg.—Mr. WYCHERLEY said he did not know who might be proposed to fill the vacancy. He asked whether something was not said at the last meeting or at a committee meeting about the Chairman seeing some person to fill that vacancy.—The CHAIRDIA.I.I: Not at the last meet- ing. Mr. Spencely went on to say that a short time ago a question arose whether a vacancy bad occurred oa the Board either through removal from the town or the person having ceased to be a ratepayer. He was ultimately asked to see Mr. Dennett and he did see him. That gentleman was not very willing to servo at first, but after much pressure he consented. Mr. Fond thought that inasmuch as a vacancy had been declared, and they were close upon the coming election, the appointment ought to left to the ratepayers. The gentle- man whose name had been mentioned had been before the ratepayers repeatedly, and he bad always been rejected. (Laughter.) lie deprecated Mr. Dennett being got on to the Board in that surreptitious manner, because he could not get on by the unanimous wish of the ratepayers. ,It was not fair.—Mr. WYCHERI.EY here attempted to say some- thing, when Mr. FOGG said: Don't interrupt me, Mr. Wycherley, I am in the hands of the Chairman.. I am going to make a proposition that this vacancy be not filled up till the next election.—Mr. PRESTON seconded,—Mi. WYCHERLEY remarked that he , was not particular about it himself. He did not know that it was absolutely necessary it should be filled up. Personally, he had no objection to it.—The CHAIUMAN observed that there was no intention of putting or dragging anybody in. One reason why, Mr. Dennett was selected was because he had been nominated and stood a contest, andtot a certain number of votes.:—Mr. Form: Yes; four or tive.—Mr. MAWDSLEY: It does not follow that because Mr. Dennett was nominated and had stood a contest and failed that he might not be a good man. —The Custamart: No, just the other way. It slowed he WU a man that a large number of ratepayers wished to see in.—The CLERK said If the appointment was not made at that meeting a special order would have to be got from the Local Government Board.—Mr. WYCI/ERLEY moved as an amendment Oat they proceed to the election of a now member.—Mr. MAWDSLEY seconded.—On being put to the meeting five voted in favour of the amendment, and two in favour of the proposition:—The amendment wass therefore declared to be carried.—Mr. WYCHERLEY then moved that Mr. T. Dennett ba elected a member of that Board.—Mt. MAWDSLEY seconded.—Mr. Fonts said it was only due to the ratepayers of Prescot that they ought to' have a responsible representative man, and he proposed as an amandment that in lieu of Mr. Dennett, who had fought some five or six bottles to get on the Bard, that Mr. James Appleton be elected. If Mr. Dennett would take his (Mr. Fogg's) sdviae, he was a great deal better off than on: (Laughter.) . He thought they ought to consult the interests of the ratepayers seeing what money they were spending. He thought Mr. Appleton who was only five votes below the Chairman at the last election had the greatest call upon that Board, and certainly he had the feeling of the rate- payers on his side.—Mr. rRESCOTT seconded the amend- ment.—Mr. MA.WDSLEY did not think Mr. Appleton had any wish to sit at the Board.—Mr. WYCHEHLEy : Nor I don't think Mr. Dennett has either. -- On the motion and amendment being put to the meeting, the former was carried, and Mr. Dennett was declared duly elected. Some desultory conversation took place in the course of which Mr. Mawdsley said that was the funniest meeting he had been at in is life.—Mr. FoGIGs remarked that it he was Mr. Dennett he would not sit.—Mr. Galloway said he would not say anything like that.—Mr. Fonts: I do say so,

-s—Mr.-Gormswontst (the surveyor) said it was a most diffi- cult thing to get a place for an hospital.—Mr. FOGG : Well, I would not send a child of mine to Chorley-house. The people have left it because it is tumbling down through the damp.—The SURVEYOR: It is not what you would really like, but where can you get another place ?—Mr. Wvcsznn- LEY : If the house had been in really good order it 'would not have been at our disposal.--111r. FoaG:, And unfortu- nately it is dot located in your local board district—Mr. WYCIIERLEY: Partly,—The Caarsattsx:" That does not matter a straw.—Mr. GALLOWAY: I think we ought to be grateful to Mr. Tyrer for letting us have the house.--Mr. FoGG: What nobody else will take.—The CHAIRMAN: It is an old house, but it does not fellow that it will not do for a purpose of this sort.--Mr. WYCHERLEY : I have known that place for fifty years and a good many families have lived its it. There has only been one death in the house fon a good many years. The Misses Chorley lived there many years. —Mr. Foote: They had no children. (Laughter.)—Mr. WYCHERLEY: Then there was Mr. Tyrer, who was over 60 years of age.—Mr. FOGG (interrupting): He had no chil- dren either. You don't know what it is to /lave children— (loud laughter)—ot else you would be more careful. (Re- newed laughter.):—Mr. MAWDSLEY at this point made some -renfark Which was inaudible at the reporters' table.—Mr. GOLDSWORTH (sharply): Is there any payment to be mad 'with 'regard to Chorley-house ? There is an insinuation at This end of the table that something is being taken out of the ratepayers' pockets, and I think Mr. blawdsley should be called upon to say distinctly-what he alludes to.—Mr. Mewiistzt : I don't attribute anything to you, sir:—Mr., Gormswonta: Well, make it plain then.—Mr.-MNWDSLEY: I *ill apologise now if you think so.—The CHAIRMAN (re. 'provingly): I am sorry, gentlemen, talk across the table! sotto weep and that sort of way. It must be 'offensive to ,1 somebody. All that nonsensical talk is ridiculous, and' people who read the reports in the papers will think we are all a pack of idiots in Prescot.—Mr. MAWDSLEY (interrupt- ing): There are a good many I know. I know what I am speaking about.—The CHAIRMAN: If you would only wait until there is a proposition before the meeting and then speak to it you would be in order. If anybody wants to make charges they should speak them out.—Mr. MAWDS- LEY: You should not surmise things not intended.—Mr. • GALLOWAY: If Mr. Mawdsley says money is being taken out of the ratepayers' pockets and put into somebody else's he should name who it is.—The CHAIRMAN: Of course; any honourable man would do so.—Mr. MAWDSLEY: I don't think it would be wise; but I am prepared, and will do so, when I think fit. (Excitedly.) I have not come here to be set down and to be ridden roughshod over.by any man, and certainly not by any member of this Board. I have come here to represent the ratepayers, and I shall.—The Caarn- MAN remarked that ho supposed the hospital was for the purpose of affording proper treatment and accommodation- for people who would not otherwise have them, and who, if they remained in their own places, would neces: sarily become a cause of infection to those around them.—Mr. GALLOWAY supposed the object was to compel People who were suffering from the disease to go into the hospital and not wait till they went in.—The CHAIRMAN said the Compulsion rested on certain points.— The MEDICAL OFFICER remarked that if he could go before the magistrate and certify that a case was not properly.iso- lated and attended to, the magistrate could make an order for the removal of the patient to the hospital.—ln answer to a question the Medical Officer stated that there was not a single case in the town which could be properly isolated.—: Mr. FOGG asked how many cases the medical officer con- sidered they were without the means of perfect isolation. He would like to know whether a cottager, paying ss. 6d. per week in rent, had not accommodation to isolate his children, —that was, where the fever was prevalent. It was a very serious matter for the ratepayers of Prescot.—The CHAIR- MAN inquired if the medical officer would tell them whether or net there were any cases in the town where there were no means in the cottages infected of properly isolating them. —The MEDICAL OFFICER said he had not known a single case which had been properly isolated.—Mr. Wycintstrzr observed that the infection might arise, and did arise, in a great measure, not from there being no means to isolate Ahem, but from no attempt being made to isolate them.—The CHAIRMAN said the parents sent their children to school just When they were recovering from the disease,—W hen the eliiñ was coming off and they were in a dangerous state.-- The MEDICAL OrridErt said he had a report as to the duties of the nurse.—Tbri' CHAIRMAN remarked that that was a matter for the doctor's superintendence. The surveyor had already spoken of the house, but they would like the benefit of the doctor's opinion_ upon it, as in the opinion of some it was not a fit place for the hospital. It was an old and damp place.—The MEDICAL OFFICER: It is not fit for a perma- nent one.—The Crtainusx We are only having a tem- porary one. The question is this, .whether you have been able to find a place suitable and proper for the purpose.—The MEDICAL OFFICER *: The only place that would answer I have not been able to examine except on the outside, there- fore lam hardly in a position 'to say whether it would do or not. I know from the view I had of it that it would answer for a temporary hospital. The Medical officer here produced and quoted a trade circular respecting thi supply and erection of tents as temporary labspitals, which could be heated by means of hot water pipes, but in answer to the chairman • he admitted that he had not experienced any of them in use. —The Cwaritaraw : They would never do this weather.— Mr. Gatmoviey : If there is any prejudice against Chorley- house, there would be much more against a tent.—The SURVEYOR: My experience is that you could not fix upon a single place but • what somebody would object to. It is a I very serious matter.—The MEDICAL OFFICER: I think Chorley-house would make a very good temporary hospital. —Mr. M.awnstEr : And yet you tell us you bave never been inside.—The SURVEYOR said both he and the medical officer had been inside the house many a time, although they could not get in When they went to look at it.—Mr. WYCHERLEY said he did not want to sit there till twelve o'clock. He did not deny that the house was damp, but there were rooms in the house that had ,been occupied by the family which he scarcely thought would be in such a state as not to be fit 1 for the purpose. He therefore moved that Chorley-hoase ; be secured as a temporary hospital until the fever was stamped out of the town. This was the second time this year, and if it went on spreading abroad among the people right and left, it would become such a town that people would be afraid of entering into or living in it. They were I told that the provision of a hospital was the best means of destroying the disease. If they were to talk till twelve o'clock he did not think they would all be of one mind as to. What was the proper place. HO was surprised at their good fortune to get a rental of it.—Mr. GALLOWAY- seconded the. motion. Mr. Galloway suggested that Mr. Wycherley should add to his motion- that the arrangements be left to . Dr. Hall and Mr. Goldsworth, and that a committee of the . Board be • appointed to assist them.—lt was understood that Mr. Wycherley consented.—Mr. FOGG was surprised that Dr. Hall should recommend such a place and Mr. Goldsworth knew no better than the doctor.—The SURVEYOR was surprised at Mr. Fogg putting it in the way be had done.—Mr. WYCHERLEY said the doctor had In- formed them that the disease was spreading, and there had been two more deaths since the previous meeting of the Board on Wednesday. He thought as men of common sense they should try to rid their town of the disease which , was causing such calamity in their midst, seeing that chil- dren were dying two and three in a family, lie considered the,y were really trifling in the matter. They had been dis- cussing it for a long time, when it might have been settled in a quarter of an hour.—Mr. Foote considered that if that motlem was passed and children were sentinto that 'damp house, instead a their lives' being prolonged, they would be buried from there. Why was it that question had cropped up all at once ?—The CHAIRMAN: Why is it the fereicame into the town ?—Mr. P 000: I don't know, but I suppose because people don't take care of themselves. Is the disease spreading 7—The CHAIRMAN: Of course it is. The doctor says so. Everybody knows the miserable state the town is In, and everybody knows that for the last fortnight or more every tradesman has suffered enormously, because people will not buy his goods owing to the fever.—Mr. FOGG moved •as an amendment, .and Mr. MAWDSLEY seconded, that Chorley-house .be not engaged for the purpose of a temporary hospitaL—On being put to the vote, the amend- ment was negatived by four votes to two.—Mr. WYCHERLEY then moved that as soon as the premises had been secured and:tlie nscesiiry :apparatus provided, that Dr. Hall engage a nurse.—This was seconded and carried.—A committee was appointed consisting of Messrs. Wycherley, Galloway, and Spencely (the chairman) to asaist the doctor and surveyor in carrying out the arrangements. The meeting then separated.

That's a handsome usher! Hasn't-she a cute little hand? Wonder what number her gloves are! They say her shoes are fives! If his hair isn't parted in the middle! Wonder what on earth she married him for! For his money, of coarse! - Isn't he handsome! He's as homely as a hedgehog! Be looks like a circus clown! No, he's like a dancing master! Good enough for her any way. She was always a stuck-up thing. She'll be worse than ever now. She jilted Strn Somebody, didn't she? No, he never asked her. He's left town, anyway. She was always a sweet little thing! How 4race- ful she walks I• Dear me, what airs she puts on! Wouldn't be in her place for a farm! I'd bet those jewels were hired. Wonder how much he'll give the minister! He looks like a culprit. His collar is choking him! What style they do pile on. Can't afford it, either. Well, she's eff of her father's hands at last ! What is her travelling suit made of? Doesn't she cling tightly to him, thought! She has a mortgage on him now. Hope they'll be happy. She'll be too extravagant, I bet. They say she's awful smart. Too smart for him by a jugful. Wonder if she got any presents. There; they're getting in- the carriage. That magnificent dress will be Squashed! The way she does look at him! I bet site worships him! Worships, be hanged, she's only making out. It's kind of nice to get married, lan% it? No, it's a sdreadful bore. • Wasn't it a stupid wedding? What 'dowdy &dais!, ru never g to another! I'm just suffo- eatedl • Tkred-to deatb,:. -4alad it's over! Oh, dear! Wish I were home !

The STIEVEYOU stated that at the meeting of the Board on the previous Wednesday evening, the medical officer and himself were instructed to make inquiries as to the best possible- site for a hospital, and it was mentioned that they might possibly get Chorlep.house.• Unfortunately Mr. Tyrer went away from home before they could see him with respect to the house.—Mr. GALLOWAY informed the Sur- veyor that he had seen Mr. Tyrer, who said he w.onld leave it entirely in the Surveyor's hands.—The Stalvavort said if Mr. Tyrer had left it entirely in his hands it weak] be all right. He and the medical officer had met and gone round the town together and examined A number of places which were at all likely for the purpose.—Mr. GOLDSWORTH gave a lit of places visited,- and said that Charley-house seetned to be the most suitable for a hoipital.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that unfortunately he was -not present at the last meeting, and he should like to know how far they got with regard to the question. Did they resolve to provide a tem- porary hospital, and that Mr. Goldsworth and the Medical Officer were to look out for a suitable place.—Mr. GALLO- WAY: Our ideas were, that if it was at all feasible it was to be done.—The SIIEVEYOR remarked that the Ishton•in- Makerfield Local Board had a lot' of hospital furnishings, consisting of beds, stoves, and other necessaries and he Lad hoped to have been able to inform the Board that night that they could have had the loan of them, but unfortunately the Chairman had gone away ff.) London. He mentioned the matter to the medical officer and others on the Tvevious day and he anticipated the Board would have no difficulty in getting the use of them at a small cost,--Mr.' MiWDS• LEY: I suppose a portion of Chorlek-house is in the town- ship of Whiston and portion in Prescot,—The CHAIRMAN I don't know. It does not matter a straw if it is.—Mr. POGO: The people have gone out of it because it was damp, and they were afraid of dying five or six years before their ordinary time. (Laughter.)—Mr. MAWDSLEY : Ido think it is the most unsuitable place they could have picked upon. Some one is benueeted_with it that has tO 'do with this Board.—Mr: PaisTox: I believe I was the person who suggested that Chorley-laouse 'would be the most suitable place we could hive in Prescot, and the members seemed to fall in`with my,Viewe. I must repudiate such charges ma4e, against ins by,Mr: Mawdsley.—Mr. MAWDSLEY All I can say is that you are a very bid judge.—The CarAlßma2lVe can't have this nonsence going OR.—Mr. MAWDSLEY rlt is I not nonsense.—The CalaudrArt i It is not before the meet- ing.—Mr. Mawnstay :It is before the meeting. (To Mr. Preston.) You are a very bad judge of a house for invalids.

On Monday evening, a meeting under the at the !Layton Quarry Church of England Temper: ciatkon was held in the If uyton-and-Roby Soh( Ref*.Canon Penrhyn, vicar of Huytort, presided, a. was a large audience.—The CHearattaw sad hat first meeting in Connection with the Huyton perance Society that had been held in that hoped during the course of the winter to hold rat a month in fluyton, either in that school or in School. They had, hitherto, during the past meetings once a fortnight at Huyton Quarry., whit be continued. It was thought that meeting once at Huyton would be more convenient for some IA tl bers, and at the same time they hoped it would 1 effect of inducing others to join the society.—The CLEarstrrs, sub-dean of Lincoln Cathedral, referred to the present position of the temperance question, position it occupied nearly half a century ago. Pot ago, when he first became a clergyman, it was a ra to meet in any society men who were total abstainet one did happen to meet them from time to, time, rarely met them without somebody, after dinner, t

and -joking them, and dealing yeti Unfairly with-thi thought. Now, all that position with them had He did not suppose there was a single class of sodi which they could enter, or a large entertainment ths , attend, where they would not find persons who wo abstainers. Not only had total abstinence greatly is its the working and middle classes, but it bad increase derabtyarnongst the upper classes, and that pat the perance question in a position it did not occupy 40 years since. -If it was unexpected it was not undeserved. He w)aat persuaded it was the result of enthusiastic, earnest, and per- sistent work amongst all classes of the community. Perhaps the Dissenters, their Nonconformist brethren, bad done more of the roughest and hardest work than the Church of Eng- land people had none. He would willingly accord to their Nonconformist brethren the praise of being the first in the field. But they must recollect that the Nenconformist bodies were something like those light troops which were very useful in warfare—especially guerrilla warfare—and which moved more quickly, and with less baggage and im- pediments, than the regular army, and consequently it was likely that great institution, the Church of England, was slow in the first instance to catch the impulse wllich Dissenters and earnest men wished to give, and that it wonld make sure of a footing before it started to move. He thought the Church had now thoroughly awoke to the work Mad duty of assisting in the temperance cause, and they were all of one mind, from the highest to the lowest, to free the country from the great national sin, which must bring down from God a curse and not a blessing. The temperance cause was like everything else worth winning, it was only to be won by hard work. The present position of the temperance cause was a very hopeful one. We never had such a Par-
rere tiaal increased
tereased con- tern-

liament as the present Parliament—he was not going to talk politics—with such a disposition to help forward temperance work. He judged them by their acts. He was not a sup- porter of the present Government. What he said he said as one who to a certain degree opposed them, but he believed if the Conservative pasty had been open in their dealings with temperance and more outspoken in desiring to put a stop to the evils of intemperance, it was quite possible that certain results of the last general election might have taken a different turn to what they did. They were all thankful a Sunday Closing Act had been passed for Ireland, and they were all thankful that this session, so spite of a large Pro- portion which Irish affairs had occupied in it, there was found time to edge in that very important Bill, which per- haps in its consequences might be quite as great and impor- tant as the Irish Land Act,—the very important little Bill of Sunday Closing in Wales. In the passing of the Jrish and Welsh Acts he saw a shadow cast before of a Sunday Closing Act being passed for England. (Loud applause.) While the position of the temperance cause was an unexpected and yet a deserved position, yet it was clear to a certain extant a dangerous position. There was a danger from those pushing on the cause of temperance, trying to tighten the Cords, which bound others, more tightly than Englishmen liked to be tied. (Hear, hear.) He was old enough to remeniber the abridging of the hours during which public-houses were open, in London some 20 years ago. He happened to bg in London on one of those two Sundays during which the Act was in operation. He did not. think it would in operation a month. There was almost a public riot in the parks. Every person of a certain class was mobbed and insulted, and the demonstrations which took Dlaci on the first Sunday, grew to a greater degree on the second Sunday. So that a serious riot in London was impending. because the hours during which drink might be obtained had been abridged. The result was that Parliament• Was obliged to eat its own words and retrace its own steps, and the temperance cause was in a worse condition afterwards than it was before. Now, be was afraid that many of them in their enthusiasm for the great and good cause might be tempted to desire to test the tightenink of the bonds which held their fellow citizens, in a way which would cause them to split and burst. He thought there was also a danger .with reference to a desire that public-houses should be en- tirely closed on Sunday. The people of this country hated anything which looked like class legislation, and he thought they hated it deservedly. He thought they wanted to feel that every man stood equal in the eyes of the law, and ,that the case of each man was equally considered by the legisla- ture. While people in a certain position were able to go to 1 their own cellars and get what they liked to drink others , could go to their clubs and do the same, but the working I man was stopped from getting that which he thFughtwas I as necessary for his food as the rich man might think 1 claret, chc. was for his. He thought they ought to avoid any i 1 appearance of class legislation in what they desired and hoped, and while hoping for and desiring Sunday closing he would not be so strict, but allow the houses to be open i an hour in the middle of the day and an extra hour in the ; evening, to allow the working man an opportunity of pur- chasing drink, but not to consume it on the spot. Referring to brewers and publicans he remarked that they- might say whatever they chose about their trade, its dangers, perils, difficulties, and trials, but they should not brand the men who carrird it on. Some of the men were better than their trade and some worse. Sunday closing would be a boon to many of the publicans, and he believed some of them vipuld tell them so. Then why say anything bitter against them -which they' could not justify and which they hid no right to say as Christian men.—Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, said he concurred with every word the last speaker had said, although he wondered as he went on whether by any possibility any- body might perchance misunderstand the position: He believed they might, and he would therefore try his best to- put the point he had in his mind clearly before them,-with a view of removing anything like misconception. Non- conformists had done an immense amount of rough Work, aye, and smooth work too for many years past in this grand movement. But he could not quite feel that the Church of England had been lagging behind to any very great extent. The Church in its corporate capacity only moved in the matter within a few years of the present time, but within his personal knowledge a very large number of ths Church's clergy scattered over toe different parishes of England were very zealous in the work long before the matter was taken up in what he had already called the Church's corporate capacity. He afterwards referred to the formation of that society.—Daring the evening songs were given by Messrs. ITate and Bernard and the Huyton Quarry Band of Hope.

COWLEY Minix &moms, St HELENS.—The Com- mittee appointed to canvaqs subscriptions towards the funds- of these schools recently recommended the governors to open the schools at once, the committee feeling sure that the required amount would be forthcoming. The governors have declined to act upon the suggestion,

CONSELVALTIVE AsSOCIA.TIO3.7B.—A. special meeting of the eXecutive committee of the Lancashire Union of Conservative and Constitutional Associations was held on Saturday, in Manchester, under the presidency of Mr. F. S. For., ell, who spoko at considerable length on the necessity for stringeilj. legislation to put down corrupt practices at elections. Condemnation of the misconduct and incapacity of the present Government in relation to home and foreign affairs was the subject of a ressiution unanimously adopted, land in support of which Mr. James Crompton, Mr. T. Nash, land Dr.,ltoyle addressed the meeting, seal a resolution on the fair-trade question was also carried. The committee decided to bold a great demonstration of county Conserva- tives in Manchester, in January next, and instructed the working sub-committee to make the necessary arrangements. LECTURE ON CROMWELL LT ST. HELEtrs.—On. Wed. nesday night the Rev. W. G. Pascoe delivered a lecture on "Oliver Cromwell, the hero of the Commonwealth,* under the auspices of the Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Associa- tion, in the Wesleyan day schools, Waterloo-street. Mr. Hewitt occupied the chair. The lecture was an eloquent resume of the rations important incidents in the life of Cromwell wham he eulogised as the greatest uncrowned king in the history of the world. He elect .etrtly defended his action in respect to the decapitation of King Charles the First, remarking that while it tiny invo been a blunder as a matter of policy, it was not wrong, as the king had afendeid in the eye of the law, and by his death the freedom of the country was eecu;ed. Mews-any MEETING kr KbTOWSLET.—On Irrot.day evening a missionary meeting was held in the GitleSehool- room, Knowsley, on behalf of the Society for the Propaga- tion of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. The Rev. Canon Fielden presided, and there was a very large attendance: The Chairman, after recommending mission work to the notice of his parishioners, introduced the Rev. Archdeacon Chiswell, who gave an interesting and lucid account of mission work in Madagascar. He painted out that the Queen of Madagascar only really ruled over one-third of the island; and it was only in her dominions mission work was carried on. The other portion of the island was simply in a state of heathenism, no mission work having been attempted by anybody. The rev. gentleman gave several interesting accounts of the habits and customs of the natives, and an amusing account of his first landing at the island. The Rev. Mr. Bridger, secretary for the society in the Liverpool district, also addressed the meeting, recommending the claims of the society. On the motion of the Rev. J. fr. Bolton, citrate of Knowsley and chaplain to Lord Derby,: r vote of thanks was passed to the Archdeacon. Atthecunktte4 a • of the proceedings a collection was made, which mo to SS 10s. 9d,

a large town as Widnes should, like St. Helens, War- rington, and other towns in the district, possess a good free public library. The subject has been dis- cussed at meetings of the Local Board, but there some spirits have been found to oppose the measure fearful of the great increase which it might cause to the rates. Those, however, who have argued against the propo- sal on this ground have thus only shown that they were not so well acquainted with the provisions of the Free Library Act as they should have been, as the maximum amount which the authorities are allowed to levy for the purposes of a free library is one penny in the pound. That being so we can scarcely imagine that there will be many persons to be found in the town who will object to pay one penny in the pound onco a year towards the support of such a valuable institution. The working classes of the town have so very few places of recreation or amusement that we are only surprised that they have allowed the subject to lie dormant for so long. There cannot be a doubt that the establishment of a good free library will be of incalculable value not only to working men but also to all classes of society, and we shall, therefore, be very greatly disappointed if, when the subject is fairly placed before the ratepayers, they will not decide, by a very large majority, to adopt the Free Libraries Act, and thus avail themselves of the advantages which their fellow citizens in other towns are now enjoying. Mr. F. H. Gossage, who is ever ready to help in any good work intended for the benefit of the town, and Major Cross, have expressed themselves as being ready to help in this movement, and it is therefore to be hoped that steps will at once be taken to petition the Chair- man of the Local Board to convene a town's meeting on the subject, so that the opinion of the ratepayers may be elicited. The question is one which concerns the people themselves generally, and it is for them to say whether they will provide themselves with the means and facilities of acquiring knowledge, or whether they prefer to remain in their present anomalous position.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

The dispute between Mr. Annett, master of Holy Trinity Church School, Runcorn, and the School Board, has excited I great interest in Runcorn and also in the town of Widnes, where the schoolmaster is very well known. The matter appears to have ended in a personal contest between Mr. John Simpson, of Frodsham, and Mr. Annett. lam at a loss to know why it was absolutely necessary that Mr. Simpson should have considered it essential to tell Mr. Annett that his statements were false, and so, in a sense, give him the lie direct. He might very easily have said that the assertions of the Trinity schoolmaster did not, as far as he could see, appear to be strictly accurate, and then ke would have escaped the terrible castigation which the attack called forth. I scarcely think Mr. Simpson would have so far forgotten himself if he had been speaking of a man who had wealth and an influential position at the back of him. He would, most probably, then have clothed his diction in a few of those graces of language which he' as a very wii.ely read and cultivated man, knows so well how to use. There are many winning features about the character of Mr. Simpson. He is a labourer in many a benevolent field, but it is said that he finds it very diffi- cult to permit of opposition to any of his pet projects. He must not suppose that people with whom he is brought in contact are prepared to sink their own individuality and per- sonal rights, because the gentleman with whom they have to do is a man of influence in a number of spheres. Such a charge as that made by Mr. Simpson might be pardoned in a young man who was ignorant of the world and its devious ways, but it is difficult to overlook in a gentleman over WiIOSO head have passed the snows of upwards of sixty winters. We are told upon very high authority to "be , courteous," but what courtesy can there be about telling a man in an almost direct style that what he says is utterly false? The question arises of how Mr. Simpson came to get, into such a 'mixed" state? Mr. Annett must, however, be a poor judge of character if he thinks that the gentleman in question will offer any apology for what he has said. In future, most of the inquests held in the town of Run• corn will take place in the Board Room at the Cemetery. Mr. Moss and Mr. Littler will no doubt win some popu- larity amongst the ratepayers of Runcorn by the proposal which they have brought forward and carried, at the Run- corn Burial Board, to dispense with the services of a second gardener during the months of November and March. . There have for a long time been serious complaints con- corning the terrible amount of coal stealing in Widnes. I have no desire to find fault with the police in that town, ; who, upon the whole, are an able body of men, but I would give them the benefit of a suggestion made to me the other day. It was to the effect that men in plain clothes ought to be detailed for such a duty so that of catching coal stealers' as they almost invariably plant a number of sentinels at various points before commencing their opera- tions, and a man dressed in the ordinary police garb, with a number of steel buttonson his raiment—apparently put there by the Government with the idea of letting the wrong doers I know he is coming—has scarcely any chance of making a capture. Perhaps Superintendent Barker will make a note of this suggestion, as there is not the slightest doubt that he I will win the gratitude of the manufacturers if he can stop the coal stealing, for which Widnes is so much noted.

The Tory party are evidently in a sad state at Burnley, for at the Revising Barrister's Court the other day they were unable to have any one to represent their interests. The party is evidently getting into a sad plight. I notice that the result of the revision of the Parliamentary list of voters for Mid-Cheshire is a net Liberal gain of 143, whilst in the borough of Warrington the Liberal party have gained 124. This is encouraging to those who desire, like myself, to see the spread of Liberalism. Mr. Hack, the newly-appointed minister in the Wesleyan Methodist circuit, is likely to prove very popular. His ser- mons are marked by considerable originality and spiritual fervour, but it is to be regretted that he does not study how to use his voice to the best advantage, and so save himself an infinitude of trouble in the way of sore throat. There is nothing gained by a speaker raising his voice until it loses naturalness, and then coming down to a falsetto, which makes the hearer wonder if the gentleman has, during his momentary wandering of thought, left the platform or the pulpit, and his place been taken by some one else. Is the idea correct that the Author of all Good requires a man to injure his body by his exertions in His service ? The body is holy as well as the spirit, and preachers ought to learn that no speaker can be effective who is wanting in magnetic power, which comes from a high state of physical health. FLACCUS.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS' ENTERTAINMENT. —The first of a series of entertainments for the season, in connection with these schools, was given in the National schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. Tne Vicar presided, and referred to the success of the entertainments last season, when £25 was realised. The glee class sang "ma Cana- dian boat song," and "Now by day's retiring lamp," in good style. Mr. F. Wilkinson gave "The British tar" and "At peace, but still on guard"; Miss Purves "Sing, sweet bird," and a selection from " Norma "; and Mr. Large " The anchor's weighed" and "Tom Bowling," both of which were loudly applauded. Mr. T. Davies, who is "up " in comic singing, entertained the audience with "The police- man " and "Gold, gold, gold." Miss Broad and Mr. Imison gave the duet "The sailor sigks," in a very tasteful man- ner. Mr. Balmer contributed a Lancashire reading; and the proceedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 15, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 15, 1881.

STORM AT RuNcom.—Yesterday, a terrible storm of rain and wind from the west raged at Runcorn. The tide was at high water about an hour and a quarter before the time fixed in the table, and much damage was done in the town by parts ef roofs being blown off and signs torn down. The wind blew so fiercely that pedestrians were in great danger from falling tiles. THE EXPENDITURE OF WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—AD extraordinary meeting of the Widnes School Board was held on Thursday afternoon. There were present: Mr. T. Sutton Timmis (in the chair), the Rev. George Holloway, and Messrs. Bradshaw, Shaw, Davies, O'Keefe, and Denby (clerk). The Chairman said the meeting had been called for the special purpose of passing the accounts for the year. Per- haps Mr. Shaw would feel called upon to give them some explanation of the balance sheet.—Mr. Shaw then read the 'accounts, remarking that he did not think it was necessary I to go into them in detail. They showed that the total receipts for the year had been £5,829 12s. 7d, and the ex- penditure £5,756 15s. 75., leaving a balance of £135 17s. The debtor side included the following items :—Parliamen- tary grant £1,367 Sc. 5d., received from the ratepayers £2,350, and school fees £1,125 19s. 11 The principal items of expenditure were : Salaries of teachers, £2,497 be. 6d ; purchase of land, erection, enlargement, or alteration of school buildings, £548 7s. 105; interest on loans £l,OlB 12s. 63.; and repayment of loans, £253 13s. 105. Mr. Shaw proposed that the accounts which embraced the financial year ending the 29th September, be passed.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously and the proceedings terminated. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Henry Coleburn presided, and there were also present: Messrs. Thomas Norman, William Littler, James Handley, George Moss, George Rhodes, Peter Briscoe, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). A statement presented by the secretary, showed that the interments for the month ending the 25th September were 13, as against 38 in the corresponding month last year. The receipts from March 25th to September 25th had been £ll7 15s. 43., as compared with £l3O 13s. 6d. in the correspond- ing period of the last 12 months. This year the burials numbered 117, as against 160 in the previous twelvemonths. The receipts for the month were £l4 ss. lid., and the ex- penditure £42 12s. 9d. It was decided, on the proposition of Mr. Littler, seconded by Mr. Moss, that the services of the second gardener be dispensed with during the months of November and March inclusive.—The Chairman said he had seen Mr. Ridgway, the County Coroner, and requested to know whether he was willing to pay the Board the same fees for the use of the cemetery offices which he paid to the persons at whose houses inquests were now held. Had received a letter from him applying for the use of the cemetery offices for the holding of inquests when the bodies lay at the receiving house. Mr. Ridgway intimated that he was perfectly willing to pay the fees so long as the county allowed them. It was then decided that the Coroner should be allowed the use of the Board room for the holding of inquests. ' RIFLE MATCH AT RUNCORN.—A friendly match was shot between the representative teams of the Hartford and Runcorn volunteer companies, on the range at Weaverham Wood, on Saturday afternoon, and resulted in a victory for the Hartford volunteers. Wimbledon targets and scoring were adopted, seven rounds being fired at 200, 500, and 600 yards. There was an unsteady wind from the right rear, and a very changeable light. STAB OF TEXPICELECE BEAU BAND, Wromr.s.—This .band has entered for the brass, band contest which will take place at the opening of the Glaciarium, Southport, on Monday. I ACCIDENT AT WowEs.—On Tuesday, a man named Davenport was seriously hurt whilst working in connection with the hoist, at Messrs. GrOssage's soap works, Widnes. Fromm FOE MB. Nowzrz, jurrion, or Rumors.— Recently a gentleman offered three prizes, one of £2O, and two of £l5, to the male students of the Manchester School of Art, for the best painting, and our Runcorn readers will be glad to hear that the second prize was won by Mr. A. T. Nowell, of Runcorn, with his picture entitled " Evening at Hale Point."

SERVICE OF SONG.—On Thursday evening a service of song, entitled " The Children's Messiah," was rendered in Bethesda schoolroom, Runcorn, by the children forming the Rev. J. D. Thomas' children's class, sixty in number. Mr. F. Fairhurst conducted, and Mr. George Lacy played the harmonium. The service was exceedingly well given, and reflected great credit on the children, and Mr. George Lacy, who had so ably trained them. SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WIDNES.:-An in- quest was held at the George Hotel, Widnes, on Wednesday, before Mr. C. E. Driffield, coroner, on the body of John Burke, a child aged two months and 21 days, the son of Edward Burke, labourer, residing at 29, Water-street, Widnes. The evidence was to the effect that the litte one died in a convulsive fit; and the jury returned a verdict of "Natural causes."

Rusconn Bunn oF GIIIIIDILNS.—The following tenders were accepted at the last meeting of the Guardians —Butchers' meat, Joseph Dobson, Warrington; beer, wine, and spirits, Robert Rigby, Runcorn; drugs and oil, Isaac Speakman; groceries, Samuel Collier; coal, W. and J. Richardson, Warrington; flour and oatmeal, John Furmston, Daresbury ; clothing, Richard Oldbury, Runcorn; boots and shoes, Edmund Ice, Earlestown ; drapery, Francis Fair- hurst, Runcorn; coffins, William Lightfoot, Dutton.

Runconn AND Tim Canons AND TARPONS= Snows. —The committee appointed to consider the desirability of inviting the Cheshire or the Tarporley Agricultural Society to hold their next annual show at Runcorn met on Tuesday. Dr. Steele was appointed chairman, and it was decided that if the Cheshire Agricultural Society agreed to hold their show at Itancorn, the committee would do every thing they could to promote its success. Intimation has been sent to the Tarporley Agricultural Society that until a reply has been received from the Cheshire Society their application could not be entertained.

METRODIST FREE CHURCH, Ruiccoßß.—The annual con- gregational tea meeting in connection with this place was held in the schoolroom, Ellesmere•street, on Monday. There was a good attendance at the tea, And also at the meeting which was held afterwards and at which Mr. M. Timperley presided. Mr. Gandy delivered an address, in which he exhorted the friends to unity and diligence in their efforts to benefit those around them. The Rev. 3. Billington, pastor, gave a description of his attendance at the Annual Assembly in London, as the representative of the Runcorn Circuit, and spoke in encouraging strains of the propects of future work in the Church. The choir sang several anthems during the evening.

STATE OF TRADE AT WIDNES DISTRICT. —WO hoar that there is a slight improvement in the chemical trade of Widnes, though many people are still out of work, and the prospect for the coming winter certainly demi not appear a very brilliant one. Some short time ago we gave a brief description of the works erected on Ditton-road, Widnes, by the Upper Widnes Chemical Co. We regret to hear that owing to the failures in the town and the generally dark look out in the chemical trade, the company did not feel in a position to start the% splendid works, which were erected by Mr. Thomas Kirkham, of Runcorn from plans by Mr. John Clare, at a cost of upwards oILIO,OOO. Some few months ago a first class auctioneer was employed, and the buildings were placed before the public at the Central Hotel, but the highest amount offered for them was £3,500, at which they were withdrawn. Our readers will be pleased to hear that Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., whose name is a tower of strength in the chemical trade, have purchased the place, and we urderstana, are making preparations to com- mence operations, so that some of the unemployed amongst the labouring population of the town have a good prospect before them. We hear a- report which we hope is well founded, that a copper manufacturing company have within the last few weeks been looking out for about 20 acres of land in the town. Another statement, for the truth of which we cannot vouch, has been in circulation, to the effect that negotiations ate In progress for:the purchase of the:Ditton Ironworks. All our readers will join us in the hope that the quietude which at present reigns at Ditton 132a7 be INA brokeny &axon Lxo Bosco IN RtlrxcOnx.—This gentleman's variety entertainment is carried out on an original plan, which seems to find much favour with the mass of the population. From the beginning to the and of the perfor- mance there is a variedness which is very charming to all lovers of amusement. Signor Bosco's conjuring is executed in a manner worthy of his father's name, though this is merely one division of the attractions. Professor Henry Miller is the best ventriloquist we have ever seen, and we have witnessed the efforts of not 'a few. Professor Smith's Punch and Judy exhibition is without doubt worth the money charged for admission. Mr. Harry Stewart assumes about eight characters. 'He changes his dresses before the audience, and the promise that he carries all this out "with- out picking anything up or throwing anything down" is fulfilled to the letter. Mr. Holliday's efforts in the way of comic representation were very well received; and his rendering of "Rocked ha the cradle of the deep" on one of the band instruments was very fine. His satirical German song we considered rather a poor affair. Mr. .1. Mortimer and Miss A. Clarisse gave a sketch which caused much amusement, though we scarcely think the girl is sufficiently old to take the part of the injinjuredwife. For several years i there has been no entertainer n the town of Runcorn who has treated the public so handsomely in the matter of gifts, many of which have been really valuable. Signor Bosco is most assuredly a man who like Sam Slick, the clockmaker, understands "'human natur'," and he will always receive a hearty welcome from the inhabitants of Runcorn. RUNCORN TRFNITY CREECH YOUNG Dinn'ti ASSOCLL. I TION TEA Priam—This annual reunion, was held on the evening of the 10th inst., in the schoolroom. The tables were presided over by Mrs': Buckley, Mrs. Rogerson, and Miss Goodwell. The company afterwards adjourned to an adjoining room, where a large collection of interesting relics, curios, tire., were arranged on tables. The articles included a view in oil of Runcorn as it was 50 years ago, when it presented quite a charming appearance; there was also a picture of Widnes taken in 1842, showing the "Snig Pie" House and surrounding neighbourhood with the river and shore, the whole being, as compared with its more modern features really a sylvan scene. There were an assegai and shield from Zululand, picked up near the spot where the unfortunate Prince Imperial fell, lent for the occa- sion; some New Zealand war-clubs of exquisite workmanship and design, brought over by the late Vicar of Frodsham ; a bow and arrows of native design and make from the East ' Indies; an Indian bow, arrows, and quiver; a digger and shield used in the Indian Mutiny; various relics of the Crimean war; Sevezal pieces of ancient pottery; a copy of the first Times newspaper, and a large number of other old newspapers; a large collection of foreign coins and stamps; an exquisite satchel made of seeds by the North American Indians; and:the Duke of Wellington's pen wiper. There were two very powerful microscopes kindly lent by Mr. Rhodes and Mr. Annett, who exhibited a large quantity of interesting objects to an admiring group. After this the Rim. J. Wright-Williams, Vicar of Widnes, delivered an address on Young Men's Christian Associations and their advantages, ctc., and the president of the association, the Rev. W. Preston, made a few remarks on the work of the association in the parish, and, owing to the indisposition of the secretary, read the report for the past year, detailing the work done by the members in its various branches. Votes of thanks were passed to the Vicar of Widnes, and those who had so willingly enriched the exhibition by the loan of their curios; the ladies presiding at tea, and all those who worked to make the meeting so great a success. Banwies-upoN-Twzga Gaamasa Saxon. The Governors have filled the vacancy in the head mastership of the above school, by the appointment of the Rev. T. W. Gibson, M.A., first class in classical honours, and late fellow of Durham University; principal of Cambridge School, Sale, and formerly one of the assistant classical masters in the Manchester Grammar School. There were over fifty candi- dates for the appointment.

CHESTER CHEESE FAIR.—The October cheese fair was held on Saturday, in the Linen Hall, when about 80 tons were pitched. There was a decline in prices of about 3s. per cwt. Good cheese sold from 50s. to 645., while two ether excellent dairies sold for 65s , buyers declaring that they could not give more in the face of the immense quanti- ties of American cheese stored at Liverpool and Manchester. There was a good attend ince and all the lots were sold save two.

REDUCTION OF RENTS IN CHESIITEE.—The tenants on the Ashton Heyes estate in Cheshire recently sent in a memorial to the trustees,among whom is Sir Richard Cross, requesting a reduction of their rents. The tenantry pointed out that rents on the Ashton Heyes estate were higher than ' on neighbouring estates, and that these exceptional rents and disastrous seasons were ruining them. After some corres- pondence the tenantry agreed to a revaluation, and named as valuers either Mr. Martin, agent for Lord Crewe. or Mr. Beckett, agent for Sir Philip Egerton, of Calton. The trustees, however, decided to appoint Mr. Coleman, one of the assistant agricultural commissioners, and no other i valuer. The terms on which the valuation were to be con- ducted were, that if the tenant's rent was raised he must pay his proportion of the cost of the valuation, but if the rents were reduced the trustees would pay the costs. Mr. Cole- man has just sent in his awards. Practically they amount to a reduction in rents to the extent of 10 per cent on the entire estate.

In the revision of the Parliamentary list of voters for the city of Manchester, which has just concluded, the Liberal party have gained 1,156 votes. In addition to this gain, a survey made by the agents of the party in the early portion of the year resulted in upwards of 1,000 claims from new occupiers or reclaims on account of removals being made, chiefly on behalf of Liberal voters, to the overseers of the respective townships.

MEDALS FOR LANCASHIRE M.—By direation of his Royal Highness the Field Marshal Commanding-in-Chief the following non-commissioned officers and men of the Lancashire regiments have been awarded the silver medal with gratuities for long service and good conduct:-2nd Battalion Lancashire Fusiliers—Col.-Sergeant J. Hogan; 2nd Battalion East Lancashire Regiment Private W. Miland, Sergeant W. Watkins, Corporal T. Williams, Sergeant W. Woolven, Lance-Sergeant J., Thompson, and Private J. Hunt ; Ist and 2nd Battalions North Lancashire Regiment—Sergeant-Instructor .of Musketry T. Orr, Band- master W. T. Trump, Sergeant J. G. Flynn, Colour-Sergeant J. Randle, aud Private M. Byrne; Ist Battalion the Man- chester Regiment—Private T. G. Owing and Sergeant W. Robinson.

GIITAT LIBERAL GAIN AT BMINLEY.—The Conser- vatives vete totally unrepresented at the annual rev:mien of the borough voters' list at Burnley the other by. The Liberals had 441 objections and made a considerable num- ber of claims. Only one person attended to defend hisv.ote, and the Revising Barrister remarked that this circumstance showed what little interest the vcters took in the .revision unless they were whipped up by agents. Mr. Moore, who represented the Liberals, said it perhaps showed another fact, namely, that the objections were justly made, and, that per- sons stayed away because they knew they had little chance of sustaining their votes —The Revising Barrister: You are entitled to look at it in that way.—The result of therevision was that 441 Conservatives, were struck off whilst the Liberal gain was about 470.

WESIAT HALL OIERCXET CLUB.—The easing match of the season was played on Saturday last, when sides.were chosen by J. Lewis and J. Warburton, resulting in a victory for Lewis's side. At 7-30 the members and friends, numbering about 30, sit down to a supper in the schoolroom, after which the Revs. J. Eglingtun and Ripon, the new ministers, each gave a short address, ;which was very interesting. The repart of the club was read, after which Mr. J. W. Horton, vice-president, addressed the meet- ing. The club have played 14 matches, winning five and loosing three, and six drawn matches, four being greatly in their favour. The following are the highest average scores : -1, Mr. T. Williams, 2P; 2, Mr. G. Ellis, 8 ; 3, Mr. G. Williams, 8; 4, Mr. J. Warburton, 7; 5, Mr. W. Byfield, 6; 0, Mr. J. Lewis, 5.

TIIE 21ST /4.14 V. AND LIEUTENANT. COLONEL GAM- nt..—The mevement:among the officers and members of the 21st L.R.V. for showing their appreciation. of Lieuten- ant-Colonel Gamble by presenting him with a testimonial is I now taking a decided shape. The great interest which the commanding officer has taken in the volunteer movement since the formation of the corps, his ready sympathy with every member, his untiring zeal, and his munificence have justly gained for him the esteem and respect of every mem- ber of the corps, while among all classes in St. Helens his name has become a household word, not only as a large employer of labour, but through being connected with every movement having for its object the moral, intellectual, and spiritual advancement of the people. After a good deal of deliberation, the officers have decided to purchase an elabof- ate album, which it is hoped will bear the borough arms aner the colonel's crest, and contain cabinet photos of the officers. The present of the general body of the corps will probably be a large oil painting of the colonel himself, on which an emindtat artist is to be engaged. PENEETII IMPROVEMENT CLABS.—The members of this class held their first meeting this session on Wednesday, in the Workmen's Club, Warrington-road. The following members gave impromptu speeches on the subjects named below :—What is your idea of the importance of truth, Mr. B. Hobson • Tell us how to live happy in this world, Mr. D. Garnett; Slow that treaties are the bond of nations, Mr. W. H. Hughes (secretary) ; Show us the virtue of the golden rule, Do unto others as we would be done by, Mr. .J. Davies ; Which is the most general, hope or envy, Mr. C. Hughes ; Which form of government recommends, itself to you, republic or monarchical, Mr. A. White; Give your opinions on the effects of controversy, is it beneficial or otherwise, Mr. J. Mainley. A very pleasant and profitable evening was spent. It is to be hoped that the young men of Penketh will rally up next Wednesday when the class meets again ; and hopes were expressed that the society would increase in its membership. The Principal amounts for the United States have been in excess during last month as compared with September in the pre- vious year, but only as 21,702 is beyond 21,432, while the total amount for the year is as 150,622 is to 155,979, show- a decrease of 5,357 though Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Charlestown have taken more than last year. Our North American districts have not only taken less in the year by 18,970, but also for September 7,006 as against 11,014 last year in the same period, though to St. John's more has been sent.
