PROPOSAL TO BUILD TUE RUNCORN SEAMEN'S Mn. SIONANY A HOUSE—On Wednesday a meeting was held in the Mission-room, Bottom Locks, Runcorn, to form a corn_ mittee for the carrying out of the necessary arrangements for bunging or purchasing a house for Mr. Wm. Shaw, the acting icer connected with the Seamen's Mission, at Run- corn. The Rev.. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also present several other influential gentlemen of the town. Mr. George Howard (sec. pro. tern.) read the minutes, and stated that at the last meeting the following resolution bad been adopted :—" That the Chairman write to the committee of the Mersey Mission and request three of them to take the trustee-ship of the house, and also to solicit a donation front the said committee in order to show ' their approval of the scheme." The Chairman said it had been strongly felt that the house ought to be public pro- perty ; and it must be built or purchased for the representa- tives of the Mersey Mission, and also that the gentlemen at the Liverpool head quarters should show their approval of ' the scheme by taking the trustee-ship. lie had received a letter from the committee at Liverpool accepting the trustee- slip, and promising a donation of LIO for the fund.—Mr. Shaw (missionary) said he had thought that the house in which he lived in Percival-lane would be a suitable one, but upon taking the matter into further consideration he had come to the conclusion that it would not be the most economical as the street was not finished and the work I would have to be done at the expense of the property owners. If a certain sum of money were collected, they might either buy or build a house in a more suitable locality.—The Vicar remarked that there was a saying to the effect that fools built houses and wise men lived in them; which meant that a Louse might be bought for less money than it would take to build one.—Mr. Taylor: I sup- pose you would prefer a house in Duke's Field P—Mr. Shaw: Yes. it would be preferable.—Mr. Williams thought it not unlikely that if Major Orred were requested, he would make them a present of a piece of land in Duke's Field on which , to erect the dwelling.—Mr. White considered this rather probable.—Mr. Williams: At any rate there could be no harm in asking him.—The Chairman: All this talk about ' the house goes to prove that we want a committee.—lt was then resolved that Messrs. Taylor, White, 11 illiams, Knowles, Pearson, ImisOn, Croley, and Littler should be appointed members of the committee, with power to add to their num- ber.—lt was resolved that the folloaing gentlemen be re- quested to act as trustees, in conjunction with the three members of the Liverpool committee.—Mr. C. W. Hazle- burst, Mr. John Simpson, Mr. Brundrit, Mr. Hayes, and the agent of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. (Mr. Meadowcroft). —At a meeting of the committee the same evening, Mr. George Howard was appointed secretary, and it was resolved that Mr. Edward Chorlton be requested to accept the office of treasurer.—lt was resolved that a Christmas tree and sale of work be held in the Public Hall in December. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBITING SOCIETY.—The winter session of this society commenced on Tuesday, in Bethesda Congregational school room. The Liberal members turued up in large numbers, but owing to some misunder- standing amongst the Conservative party, there were only about three present. The house was nevertheless formally opened, and the Queen's Speech read as follows :—"Gentle- men of the House of Commons,—The customary period having arrived for your assembling in order to deliberate upon measures affecting the prosperity and happiness of my people, I hasten to assure you of my unabated interest in your proceedings. It is with feelings of the deepest sorrow I refer to the death, by the hands of the assassin, of General Garfield, the President of the United States, who by his noble and Christian conduct gave promise of a successful administration of that mighty Republic; and I am assured you will unite with me in my expression of sympathy and condolence with his widow, and the American people generally, in their sad bereavement. The improvement in. trade and commerce to which I directed your attention at the commencement of the last session, has, I am thankful to say, continued ; and the long season of depression which pressed so heavily upon a large proportion of my subjeCts is, I trust, gradually passing away. Although a section of my subjects in Ireland give cause for anxiety, yet I am sanguine to hope that the measure which recently received my assent will so ameliorate the condition of my people, that contentment and prosperity will permanently result, and the necessity for exceptional measures for the protection of life and property in that portion of my dominions cease to exist. My relations with all the Powers continue to be of a peace- ful, amicable, and cordial nature, and as a result of the , united action of the greater Powers, aided by my Govern- ment, Greece has entered into possession of a considerable accession of territory, which I trust will be a strong guarantee of peace in the future. Though I have not yet been able to withdraw my troops from a partial occupation of the Transvaal, look with hope for the ratification of the Convention entered into between my Government and the leaders of that State by its Legislative Assembly. My Government intend submitting proposals for your considera- tion, having reference to a further extension of a national system of education, the conditions under which land is at present held and cultivated, and the representation of the , people by a re-distribution of seats. .If the state of public business will admit, your attention will also be directed to the incidence of local taxation, and the establishment of representative county boards.—On the motion of the Premier, seconded by the member for Walsall, the ,house adjourned until Tuesday evening next, at eight o'clock, when the address in reply to the Queen's Speech will be moved and afterwards Commented upon. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The meeting of.this Board was held on Tuesday. Major Cross presided, and there were also present Messrs. Gossage, O'Keeffe, Kershaw, Shut, Heworth, Sadler, Pankhurst, Heyes, Gaskell, Handley, Forster, Allen (clerk), Roberts (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector.) The proceedings only occupied ten minutes.

div.head: BOILERS ON THE FAIRGROUND.
div.p: BOILERS ON THE FAIRGROUND.

Mr. HASKELL asked what instruction had been given with reference to boilers upon the fair ground.—Mr. PARKHURST said that under existing circumstances, the officials of the Board did not bind themselves to give a certificate, or receive a fee, in the case of any boiler used upon the ground. Dn. COOPER'S APPOINTMENT. Mr. CAREY reported that the Government auditor had drawn the attention of the Board to the fact that as Dr. Cooper had sometime ago been appointed medical officer to the 'Union, an application ought to be made to the Local Government Board to sanction his occupation of the office beheld under the the Local Board, under section 191 of the Public Health Act. He proposed that the application be made.—Mr. HAYES seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously.

div.head: LEVEL CROSSINGS.
div.p: THE LEVEL CROSSINGS.

The CHAIRMAN reported that a communication had been received from the assistant secretary to the London and North Western Railway Company, stating that the letter from the Board on the subject of level crossings had been received, and it would be laid before the next,meeting of the directors.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COM3fITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COM3fITTEE.

_ The minutes of this committee were passed, on the mction of Mr. (Imam They showed a decrease of 5444 per cent. in the quantity of water delivered during the four weeks ending 21st September, as compared with the corresponding period last year ; and of 10.56 per cent, in the gas delivered. It had been resolved that in future dry meters should not be supplied by the Board.—Thg following contracts had been signed: Messrs. Brunner, -Mond and Co for gas liquor; John Culpan and Sons, for tar; and Smetherst and Co., for coal. It bad been also resolved that A special meeting of the cominitcee should be held on the 24th October, to consider the General Purposes Committee's recemmendations as to the staff, and the question of private plumbing and gas fitting.

div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

These minutes were passed, on the proposition of Mr. KERSHAW' seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. They showed that a letter had been received on behalf of Mi. Bibby, enclosine, an agreement for widening roads and constructing new rail- ways.' The consideration of the letter was postponed. • THE:HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Mr. PANKIIIIRST moved, and Mr. HEYES seconded the motion approving of the minutes of the Health Committee which was passed. They contained the medical officer's re- port, from which it appeared that the births during the month had been 102, or 48 96 per 1,000; and the deaths 23, or 11.04 per 1,000. The deaths included those of seven children under one year, and six between one and five years. Mr. Dickson reported that the cases of fever were now all convalescent. Two cases of scarlet fever had been reported, and both patients were now recovering. The Clerk had been instructed to write to the St. Helens and Sutton Building Society, and Mr. John Houghton, stating that unless the arrangements of their property in Elizabeth and Margaret. streets were at once made good, the houses would have to be closed.—Mr. CAREY congratulated the Board on the fact that the attack of infectious disease from which West Bank had been suffering had ceased. He spoke in high terms of the manner in which Dr. McClellan had acted in reporting the case.

div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Under the presidency of the Bev. Canon Barclay, a Special meeting of this Authority was held on Thursday at Dutton Workhouse, to:consider a letter received foam Messrs. Wrigley and Moscroft, solicitors to Mr. E. A. Wright, of Frodsham, the owner of certain lands at Frodsham, across which the Authority propose to lay sewer pipes in accord- anee with plans approved by the Authority and the Local Government Board. There were present Messrs. T. Andrews, Weir, Challoner, James Derbyshire, C. Mounfield, H. Lima- ker (clerk), and W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Clerk said he considered the letter he had received of such impor- tance that he at once sent it and the accompanying plans to Mr. Bancroft, the engineer, asking his advice as to whether a special meeting should be called, and he replied in the affirmative. He therefore (lid so. The letter, which was addressed from /2, Clegg-street, Oldham' and dated Oct. 7, stated that the writers were concerned for Mr. Ed. Abbey Wright, of Castle Park, who some time ago handed to them the Authority's letter and notice of the 19th January, 1880, and the plans which accompanied that notice, and also their letter of the 7th July last enclosing plan and section show- ing the line of the proposed sewer. It was not till Mr. Wright was furnished with the last-mentioned plan and means of knowing what maa pro- section that & had any posed to be done nor in a position to judge of the way in whieh his estate would inevitably be effected if the proposed scheme was carried out; and it could not have surprised either the Board or Mr. Bancroft that he should ha.ve taken every opportunity to protest against it in the strongest terms. Against the carrying out of the scheme he would struggle to the utmost of his power; and if it should be forced upon him they did not hesitate to say that the hardships of the case would bring it within the words of Mr. justice Am- pladd as a" thing do..ie vexatiously,' for which very heavy damages would be given. In taking this stanch it was incum- bent upon Mr. Wright that he should point wit some alter- native scheme, and he had accordingly been at considerable pains to do so. The enclosed plans had been prepared by Mr. Wright's surveyor, George Heywood, after conferences between him and Mr. Bancroft, and would elucidate the alternative schemes. There was nothing to prevent the sewer being constructed along the highways, as indicated on one of the alternative plans. The expense would, of course, be greater; but mere saving of expense did not warrant in- terference with private property. If the Authority would adopt the alternative plan they would escape the payment of heavy damages and compensation, which under the pre- sent scheme, Mr. Wright would obtain. Ile would contribute £lOO towards the extra cost of the scheme he submitted, with the stipulation that no manholes or lamplioles should be constructed on his land. Aathe matter was one of oon- siderable anxiety to Mr. Wright, and had now arrived at a stage when it must be specially dealt with, they trusted the Authority would give it thtir best end immediate attention. —Mr. Bancroft was presunt, and explained the alternative schemes proposed by Mr. Wright, stating that the course approved of by the Board would cost £lO3 4s. If they went round by the retad, as suggested by Mr. Wright, it would colt £Bl6 9s. 3d.; bat, deducting the amount promised by Mr. Wright, would leave it £716 3s 9d. The second alternative scheme suggested would cost £730 3s. 9d., besides way-leave. —Mr. Challoner : It is preposterous to suppose that the Board are going to pay £BOO more than they had originally agreed.—Mr. Derbyshire said the plan suggested by the Board, and approved by the Local Government Board, was undoubtedly the bes• one. Mr. Wright wished them to spend £BOO, which could not be.—Mr. Bancroft, in reply to a question, said the way-leave might cost 25. per running yard.—Mr. Weir proposed that the original plan be adhered to, and that the clerk write, in reply to Messrs. Wrigley and hloscroft, that ample notice was given to Mr. Wright of the Board's intention totcarry out the sewer, and that he should have stated his objection to the Local Government Board inspector when he held his inquiry at Frodsbam ; and that the Board enter into arrangements for carrying out the scheme. The Authority's plan was a most satisfactory one, and they did not feel justified in altering their original plan, on account of the cost to the ratepayers.—Mr. Derbyshire seconded the motion, which was carried unaniumusly.—Mr. Bancroft was instructed to proceed with the work according to his own discretion; and the meeting concluded.

div.head: FROD SHAM.
div.p: FROD SHAM.

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—The annual meeting on behalf of these missions was held in Trinity Chapel, on Thursday, when Mr. Thomas Norman, of Runcorn, pre- sided. There was a good attendance considering the very unfavourable weather. The Chairman expressed the hope that notwithstanding the unfavourable weather the meeting would be the best that had been held in Frodshim. He was very much interested in missionary WI:Mk. It w —L. work in which every oae c3uld take a part f- 'in the child in the Sur4ivc school .o !!!.`; '.(111.1t t:f. . mature .v age. He was pleased to see that tl.e children ill the 'Sabbath schools contributed so largely by their eartions to secd the Bible to the heathen. They could not all preach or make missionary speeches, but they could do their utmost to promote the cause. He trusted that from that night all would make up their minds to do more than they had done before.—The Rev. J. M. Bamford read extracts from the 64th annual report of the Auxiliary Missionary Society for the Liverpool district, and regretted that a very large deficit existed in the funds of the parent society. The amount collected daring the past year in the Frodsham circuit was £B4 9s. 10d., or an increase of .£1 170. over the previous year. lie confessed to being disappointed at the unfavourable weather, but felt convinced that the meeting would not prove a failure, as the chai•lnan and deputation, he was sure, would not fail in their duty, and the responsibility, therefore, rested with the congregation. If a little self-denial was practised, the meeting would be a success, and it was not up to the standard of Gospel .teaching if self-denial was not practised. He hoped that all would help forward the cause of Foreign Missions which benefited so many lives.—The Rev. Alfred Johnson, of Wrexham in a telling speech, re- viewed the difficulties which the Wrexham, had to contend with in carrying out the command to make disciplcs of all nations, and traced the progress and Buenas which had attended their preaching of the Gospel.—The Rev. Allen Rees, of London, the deputation appointed by the Confer- ence, in an eloquent speech, explained what had been accomplished by the Wesleyan Missionary Society since it commenced its labours, and dwelt upon the difficulties and prejudices which had to be contended with in different parts of the world.—The Rev. F. F. Edmunds proposed a vote of thanks to the collectors and deputation, which was seconded by the Rev. J. M. Bamford and agreed to.—A vote of thanks was also accorded to the Chairman on the motion of the Rev. J. M. Bamford, seconded by Mr. Turner. The collection amounted to £6 63. 9d.'

• MEETING OF THE BIBLE SOCIETY AT FRODSHAM.—The Frodsham brapch of the British and Foreign Bible Society held a meeting in the Town Hall, on Monday. The Rev. J. B. Blogg, vicar, presided, and on the platform were the Revs. J. Burbridge (deputation,) W. Knocker, E. Marsden, and J. Schofield. The Rev. E. Marsden read the report which showed that after defraying all expenses there was a balance of £5B 83. There had been £lO 133. 21. worth of books sold during the last year. The number of Testaments sold was 19, and of Bibles 82, being a total of 101, Wing double the number disposed of in the previous year. He desired to acknowledge the pleasure the committee felt at seeing Dr. Weaver present, and they were glad to find that he had recovered from his serious indisposition. (Hear, hear.) They trusted that he would show the same interest in the society as he had done heretofore. The committee desired to thank Mr. Dunsford and the lady collectors for the assistsnce they had rendered the society by taking the trouble to collect subscriptions. On the motion of the Chairman, the retiring committee was re-elected.—The Chairman said last year was the first time he had ever been present at a meeting of the Bible Society, and on that occasion he was very much struck with the address they had from the depu- tation. He was very much pleased to have been present and to help the society in any way be could. During the past year .he had rather been taken to task for doing so, but he could not see why a clergyman of the Church of England should refuse to support such a society. (Applause.) He bad no cause for regret and he felt that in attending that meeting he was only doing his duty. Referring to the revised version he saiUe believed it had had a very strong and powerful influenSlion the Christian world, and con- cluded by saying the Bible Soc'ety had his hearty support. The Rev. J. Burbridge gave an account of the working of the society, which has already appeared in these columns, and the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

THE ELECTION OF MAYOR.—It is rumoured in official quarters tl at there is some probability of our worthy Mayor, Alderman J. R. Pickmere, being again requested to accept office for another year. During his term of office as Chief Magistrate, Alderman Pickmere has won the esteem of all with whom he has come in contact, and his re-election to the mayoralty will give generally satisfaction. THE STORM AT WARRINOTON—The storm, which commenced on Wednesday, increased in violence on Thurs- day, and in the evening the wind rose to a gale, which continued, accompanied with heavy showers of rain, throughout the night. Yesterday the storm raged with unabated fury, and did considerable damage to property. Chimney pots and slates were loosened and blown down in all directions, rendering the streets exceedingly dangerous: and in many instances large squares of window glass were shattered, the window frame at a house in Arpley-street being completely blown in. A chimney stack at No. 2, Dixon-street, was blown down, and fell through the roof of the nest house, into a bedroom, the furniture in which was much damaged by the di,bris, which found a lodgment on the landing of the stairs. As may be imagined, a hole of considerable dimensions was made in the roof, and the por- ..tion that remained was swayed to and fro by the wind in a manner that portended its demolition. A portion of a chimney stack at 75, Butterrnarket-street, was blown into the street, and in Bewsey-street part of the roof at Litton's mill was destroyed. The ornamental tiles on Wycliffe Church also showed evidence of the force of the gale, as a large number of them were hurled into Edgeworth•street, damaging the roof of the church in their fail ; and in Rolleston-street a quantity of timber at Mr. Wright's yard was blown over, and partially demolished a wall abutting the footpath. Damage was also done to the trees and shrubs in the Park, several tall trees being torn up by the roots. The river has risen to an unusual height, and about three o'clock yesterday afternoon 20 feet of water was registered above Warrington Bridge.

div.head: MORE ATIRPSTS IN IRELAND.
div.p: MORE ATIRPSTS IN IRELAND.

Mr. J. P. Quin, assistant secretary of the National Land League, was arrested this morning, at his residence in Dublin, by a detective on a warrant signed by the Chief Secretary. A warrant has been issued for the arrest of Mr. Arthur O'Connor, M.P, for Queen's county, but up to the present he has not been come up with. Other arrests are expected.

div.head: SHOCKING DEATH FROM SUFFOCATION.
div.p: SHOCKING DEATH FROM SUFFOCATION.

Yesterday, at Flint, William Griffiths was walking across one of the saltcake pits at the Flint chemical works, when he slipped into the seething mass, and was instantly suffo- cated by the fumes of gas.

LAVERPOOL COTTON.—Spot : The demand has ages: been very good. but holders are free sellers at previous prices. Bales 12,000 bales, including I,COO on speculation or for export. The sa,es for the week have reached 69,580 bales. Spinners have taken 70,800 bales, including 6,210 forwarded direct. The im- 'port is 54,016 bales, including 28,432 American, The export is 4 688 bales. The stock is reduced 21,520 bales. The visible • supply is 357,610 bales more than at this time last year. LIVARPOOL PROVISIONS —Beef firm at the quotations. Bacon has rather more inquiry for the home trade, met freely by sellers. Pork dull and easier. Hams flat at previous rates. Shoulders slow of sale. Lard easier in value by 60. Cheese very dull. Butter inactive. Tallow steady. MANCHESTER COTTON.—Whatever the remon the market opens duller in tone than it closed yesterday. In some measure cotton reports, rough weather, and bad telegrarus from Cal- cutta are, no doubt, accountable for the change, which amounts to the total loss of any Imprcvement which was re- ported yesterday. Sellers are easier to deal with, but buyers h Ad aloof.

LIVICRPOOL CORN.—There was a moderato attendance at our Exchange to-day, but the market remained veryecpalet, and only a small business was transacted in wheat at a general decline of ld per cental since last Tuesday. Although the prices for flour was slightly weaker, there was not much in- quiry. Indian corn was very slow of sale at 63 to 8s Ofd for new mixed, 6s 2;cl to 63 4d per cental for round. Batas re- mained very quiet at late quotations; Egyptian gelling at is 10d to Bs, and mixed at is 9d to is 10d per cents'. P,as were dull at is 2.1 to is 3/d per cental. Oats audoat meal experienced very little demand; values unchanged.
WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT, THURSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Finnlkes.

DISPUTE ABOUT A SHEEP.—This Was an action in which John Cross, butcher, Corporation-street,'Warrington sued John Goodier, also a butcher, for £2 45. 6d., value of a sheep. Mr. Percy Davies, appeared for the plaintiff. and Mr. Slater (from the office of Messrs. Robert Davies and co.) for the defendant.—Mr. Davies stated that on the 10th January plaintiff went to Mr. Joseph Taylor's periodical sale. at the Norton Arms, and purchased amongst Oler cattle a pen of five sheep. The beasts were delivered on the day of sale, but he left the sheep in the yard after seeing they were marked with his private mark. Next morning plaintiff sent his son John for the sheep, and also five he had purchased at a previous sale. When plaintiff's son got to the yard he only found nine sheep, and afterwards went with a man in Mr. Taylor's employ to several slaughter-houses to look for the missing sheep. It was found in Zlelendant's slaughter- house, and plaintiff's son 'anted to take the animal away with him, but be. "was informed defendant was away frorn home, and 1013 man in charge weuld not let him take the ..a haver got tne aneep, anu ..as reasonau.. to suppose defendant had converted it to his own use.-- Plaintiff, his two sons, and another witness gave evidence in support of this statement. A witness named Tilley stated that the yard where the sheep were left was one from which a sheep could be taken away, or make its escape. A sheep escaped out of the yard after a sale a month ago.--Mrs. Taylor, wife of the auctioneer, having been called in refer- ence to an interview with the defendant's wife, His Honour said he did not see that there was a cave. The point in the case was identification of the sheep. Whether the yard was an open yard or closed yard did not matter much. The question was whether or not a sheep belonging to plaintiff get into defendant's possession. It might have got into, his possession quite innocently. If it had, and he refused it on demand, it would be evidence of conversion. But there was no evidence of it, because neither plaintiff's son nor tl.e man who picked out the sheep could identity it.-.... Judgment was therefore given for defendant. MASTER AND SERVANT'S CASE.—Mr. G. T. Illooore ap- peared for plaintiff, Thomas Samuel Weoliscroft, and Mr. T. J. Ridgway for defendant, Joseph Stott, farmer, Lymrn. —Mr. Moore said plaintiff claimed 15s, for five days' wages due and 21s. at the rate of 35. a day, for seven days' wages in lieu of notice. Defendant. who was a farmer in Lyrom, advertised for a teamsman, and came in contact with the plaintiff, who accepted his terms of 18s. a week, with a cot- tage free, and 2s. 6d. every time he went on a journey to Manchester. On the sth August plaintiff entered defendant's service and remained there four or five weeks. Defendant paid plaintiff for four weeks, and on the Bth or 9th Septem- ber plaintiff was dismissed without notice. He therefore claimed five days' wages for work done, and for which he had not received payment, and also a week's wages for being dis- charged without just cause.—Plaintiff in giving evidence, said he had been fined at the Lymm Petty Sessions for being drunk in charge of his horses, and was also summoned for using defamatory language to plaintiff.—His Honour could Rot see, on plaintiff's evidence, that there was any case. After the language used by plaintiff, defendant was justified in dismissing him, and le gave judgment for defendant. PLAINTIFFS AND THEIR DOM.—Daring the hearing of a case for groceries supplied, it transpired that a plaintiff had not brought her hooks, and hie Honour remarked this was the fourth or fifth case that had COW l‘efare him that day in which the plaintiffs had not thought fit to bring their books.—The Registrar said there had been several cases before him in which the parties did not even know the amount of claim.—His Honour said he could not see how the plaintiffs could expect to obtain judgment if they did not bring their books, and he would mark his sense of dis- approbation of these proceedings hy adjourning the case, and ordering the plaintiff to pay the defendant's costs. ACTION AGAINST A GLAZEBROOK FARMER—In this case the plaintiff, William Boardman, was represented by Mr. W. Whittingliam. of Leigh; and Mr. G. T. Moore ap- peared for the defendant, James Parsonage.—Plaintiff is a carrier residing at Farnworth, and the defendant a farmer living at Glazebrook. On the 31st August last the parties met and were introduced to each other in a public-house in Pendleton, and a conversation ensued which turned upen a mare which plaintiff had to sell. Plaintiff mentioned that the animal had been out to grass for some time and had been strained whilst carting, and the result of the conversation was that they entered into a bargain to the following effect: That the defendant should purchase the mare in question for the sum of £l5, and if at the end of one week the mare did not suit he was to return it, but if he did not he was to pay the price agreed upon. Nothing was heard for 12 days, and on the 12th September plaintiff sent an invoice for £l5 to defendant. On the following day defendant returned the mare, but it was refused; and as plaintiff said there was an actual contract within the meaning of the Statute of Frauds, he therefore brought the action.—Plaintiff and Mr. Lever, who introduced the parties, supported the above statement.—Deftndant was then called, and said he was to have the mare a fortnight on trial, and if it did not suit him he was to put it out to grass for plaintiff until November. —After being examined for a short time, Mr. Moore said be had COM to the conclusion the defendant was not in a fit state to give his evidence.—His Honour: He is not fit.— Mr. Moore said it was therefore his duty to plan the case in His Honour's bands and to suggest that the case be ad- journed.—His Honour: No, I can't do that. If defendant chooses to conduct himself in this way he must take the consequences of it. I cannot adjourn the case for a drunken man.—The case was then proceeded with, and a young man named Simpson, employed by the defendant, said he heard the conversation between plaintiff and defendant. Defendant was to have the mare on trial a fortnight. —Mr. Moore con- tended the sale was never concluded, and if the mare had suited defendant he would have had her. But as soon as defendant saw what the mare was he put her out to grass according to agreement.—His Honour could not disbelieve the evidence of Mr. Lever, an independent witnes, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

The annual meeting of the National Federation is to be held at Liverpool, on Tuesday, the 25th instant, and it is stated that Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., will address the meeting. The Warrington Liberal Association will meet on Friday next to elect delegates to attend the meeting. NEW VIADUCT AT EARLESTOWN.—The level crossing near the London and North-Western Railway Company's wagon works at Earlestown i 3 to be abolished and replaced 14 a cast iron viaduct. The iron work is being constructed by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., and on S.unday last two main girders, each weighing about 19 tons, were lifted into position over the main line. The viaduct consists of six spans, five being formed by cast iron girders and brickwork, and one by wrought iron girders and a wrought iron flooring. The total weight of the irodwork is about 300 tons. The largest span is across the main line, and is made by two main girders and 15 cross girders. The main girders are of the box description, and each girder is 63 feet 8 inches long, and 8 feet 6 inches deep.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON CONSTABLES.—MichaI Kelly and Ellen Lavelle were charged with being drunk and disor- derly in Bewsey-street, and with assaulting P.C. Chantler and others. Kelly was also charged with being absent with- out leave from the Bth Foot, stationed at Salford. About one o'clock on Sunday morning P.C. Evans was passing along Scotland-road, in plain clothes, when he heard the prisoners creating a disturbance, lie advised them to go home, when Kelly unfastened his belt and struck him on the shoulders. Evans struck prisoner on the arm with a I stick, and blew his whistle. P.C.'s Chantler and Street then i arrived, and Kelly " tupped " the former on the nose, and kicked him most violently, and he was "hardly able to lie in bed on the Sunday." Lavelle also kicked him on the legs. Both prisoners were drunk and assaulted the three officers. Prisoners had to be carried down to the police station.—Mr. Hunt said he was at the station when the pri- soners were brought.in, and he never heard worse language used.--Kelly stated Evans was the assailant, and struck him with a stick.—Prisoners were committed to gaol for a month hard labour. DREADFUL ATTACK UPON A BAILIFF WITH A CLEAVER.— John Loughlin, a middle-aged man, was charged with having unlawfully assaulted Were. Burrows, a county court bailiff.—Mr. Percy Davies who prosecuted, said that on Saturday, the let inst., at 7-'3O p.m., Burrows 'sent to execute a warrant on the prisoner at his father-in-law's house, in Bakehouse-yard, Latchford. When informed of the bailiff's intention, prisoner threatened to split his head open if he laid a hand on him; and with an iron cleaver which he held in his hand struck a most savage blow at the officer. Had not Burrows partially parried the blow with his arm, there was no doubt the blow would have killed him. It, however, struck him under the eye, making a gash from which blood flowed freely, and rendered him senseless. A man named. Astbury entered the house, "jumped upon" the prisoner, and ' took the cleaver from him. Prisoner with much malice then rushed upon Burros s, who was "dazed," and with his clenched hand, knocked him to the floor, kicking him most savagely. A severe struggle took place, but the war- rant was not executed. It was very fortunate that the ' prisoner had not been charged with murder. Burrows wished for the protection of the Bench in • a case of this sort.—Burrows confirmed his advocate's statement and said his head and legs were still sore with the blows which were showered upon him.—P.C. Lawrence said he apprehended the prisoner on Sunday. When he entered the father-in-law's house prisoner pre- tended to be either asleep or drunk, and his mother-in-law said his name was James Cummins' but Burrows recognised him. Prisoner said "I am sorry I did not give him as much more. I didn't give him half enough."—The Mayor said it was a dreadful attack upon a man who was doing hi duty, and he was only sorry that the law did not allow the Bench to inflict a heavier penalty.—Prisoner was fined £5, or a month's imprisonment in default. Ile was also bound over to keep the peace for 12 months, himself in £2O and two ' sureties in £lO each or two months' additional imprisonment. ...Prisoner went to gaol. William Preston, and Bridget Fleming. • DISGRACEFUL FEVER Bridget Nixon, keeifer of a *, •registered lodging-house in Edward-street, was charged with ' keeping more lodgers than allowed by the Sanitary Cons- ' mittee. Inspector Church said be visited the house on the sth inst., and there were 11 persons in the house, four per- *--, . sons being in a room only adapted for one. The house was only registered for ten persons. Defendant was ordered to co. pay chsts.—John Monaghan was fined 103. and costs for keeping an unregistered lodging-house. The house was only adapted for seven persons, and there were 11 persons inhabiting it. —Patrick Flynn was charged with taking lodgers without having his house registered. Inspector Norman said the defendant occupied the house 56, Gaskell's Yard, which was without thorough ventilation. When he visited the house on the 2nd October there were, in two rooms, 11 persons grouped together, without any regard to age or sex, whilst the house was only adapted for four per- sons. Sinenhis visit a malignant case of scarlet fever had . broken out In the house, and had been removed to the hospital.--Councillor Crosfield (to defendant): So the lives of the inhabitants are to be sacrificed because you break the . law in this manner !—The Mayor said it was a most dis- graceful case. It was through crowding houses ia this , . manner that people suffered from fever. Defendant was .fined 20s and costs, or in default a month. Prisoner met witness in the street some time ago, and accosting him professed to give information of the p ' w ereabonts of Morris. He did not know prisoner personally, and he believed it was done to throw the police off the scent. P.C. Bowen said he apprehended the prisoner in Wishaw, Lanarkshire, Scotland, where he had been working for twelve months.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for three months ' With hard labour. LOUCH. An interesting meeting, which was well attended, was held he 'Sf- eMetry'ef, Mission Church, Warrington, under the presideney •of Mr. H. B. White. The occasion was the presentatien. to the Rev. Thomas Louch, curate of Holy Trinity Church, of a handsome inkstand, inlaid with yr, a stenographic pen, and a purse containing £2O lie. The inkatand,bore the following inscription:—" Presented to the Rev. Thollras Loucb, together with a purse of money, by the congregation and friends of Holy Trinity ani St. Mary's Churches, Warrington, October 101.1; 1881." For two years I Mr. Louth has. laboured ,in connection with St. Ifary's I branch of Holy Trinity . parish, and his earnestness, kind- nessl and affability have, won for him the regard of all sections of the parishioners. The Cnatitetaist said whert,he wad, asked to take the chair that night he consented to do so 'with very great pleasure, because if he could contribute in any way to evincing the esteem felt by the parishioners of :St. Mary's district towards the Rev. Mr. Louch on his leaving them; he was only too glad to be able to do so. Mr. Louch must be grati- fied to find that there were so many who took an interest in. him and in his future, and who went there that night to express their feelings towards him, and bid him God speed. in his future career. (Hear, hear.) He called upon Mr.' Ray to make the presentation. Mr. Ray had been a most. able assistant to Mr. Leuch, and a more fitting person could not have been appointed to perform this pleasieg duty. (4planse.), Mr. WALTER RAY said the subject whicla was brought prominently before them that night was change. It was a strange thing, but look where they would, everything was stamped with change. If they looked at nature, every day gave new phases of the same thing. Spring gave way to sunamer, summer to autumn, and autumn to winter. Changes occurred day by day, hour by hour; circumstances never twice looked the same. There were changes in ourselves, in our circumstances; our own body was continually Changing. Thbrefore it was no wontler that we should be brought in contact with a change of circumstances and conditions of those that were about us. They were met in a rather sorrowful mood at haying to part with one who had been to them as good as a father. (Hear, hear.) He went to them a young man fresh from college, with a determination to do his duty, to speak feelingly and openly; where he saw there was need of correction he would 'Administer that correction, where he saw a need of praise and encouragement he gave it. And so it had been that they had got on together very well. When he first went he told them that he certainly was not favourably impressed with the place. He saw the atmosphere was rather smoky, and said to himself, "I am afraid I shall not like this place ;" but when he got amongst the people, to know them, and be known by them, he found that there was a great deal more to be admired in the Bank Quay district than he had ever dreamt of. The people knew how to appreciate a good man; and although they might be poor they were always ready to stretch forth a hand to help him, and give him encouragement in the work he had to do. Now he was going to change his parish, and they were going to change their minister. It had come upon them rather unexpectedly. Until a few weeks ago they bad not dreamt of any such thing as change in that direction; they had been flattering themselves that there could not be such a thing as separa- tion. But, alas for human hopes, something came across the path. He did net know whether it was a prospect of future greatness, or whether he looked upon removal from there as a stepping stone to something better,' or that he thought he could do more good in another district than he was doing there. He must have some good in view or else, he would not have left them; and it was as the rending of sensitive cords to tear himself away. He I (Mr. Ray) hoped Mr. Leuch would for ever remember his connection with St. Mary's. In order to make him do so, and to show their appreciation of his worth, the parishioners had voluntarily subscribed towards the pur- chasing of a memento of his departure. Those who had I -much bad given according to their means, and those who had little had contributed their mite, and it would please afr. Lunch to know that all had been given with that hearty 1 good feeling that made anything acceptable to the recipient. (Hear, hear.) He left Warrington with the hearty good ' wishes of everyone that dwelled in the district, not only of Church people, but of those who differed from them in points of faith; for all had admired him. The little 1 'differences they had had only cemented them the closer to- I 1 gether, for they felt that in their differences there was agree- I ment. He always acted as a brother and a gentleman, and it was with the greatest sorrow and regret that they were parting with. him that night. '(Hear, bear.) He asked hint in the names of the parishioners of Holy Trinity and St. Mary's Churches to accept that inkstand, pen, and pursi containing money as a small token of the esteem in which they held him, and their best wishes for his future welfare. NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. A. VOTE V.NDEII DlrrtenurrEs.—At Newton Petty SessionS, on Saturday, a man named Ratcliffe was summoned for being drunk and disorderly at the Revising Barrister's Court, at Newton.—P.C. 336 stated that defen- dant was very disorderly and would not be quiet. The Re- vising Barrister ordered defendant to be quiet, but he would not do so, and witness was told to put him out.—Defendant said he came to claim his vote. He had been objected to year after year, and had always to be put to the trouble of coming before the Court to claim it. He was annoyed at this, and thought it was getting a vote under difficulties. He had not much drink, but was excited because they were ' " chaffing " him. He wished to leave the room, but the policemen would not let him out.—He called a witnnas, who stated that he was not drunk, but only excited.—The Bench gave defendant the benefit of the doubt, and dismissed the Case. FIJNEILAI Or TIIE LATE Ma. S. H. BIIaLE:Y.—Th(II remains:of the late Mr. J. H. Birley were interred on Satursi day at St. Peter's Church, Newton, amid every dentOnstra- tion of respect and esteem. The body was enclosed in two I coffins made by Messrs. S. and R. Johnson, of Warrington, the outer one being of oak panelled with ebony and heavily mounted with brass. The coffin was literally covered with wreaths and crosszs of white flowers, and was carried with- out pall by the, workmen of the deceased to the church, followed by Mr. Frank Birley, Miss Birley, and Mr. W. Birley, sons and daughter of the deceased, as chief mourners, Mr. Birley, M.P. and there were also present Mr. Gooch, Colonel McCorquOciale, Mr. Wood, Mr. James Fairclough, Mr. Winstanley, Mr. Worsley, Mr. Brierley, Mr. H. Hough- ton,"Mr. Crabtree, Mr. Pearson, .LP., Mr. Houghton, J.P., the Rev- J. Sherlock, the Rev. H. Siddall, the Rev. Richard Smith, rector of Lowton ; the Rev. J. Carson, Winwick ; the Rev. T. C. Quirk, rector of Golborne; the Rev. T. R. Matthews, Earlestown ; the Rev. 3. Whitley', Wargrave ; and Messrs. Gillespie, R. Davies (Warrington), Borrow, Thomas Stone, John Stone and D. Stone, Brewis, Lowe, Stock, Thomson, and John Jones, Mere House Newton. A number of Iworkmen assembled at the gate and followed the cortege to the church with heads uncovered. The streets were crowded with spectators, who manifested the greatest respect to the memory of the deceased. The funeral cortege was met at the church by the Rev. H. Monk, and his curate, the Rev. W. B. Sham. _The funeral service was most impressively read by Mr. Monk and Mr. Sisam, and the hymn, "When our beads are bowed with woe," sung by the choir in a solemn manner.— At the Newton Petty Sessions, before the commencement of the business, Colonel McCorquodale said he was sorry to have to state what was now generally known, that their friend and colleague, Mr. Birley, was no more amongst them. He paid a high tribute to his memory and to the manner in which he had acted as a magistrate. They would all feel his loss, and he would feel it very much personally. They would not see the face of their late friend, Mr. Birley, in this world again; and it would be very difficult to replace him and repair the loss. The Colsnel appeared to be very much affected.—The other justices on the Bench concurred in what bad been said by the Chaim-mgt.—Mr. Moore, on be- half of the legal profession said they offered their sincere sympathy to the widow and children of the late late Mr. Birley. They had always experienced kindness and courtesy at his hands, and they all deeply deplored his loss. He would be missed in various ways. He was always on the I spot, and ever ready to perform his duties as a magistrate. To the cases that came before him he always paid great at- tention, and always did his best to sift out the truth. He always showed the poor great kindness; and though it was not generally known, it very often happened that when per- sons came to him who had cases against them in court, if he thought legal assistance was required and the parties were not aloha to provide it, he would engage a solicitor himself to appear in the case so that justice might be done. They- would miss him as a magistrate; but the poor would miss him as a kind and generous friend; ad the people of New- ton would that day follow the remains of departed worth with feelings of sorrow and signs'of mourning to their last resting place.—Mr. White (the Clerk to the Magistrates), on behalf of Mr. Buckton and himself, also expressed his re- gret at the death of Mr. Birley.—Mr. Swift (St. Helens), the only other solicitor present, endorsed all that had been said Mr. Moore.

"LONDON, AND LeNDON LIFE." , INTERESTING LECT' . CBE AT WIDNES. On Tuesday evening a ver- the Rev. J. Billington, f interesting lecture was de- livered in the Zion School- room, Oakland-street, Widnes, by i " chair was o? . Runcorn, on "'London and London lire. The cha oCcupied by Mr. Richard Webster. In commencing his had such a meititu'e of i acture' Mr. Billington said that London aspects that t was a subject always new. It was not a study for an evening, but a lifetime. It was a volunae finger of time which was being constantly written by the same new ir , day by day bringing some new phase, adding j ect for ti'Aerest, and opening to the light some new sub- dffer!ta t .ought. It was a different place in the eyes of some i . people each one viewing it through the medium of „A. Articular pursuit. It was the world's city, and cone- Aended the whole human life in all its varieties—the aggar, the millionaire, the honest tradesman, and the dis- reputable thief, together with representatives of every nation, and people, and language, making it a veritable Babel. Law-makers and law-breakers, wealth and want, virtue and vice, all found a place in the vast metropolis, constituting it a study at once inexhansted and inex- haustible. London was continually undergoing a process of change. Explorers were needed to pry into the mysteries of the great city, and the maps and guide books required as frequent alteration as the almanac. As a proof of the ex- pansive nature of London traffic, he might state that it was supposed that, when the Metropolitan Railway was opened, all the city and Paddington omnibuses would be run off the ground, but although it carried forty-three millions of passengers in one year, it had been found neces- sary to increase the number of omnibuses on the southern route. It was more dangerous to walk the streets of Lon- don than to travel by railway or to cross the Atlantic. In the year 1874, 125 persons were killed and a larger number injured by vehicles in the streets. Other tokens of the immensity of the population were that 750,000 business men left the city every evening for their suburban residences. There were 10,000 police- men and as many cab-drivers, and the same number of per- sons connected with the post-office. When London made a holiday there were several places of resort, such as the Crystal Palace, the Zoological Gardens, Kew Gardens, etc., which absorbed from thirty to fifty thousand visitors each. The cost for lighting London was t 2,500,000 annually; the water supply 100,000,000 gallons per day, and 314 daily and weekly newspapers were required. What London would eventually become it was idle to predict. It already stood in four counties and was fast striding on to a fifth. So he might go on detailing facts and figures, and at last have to give up in despair saying with the Queen of Sheba, "the half has not been told me." Whatever', the future of the metropolis might be the past history might soon be told. Although the true origin was unknown, it was probably founded in days long prior to the Christian era. In the reign of the Roman emperor Nero it was a place of considerable importance. Proofs of the occupation of London by the Romans were seen in •the remains of buildings, tesselated pavements, coins, rings, and earthenware, which had been dug up in the heart of the city. At the conquest London submitted to William the Conqueror, who was crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day, 1066. In 1218 the forest of Middlesex was cleared, and buildings began to appear north of the river. In the fifteenth century lamps were used to illuminate the streets, the principal of which were paved, and in the same century wooden houses gave place to brick buildings. The year 1604 was notable for the horrible conspiracy called the gunpowder plot; and in 1665 the great plague occurred. For more than twelve months this pestilence raged, mocking alike the skill of the physician and the exertions of the gravedigger, who stood aghast, spade in hand, before the increasing piles of corpses waiting to be buried out of sight. The plague swept away rich and poor, the strong man and the youth, until not only families, but whole streets were empty. Business was so completely stopped that grass grew in many of the streets. Such were a few phases of the calamity,that in one year swept away 100,000 sduls. The year following this catastrophe they found that what in history iet called "The fire of London," broke out. It began on the morning of Sunday, Septembcr 22nd, 1666, and raged, with irresistable fury for four days and nights, swallowing up many buildings, churches Jtc. It laid bare a space equal to 336 acres, and destroyed property to the value of £10,000,000. In many respects, however, this fiery scourge was a blessing to the populace, for afterwards an Act of Parliament was passed for the rebnilding of the city, which took place within four years, commodious and healthy dwellings taking the place of filthy and unwholesome houses. Frightful havock was committed in the year 1700, when the Gordon riots took place, and the mob were in possession of the city 4or two days. Since that time the peace had never been seriously disturbed, and the improvements which had been effected during the present century were of greater impor- tance than any which had preceded them. London was bne of the healthiest of the large cities of Europe, and there were few places in the kingdom where less rain fell. In the beginning of winter it was often enveloped in dense fogs, which sometimes were the cause of great danger, and almost entirely stopped the traffic. The young streejkArabs turned them to good account in guiding people home, by the light of torches, for which service they cfaimed a few coppers as payment. The river Thames was spanned by nine bridges for foot passengers and vehicles, and six railway bridges. The chief one—London bridge—was 56 feet in width, and it was supposed that no fewer than 8,000 foot- passengers and 900 vehicles passed over it ever hour. Below Londoeßridge were the docks and wharfs, in which were to be found vessels of every flag,, hailing from almost every port in the world. Above the bridr the steamboats plied for the convenience of the masses. The passengers on board one of these 'would furnish food for a study in them- selves. London was, not the vrildern ss of bricks and mortar country people sometimes imagine lit to be. It abounded in parks, squares. and gardens which were some- times surrounded by splendid residences The west end had the greatest share of these. He was g' ‘d to say that the poor were not neglected. lathe east r • of the city there was the Victoria Park, a most beautiful ,ot, with well laid- out flower beds and spacious recreation ;rounds. London was thickly studded with public buildh..3, halls, and insti- tutions, each of which would afford ma t‘r for more than one lecture. His remarks, however, w • rid be incomplete without reference to the inhabitants of the mighty city. It was a very common thing to find several familes living in the same house, as the rents were so high. One feature of the street life pleased him wh'en he visited the metropolis, viz,, the almost total absence of oaths and profanity amongst the ordinary foot passengers. Some of the streets were sights worth beholding. Taking the outside of a 'bus along Cheap- side, one was struck with the idea of being in an inextricable maze, but a little patience and the skill of the driver would take them out in an incredibly short time. Much might be said about the various occupations that were constantly carried on in the streets. Time would not permit him to dwell upon any one of those subjects, which were so numer- ous. There was the crossing sweeper' who could often tell a sad story of reduced income; the flower girls, who had perhaps been out early in the morning to cull the flowers of which the Londoners were so fond, and then there was that public nuisance, the organ-grinder. Then came the professional mendicants, many of whom deluded the people with their sad stories and by exhibiting ugly wounds, which were, however, frequently merely clever works of art. Com- ing to the religious phase of the subject, the lecturer said that a man might worship God according to the dictates of his own coiascience in London, for there was every imaginable branch of the Christian Church to be found there. Street preaching was very prevalent in the summer time, and ssmetimes very strange places were used for the purpose. The thought was a very sad one that there were so many in the city who tramped, with weary feet, the cold and pitiless streets, spending long hours of the day in some- times fruitless efforts to earn a few coppers with which to buy a crust and hire a dirty bed in some filthy garroter cellar, and when they failed in the attempt they were forced to spend the dreary night beneath some lonely arch. Yet, while their hearts went out in sympathy for these, they ought to feel grateful to Him from whom they received daily bread, and the ten thousand little, yet all necessary comforts of life. (Applause.) The proceedings concluded with 'a rote of thanks to Mr. Billington, who was frequently applauded. •

A BRUTAL HUSBAND RIGHTLY SERVED.—Michael Carney, a labourer, whs charged on remand with unlawfully wounding his wife Margaret. on Saturday night.—On the prisoner being brought up on Monday, the wife made a statement to the effect that after twelve o'clock on SaturdaY night she went to fetch her husband out of a neighbour's house.' She spoke to him about it being time that he was at home, and asked him how it was that te was out at that time of the night, when he hit her in the mouth with his fist, loosening several of her teeth, and then threw the salt cellar at her, cutting the left side of her face.—Complainant now said that the wound on the side of her face had been caused through her falling against the wall, and not by her husband striking her with the salt cellar.—Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, reminded her of the statement she had made on the Monday, but she adhered to what she had said.—Superintendent Barker (to complainant): Why did you give that salt cellar to the policeman if your hus- band had not struck you with it? Because I was in a passion. —Answers the question, what was the reason you gave it him? Because I found it on the floor.—P.C. Thom said that about one o'clock on Sunday morning he went to the house where the complainant was, and found she had a cut on the left side of the face, and blood was flowing from it and her mouth. She was present when he took the prisoner into custody, and stated that her husband had hit her in the mouth with his fist, and also thrown the salt cellar at her. On charging the man with having done these, he said, "All right."--John Lally was called for the defence, and said it was his house into which the complainant came on the night of the alieged assault. She blackguarded her husband, lon which he struck her in the face and she fell against the swab. He could not say what gave her the cut on the eye. —Mr. Gossage: Prisoner, .there is no doubt that you struck your wife in a most unprovoked manner, and you will be committed to gaol one month, with hard labour. • STEALING A LOAF AT PRESCOT.—John Howard, a tramp, was sent to gaol seven days for stealing a loaf from the shop of Mr. Philip Reichardt, baker, Prescot.—The manager to . the prosecutor saw the man walking out of the place, with something bulky under his clothes, and, on stopping him, I found the loaf in his possession. ALLEGED CASE OF GROSS INGRA-TITUDE.—A respectably dressed young womarf named Louisa Nicholson, was charged with stealing, on the 10th inst., two gold rings, one silver ,brooch, a silk scarf, a purse, and a penknife, value 275. 6d., the property of Mr. Wm. Harascow, of Halton-view.—The wife of the prosecutor stated that on the 10th inst. the prisoner came to her house, and stated that she had been working at Warrington, but she was then without a home, and should be very much obliged if she would let her stay there. She consented, and the prisoner remained until the morning of the 10th inst., when she decamped, taking the things with her.—Mr. John R. Carver, manager to Mr. Thomas Greaves, Church-street, Warrington said that on the 10th inst. the prisoner brought him a scarf pin and gold keeper, upon which he advanced her 2s. 6d.—The manager to Mr. J. B. Imison, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road, said that on Monday she brought two wedding rings to the shop, and he advanced ss. upon them.—P.C. Strickland proved appre- hending the prisoner at - Warrington, on Tuesday, and she admitted having stolen some of the things.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

• • -- • -- - --- TEMPERANCE MEETING AT ,OTETL.—In connection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Littler Over, a Band of Hope meeting was held on Tuesday, when a host of speakers recommended the principles of Rechabitism, especially in reference to the young, who Can be thus got to practice thrift and temperance at the same time. • • • • •

WINSFORD IMPROVEURNTS.—The manner in which the Winsford Local Board does its work is an evidence that its desire is the conciliation and satisfaction of all, or the greatest portion, of the ratepayers. The main streets are being macadamised, and the causeways are being paved except here and there, and those parts are to be included in the forthcoming estiroates,-and will be done as speedily as will be convenient no doubt.

Those officers are sent by the "General," and are billet ted on the local friends, who sustain them by collections, and thus the movement keeps afoot. - - - Fizonsusst Vastest, SoarrY.—A public meeting was held in the girls' school, Church-street, on Friday, to receive and consider the report of a provisional committee appointed at a previous meeting as to the prospects of the successful formation of a musical society for Frodsham. The Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., presided, and there were also present, Mrs. C. Reynolds, Misses Latham, Ashley, James, Chat- loner, Potts, Birtles; Messrs. J. Bolderstone, C. E. Linaker, H. G. Linaker, Thomas Riley, Samuel Davies, George Riley, Peter Riley, Henry They, T. Fairhurst, H. E. Heyweod, W. C. Collinson, P. Nickson, John Stead Rimmer, B. A. Rigby, George Sharrock, Major Corker, and others. The committee subrhitted a list of 80 persons who were desirous of joining a musical society, when it was unanimously resolved that a society be formed, called the Frodsham Musical Society. The hon. sec, to the committee, Mr. Thomas Riley, read correspondence which had taken place between himself and Mr. Argent, of Birkenhead. After some discusior, the subscription was fixed at ss. per annum, and the girls' school, Church-street, was selected as the place for weekly rehearsals. The following officers and committee of management were appointed :—President, Rev. H. B. Blogg, ' M.A., -vicar ; hon. secretary and treasurer, Mr. Thomas ; Riley ; committee, Mrs. Charles Reynolds, Mrs. Col- linson ; Miss James; Messrs. Henry Tiley, GeorgAtiley, T. Fairhurst, and J. S. Rimmer. SfAnR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETII.—A lecture was Riven in the Town Hall, Frodsharn, on Wednesday, by Mr. W. Bancroft, on Starr-Bowkett Building Societies, their rules, working, and advantages. Mr. Thomas Davies, builder, Frodsham, presided, and there were about fifty persons pre- sent.—The lecturer explained, in a very lucid manner, the rules of the society, by which if a member paid sixpence per week for each £lOO share he would be entitled to take part in the ballot on the next apropriation, when, if successful, the amount of his share would be advanced without interest for a period of 121 years, repayable by instalments, the first quarterly instalment being due five months after the date of appropriation. The amount received might be invested in actual building, or onbnilding in course of erection ' • and power was given in the rules to sell an appropriation to the society or to the highest bidder. The amount of weekly payment on each share have to be paid until it amounted to the sum of £27 Gs., which would take 21 yew s to accom- plish, in which time the society would be brought to a ter- mination, and the amount of weekly subscriptions returned to each member, and if any balance remained in hand as the profits of the society, it would be distributed as a divi- dend to the members in proportion to 'the number of shares held. The lecturer contended that in addition to being ran encouragement to thritrand self-help, the contribution to the society was a good investment, which fact ha demon- strated. The principle upon which the Starr-Bowkett Societies were worked was co-operation, and much could be attained by its means which would otherwise be impossible to workingmen. div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

_ At a meeting of this Committee accounts amounting to £2lB 15s. id. were examined and recommended to the Board for payment. On account of manual labour and team labour there had been paid :—Main roads, £l5 13s. 7d.; district roads, £173 19s. Id.; total, £412 15s. Bd. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £1,209. 11/NPAID CALLS. -

The CL Enx said the calls for Barnton, Halton, and Walton Inferior had not been paid, and on the motion of the Cairn- XAN, the Clerk was instructed to take proceedings if the arrears were not paid in a fortnight.

div.head: – ENCROACHMENTS ON-THE HIGHWAY.
div.p: - ENCROACHMENTS ON-THE HIGHWAY.

The SURVIC-7017resented a report as to the alteration and forming of fences in the Board's district, pointing out an encroachment on the road at Preston Brook.—Mr. Masou said these encroachments ought not to be allowed. Mr. Lyon, of Dorothy Farm, Stretton, had encroached upon the road, but he had no doubt, if asked, he would allow them some land to make an improvement.—A MEMBER: The road is 30 feet wide.—Mr. MASON: They seem to think that if it is 30 feet wide the Board have no right to interfere. It is a good fault to have a road too broad.—The CHAIRMAN said the jurisdiction of the Board was from fence to fence, and if the Surveyor saw any alteration in fences being made he ought to inform the parties they did it at their peril. The Board should have plans as to what alterations were intended.—Mr. Masort proposed that a committee be ap- pointed to see Mr. Lyon and endeavour to get a little land to improve the read.—The CHAIRMAN: He has not en- croached where you mention but the Committee can say, "You have taken certain portion from Stretton Highway, cannot you give us a little here."—The motion was seconded and carried, Messrs. Barber, Parr, and Mason being ap- pointed.
A. BROOK IN THE ROAD.

Mr. TROIKAS Slant BURGESS, sub-agent to Sir Gilber Greenall, appeared before the Board with reference to the brook in Rose Wood-lane, Walton Superior, and said Sir Gilbert Greenall had intimated his intention of giving a subscription towards defraying the cost of diverting its course and erecting a bridge, but "like all wise then he had changed his mind, and doubted whether it would be wise unless other landowners did so in proportion. The brook was a very dangerous place, and there had been many an accident there. At present it ran along the road for a dis- tance of 112 yards, there being a footpath on one side. Sir Gilbert would give what was necessary for its improvement, but he brought it before the Board on public grounds. Did rfot the Board thing it a dangerous place; that it required improving; and were not the Guardians of the Poor liable for the same.—Mr. BENNETT : I say no. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BURGESS said the cost would be from £5O to £l2o.—The CLERK: I don't see what we have to do with the brook at all.—Mr. BARBER: It ought to have been done 30 years ago. There has been a great many accidents tlywe.—Mr. PARR said the brook required no bridge, but it offght to be culverted if Sir Gilbert would allow them to go through his I land.—Mr. BURGESS said Sir Gilbert would allow a cutting to be made though his land.—Mr. WILKINSON said Cox- shall's at Comberbach 'Was much worse ; it took horses off their feet; and if they took steps in one they would have to do both.—The CHAD:maw said the Board were not in a position to do anything at present. They must have plans and an estimate of the cost, and some arrangements made between the different landowners as to the exchange of land; then it would be for. the Board to say whether they would build a bridge or not.—Mr. CLIEFE : I say the Board ought not to build a bridge. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. PARR: Well that brook is impassable when it overflows.—Mr. WILKINSON: There is another road not far round where you can always pass.—Mr. MASON thought that brock and Cox- shall's brook wanted putting right.—Mr. WILKINSON: I move that the landowners put the road in proper repair, and then we take it—(laughter)—and keep it in repair.—The CruarateN : The brook was in this state before the Board existed.—Mr. MASON: But we are a Board now and the brook is dangerous—Mr. WILKINSON: No more than it always was.—Mr. WEIR: It doesn't require a bridge. The thing can be remedied at a cost of nth—The CHAIRMAN informed Mr. Burgess that the landowners must come before the Board with all arrangements as to the exchange of land made, and plans of what was proposed to be done drawn to scale ; and the meeting terminated.

div.head: BAZAAR AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: BAZAAR AT ST. HELENS.

On Monday a three days' bazaar was ,opened by His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the Primitive Methodist School-room, Kirkland-street. For some time past the worshippers at the Primitive Methodist Chapel have been endeavouring to wipe off the debt on the West- field-street chapel, which encumbers them, and which amounts to about £l,OOO. The chapel was erected at a cost of £2,500 five years ago, and by means of lectures and other meetings, and through the benevolence of some of our pro- minent townsmen, 03 debt was reduced to £l,OOO. To further reduce the encumbrance a bazaar WAS projected, which was originally intended to be held last Easter, but it was found necessary to postpone it. Some of the friends and members of the chapel assiduously exerted themselves to accumulate a stock of goods while others instituted and sustained a canvass of the neighbourhood, the result of which has proved very satisfactory. At half-past two on Monday' His Worship the Mayor, arrayed in his gold chain, took up a position on the platform; and after singing and prayer, The Rev. T. WiLsrasw said he was sure they would all be delighted to know that they bad in their midst the chief Magistrate of that borough. (Applause.) Alderman Harri- son had shown very warm interest in connection with the affairs of that bazaar and the endeavours they were making to liquidate the debt on thetr chapel. Of course they all knew how he took the chair for them at one of their lectures in November or December ; and he then said he hoped they would go heartily into the matter, and promised his full sympathy and support. He was very pleased to stT His Worship the Mayor present, and they would give him a hearty welcome. (Applause.) The speaker said that the object of the bazaar was the reduction of a debt of £l,OOO remaining on the chapel in Westfield-street. Towards its reduction Majors W. W. and R. Pilkington had, in addition to valuable assistance previously given, offered a donation of £5O on condition that £5OO is raised. Messrs. Canning- ton and Shaw had offered a donation of £25 on the same conditioa, Colonel Gamble £lO, Mr. Walker £lO, and Mr. B. B. Glover bad promised to give the last £lO of the £5OO. The following list would represent somewhat the support from outsiders, in addition to the foregoing : Mr. B. B. Glover, £10; Major Bramwell, £6 103. ; Atder- man Cook, £6 • Messrs. Thomas Cook, ;D. He had never in'pre- vious times been more encouraged with a general canvass than he bad been during the last three months, and it was worth all the toil and effort to have the kind wishes and sympathy of the various gentlemen who had been waited upon. (Applause.) The Mayon, who WAS received with ipplause said that when he was requested by their pastor to open that bazaar, he thought, as mayor of the town, it was part of his duty to do what he could to help forward the movement and promote the object in view; and that was the reduction of the debt upon the chapel. (Hear, hear.) It would afford him great gratification, and not only him, but their minister and the congregation, if the efforts now made succeeded.
