div.p: TRA VEL§ IN THE EAST.

BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE G73TLEMAN. ISpnciarn] NO. XX. LERONAII TO NABLOUS. We were sheltering from the burning sun under the open saloon tent when Mr. El. Carry was int-educed by Mr. Hoelen. He very cocrteously offered to go with us to see the Samaritan MSS. of the Pentateuch. Through filthy, stinking archways-and narrow streets, in which we had to pick our steps between heaps of refuse, he led the way to the ynagogne. We had to wait a few minutes in the small I courtyard adjoining (in which an orange tree was growing laden with fruit), while one of the children ran to bring the High Priest. He was-in no hurry to make hie appearance. When at last he came we beheld a handsome but pensive ; looking Jew, about 35 or 40 years of age, who professes be a lineal descendant cf Samballat, who set cp a temple, le and worship in opposition to Nehemiah and Ezra,, they a the rebuilding of the tennple and city of jermsa we m wives. y re- The quired the people to put away their strange gentleman first brought out . from behind a calico screen, which spanned a recess in one of the plainest and barest of edifices, a covered reit. On Mr. El. c arry objecting, he went back, and while he was absent Mr. EL Carry remarked that he was going to deceive us by exhibiting a sae simile of the more ancient one. When the real MSS. appeared, we found it composed of two large rolls festered together and covered with crimson, but leaving exposed a few lines of the text. With a complacent smile the High Priest told us the MSS. was 3,472 years old. Of course we smiled in re- turn, a smile of incredulity. Mr. El. Carry, standing in the place of an interpreter, gave a version very different to the original words. He said, quite audibly, that it probably dated back to the fourth century of the Christian era. The interview was closed by this high sacerdotal dignitary • haggling with our guide as to the amount of " backsheesh " he was entitled to, not losing hia hold until some addition .was made to a very liberal bonne. Mr. El. Carry then con- ducted us to his own house and introduced us into a large airy room furnished in Eastern style, with broad divan seats all round, and large square cushions reared at the back. Thic room, he said was used for meetings on the Lord's day, for mothers' meetings through the week, and for a general reception room. The little church over which he presides, has a membership of fifteen baptised believers. Mr. and Mrs. El. Carry have about sixty girls under tuition, and are anxious to build a place for schools and worship. He had raised about £250 to which our party added about £23. We spent every pleasant evening in listening to the many thrilling incidents he had to relate of his mis- sionary life. Mr. El. Carry accompanied us to the summit of Gerieziin the same evening. A more difficult ascent on horseback it would be difficult to imagine. The loose stones and precipitous paths made it a perfect scramble. But the view we bad from this grandly situated mountain amply repaid us, if it did not the poor ponies for the toil of ascend- ing. Seated on the top of an old tower within the ruins of a castle, dating back to the time of Justinian, and elevated 2,850 feet above the sea level, we looked round upon a lands- cape which, once seen, can never be forgotten. The sky above was an unbroken vault of blue with but " one little cloud no bigger than a man's hand." The whole area of Palestine, -from Dan to Eeerskeba, seemed to he within the range of our vision. Just below was the beautiful plain, divided into squares and oblong patches of the brightest green, and the richest brown; far beyond the hills by which the plain was; bounded rose the purple mountains of Gilead and Moab over the Galilean hills to the left, the snow-clad peak of Hermon was shining like silver in the rays of the declining sun; Away to the south the hills of Samaria and Judea receded in an interminable perspective of sober grey; while stretched out behind us was the valley of Shechem, with its mountain ranges on each side ending in the deep blue waters of the Mediterranean sea. We raw, on the top of the mount, the altars and stone erec- tions on which the sect of the Samaritans had been sacrific- ing the week before. They go up once a year to the number of 120, and tent out for a week, preparatory to the Feast of the Passover, on which occasion twelve lambs have their throats cut in the twinkling of an eye, as the High Priest, standing on a stone with his face towards the setting sun, repeats, "And the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening." Then they dip their fingers in the warm blood, and instead of sprinkling it on their door-posts they draw a line with it from the forehead to the tip of the nose on their children's faces, with many other perversione of the law of Moses. I purposed giving a more particular account of this annual feast, but I feel that my readers must, with myself, have felt too much disgust with the high priest's proceedings, to make it of much con- sequence how such men conduct their worship. I have only to say further that we got safely down the hill on the opposite side to that we asceeded, our friend Mr. El. Carry making the valley ring as he sung in splendid voice, "For ever with the Lord." Shechem was a city of importance four or five hundred years before Jerusalem was known as the capital of Judea. Its natural surroundings are perhaps the most picturesque of any in Palestine. It seems to have grown into a town between the time of Abraham's sojourn and that of Jacob's, when he came from Padan-aram. To stand within a city of such undoubted antiquity—a city with which Jacob and his family formed a treaty of peace, and which has existed, in spite of its tur- bulent and bloody history, ever since—was something wonderful for speck and span English blood. In the midst of such hoary surroundings, grey hairs are but the down on the cheek of infancy. Shechem was the centre of Joshua's operations for the consolidation of Israel when the tribes came into possession of the promised land. It was the seat of government when the ten tribes threw off the yoke of Rehoboam and accepted the servant of his father as their king, the wicked Jeroboam, whose baleful influence seams even yet to cling to its gates and walls— "the son of Nebat who made Israel to sin." Although we were encamped quite outside of the city, the howling of the dogs as they prowled about the streets inside, was so loud and incessant that it would have been impossible to sleep during the night if shear exhaustion had not in the long run steeped us in eblivion. The dogs of the city, Mr. El. Carry informed us, are almost innumerable. They breed and nurse their offspring in the public thoroughfares; and, being the acknowledged scavengers and guardians of the city, are seldom destroyed except by each other. They prowl about the narrow streets at night growling and fight- , ing over the garbage thrown out to them. Any inhabitant going out at night without a lantern is in danger of being torn to pieces, and his only safety is in sitting down quietly until a chance passer-by with a light comes to his relief. The dogs skulk away from the light. I suppose they are the lineal descendants of those that growled over the limbs of Jereoboam, Jezebel, and others, against whom the woe was pronounced,—" Him that dieth in the city shall the dogs eat ; and hint that dieth in the fields shall the fowls of the air eat." As we stood next morning in con- versation just before starting, Mr. El. Carry pointed to an overhanging fig tree, and spoke of its great utility. He said the fresh young leaves as they were then bursting out, were an excellent aperient; that the young figs they bore in the early spring were a wholesome vegetable when plucked and eaten with salt, and which did not at all interfere with the fruitfulness of the tree, as, later on in the year, it bears the richer fruit for drying and preserving. At some little distance from our tents, a number of lepers gathered about seven o'clock on the morning of our departure. They were squat- ting in a semi-circle as we turned out after breakfast. Al- though many of the poor creatures were sad pictures of human misery, none presented leprosy in its worst aspects. Dr. 'Vern° went ronnct and examined every one; handling their limbs, and lifting their eye-lids etc. He seemed to think they presented no features of skin disease that he bad n3t had under his care or observation in St. Bartholomew's. In England, as in Palestine, the disease, he said, was generally traceable to filthy habits and poor living. NABLOUS TO SAMARIA, We leit a egbt o'clock, and proceeded up the valley to- wards the west. After travelling one or two miles we struck over the hills to the right on our way to the ancient city of Samaria now Sebastieh, The way was toilsome, but much of the scenery was so fine that we thought little of the labour. The convexity of the hills was still a pleasing feature, and, being cultivated to the summit were already giving evi- dence of great fertility. The views were enlivened by many beautiful glimpses of the Mediterranean. The ten tribes had, in their day, a splended inheritance in the soil, the streams and climate of Samafia ; with ordinary industry in its cultivation it was sure to become a land "full of corn and wine," a land "flowing with milk and honey," We dis- mounted about noon at the village of Sebastieh, close to the ancient bill of Samaria; and first visited the church of St. John, now a Mosque. It is a large edifice. 153 feet long and 75 feet wide, with one end resting on a precipitous rock 100 feet high, which gives it, at that elevation, a very command- ing appearance. It is supposed to have been built by Queen Helena, but its architecture has too many characteristics of the period of the crusades to claim such antiquity. Whether it belongs to the earlier or tlater date, I should think there is no certainty at all that it covers the dust of John the Baptist. Josephus states that John was beheaded in the castle Ot Machceus, on the east of the Dead Sea. If Josephus be correct, I think we may safely give Queen Helena the honour of its erection, as it would require all her unapproachable ingenuity and credulity to effect s.uch a union between the deith and Lariat of the Baptist. It was rather a steep climb on foot to the hill on which, and around which, the ruins of the old city of Samaria are found ; the city whose wars and idolatries and will-worship, in rivalry with Jerusalem, make "n so much of the history of this ancient land. The hill is along and regular in form. The situation is wo-,derfully beautiful, it stands in the midst of a broad and fel t-e valley; I the 0110 we entered as we passed up between %hal and I Gerizirn to Shechem, and which here expands to a bre•lLth of five or six miles. The hills that encircle th 2, Talley at.) not reach the altitude of the hill of Sapar2- .., although they stand as a wall around it. Therefor, instead of Intercepting the vision they form the inner border to a magnificent land- scape, In which the broad Mediterranean is a conspicuous feature. It David had lived here I almost think his lyre would have been struck to higher and sweeter notes than Bethlehem or even Zion inspired him to sing. The hills around are either covered with the fresh green corn, or, ter- raced from base to summit for the cultivation of the richer fruits. In ancient times it was the amazing fertility of the vineyards on these sunny mountain sides that became a curse to the inhabitants of Samaria. Can anything exceed in appaling vividness of description the account which Isaiah gives of the city in his day : "They have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong

div.p: ------ drink, they are swallowed up of wine,,they are out of the way through strong drink ; they err iu vision, they stumble in judgment. For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean." I well remember our revered friend and companion, Mr. Frost, standing on the i face of the hill, and repeating n his rich and tremulous voice, the opening verses of the chapter in which the above \ quotation is found: "Woo to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, whose glorious beauty is a fading flower, which are on the head of the flat valleys of them that are overcome with wine." (To be continued next week.)

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick (chairman), and Mr. Henry Reynolds. A. COUPLE OF FIGHTING RELATIVES—David Beckett, Northwich, and Peter Beckett, Runcorn, two brothers, were charged with fighting, and being drunk and disorderly at Weston, on the 4th instant. bergeant Dalziel proved the case.—Peter was ordered to pay a tine of 10s. and 93. 6d. costs, or, in default, be imprisoned 14 days, with hard labour. The costs in the case Of the defendant David being heavy, he was only fined ss. and 185. costs. PUNISHING FOR HER AMUEEMENT.—Mary Ann Lovell, a young woman, was charged with assaulting a lad named Michael Callighan.—Complainant said that on the 27th ult., he was passing the house of defendant's mother, when she hit him with a fluke. He struck her back and then ran away. Some time after the defendant caught him, took him into the house, and locked the door. She gave him a good thrashing, and, on putting him out, struck him with a large shell, and cut his head. Defendant, who had paid the medical fee, and the cost of the summons, said she had arranged with the complainant's mother that the case should be withdrawn.—The Chairman said that as defendant had chosen to take the law into her own hands, she would be fined 20s. and costs. THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT HALTON.—Michael Duffy, an Irish labourer, was charged with attempting to commit suicide at Halton, on the 23rd ult , under circumstances pre- viously reported in The Excouiner.—Evidence was given by Thomas Feeney, brother-in-law of the prisoner, after which Superintendent Williamson said that from enquiries made, be found that the prisoner had, some years ago, an attack of sunstroke, and was subject to mental aberrations. He had received a medical certificate stating that the man had not yet recovered, and, ander these circumstances, he did not consider lie was fit to undergo a trial for the offence of which he had been guilty. He asked the Bench to remand the prisoner to the workhouse, where he had been since the 23rd ult.—Feeney asked that the prisoner might be set at liberty, so that he could be put under the care of his own wife.—Superintendent Williamson stated that he understood the wound from which Duffy was suffering required daily dressing, and would be far better in the workhouse until he recovered.—Prisoner was then removed under remand for a week. CAPTURE OF A GANG OF ALLEGED ROPE STEALERS.— John Roylance and Thomas Massey, boatmen, were charged with having, on the 7th instant, whilst in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, stolen ddlbs. of new rope, the property of their employers ; and they were also charged along with George Betley and Stephen Hough, boatmen, with having stolen and received it knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. Meadowcroft, the Runcorn agent of the company, watched the proceedings. —Superintendent Williamson having opened the case, James Weedall, canal constable, said that on the previous Saturday night, he went to the Eat Sarah Ann, of which the prisoner Bentley was captain, and in the berth of the prisoner Hough, who was a hand upon the vessel, he found the rope produced, which he saw from a particular strand in it, belonged to the Bridge- water Navigation Co. He took charge of the prisoner, and afterwards showed him to a police sergeant.—John Bailey, storekeeper at the Old Quay, said that on the Bth July he supplied the prisoner Roylance with the rope produced for use upon his flat—Mr. W. H. Chadwick, manager of the company's ropery, said the stolen rope was the property of his employers. It was worth 235. and had never been taken out of coil.—Sergeant McMichael stated that on Satur- day night, about 11 o'clock, he received the prisoner Hough into custody. At the police station Hough said the stolen rope had been brought on the flat at the Duke's dock, Liverpool, on the previous Friday night. It was purchased for 105. from the captain and hand of the flit Clyde. He then went to Betley's house in Mill-street and apprehended him, and at the police station confronted him with Hough, who made a similar statement to what be had said before. Betley replied "I know nothing about it." Sergeant Walley proved apprehending Roylance, and, placing him before Hough at the police station, and asking him " Is this the man you bought the rope from ?" Hough said, "Yes that is the captain." Roylance reylied, "No, don't say that." Hough answered, "It's the truth." Roylance said he knew nothing about the rope. He next apprehended Massey at his house in Queen-street, and on confronting him with Hough at the police station he said " Yes, that is the other man, and we divided the brass." Massey re- marked, Yes, it is quite true what he says. Roylance and me divided the money. It's a very bad job."—On being , formal*. charged by the Deputy Magistrate's Clerk (Mr. I Johnson.) similar statements to those given above were made by three of the prisoners. Betley said he had never had any intention of stealing rope belonging to the company, as he had seen the folly of such conduct in the past. Be alleged that Hough had persistently asked him to be allowed to buy the rope, but he (Betley) had strongly urged him to have nothing to do wills it, on the ground that he would be sure to get into trouble. He, however, admitted that on the day when the rope was taken on the vessel, Hough asked him if he might bring it, and then went away for it. He imme- diately afterwards " went to tell " him he must not bring it on the flat, but could not see him. Henext went to sleep, as he was very tired, and now alleged that the rope was taken on the boat whilst he was in that condition.—Hough did not support this tale, but said the only objection which Betley had raised to having the rope was that he bad only Bs. 6d. with which to pay for it. Betley saw it taken on board, and told him where to stow it away. —Prisoners were committed to Knutsford Quarter Sessions, which commenced on Mon- day, for trial.—George Betley and Stephen Hough were brought up on Thursday, charged with stealing 18Ibs. of rope, the property of Messrs. Thompson, McKay and Co., of Manchester, It was proved that the rope was l'eflt to the prisoners by the captain of one of the prosecutors' flats, arid they had not returned it. The charge against them was, therefore, dismissed.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, EDGE GREEN. - Tha Edge Green Primitive Methodists celebrated their chapel anniversary on Sunday last, when sermons were preached afternoon and evening by Mr. H. Fisher, of Wigan. Mode- rate congregations attended both services. The singing was good ; the choir giving an anthem at the evening service. The sum of £8 93. 41d. collected will be applied to the trust fund.

SELLING DRINK ON SuNDAr.—At Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday, Peter Boardman, landlord of the Mill- stone, Golborne, was charged with selling intoxicating liquor during prohibited hours.—Mr. Swift defended.—P.C. Beardsworth said that on Sunday morning, the 11th instant, he concealed himself to watch defendant's premises. About half-past seven o'clock defendant and his son-in-law, named Skelhorn, were observed walking in front of the house. I Two men named Brown and Allen came up, and they com- menced to talk. Something was said to Skelhorn and he went round to the back. He then came to the front window and Brown and Allen gays him something out of their pockets. Skelhorn handed them a pint jug and they drank the contents. They went back to Boardman, who was stand- ing on the road and appeared to be looking out for someone, and Skelhorn also joined them. Three men named Burrows, Clubb, and Hayes came up afterwards and spoke to them. Skelhorn again went into the back premises and returned with half a gallon jug. He called to the men, and they went up to the end of the building and drank the ale. Wit- ness and the constable who was Wit h him then made a rush. Boardman shouted to Skelhorn, who took hold of the jug, emptied some of the ale upon the ground, and ran inside. The others went away in all directions. Witr ess tasted what I was poured out of the jug on the ground and found it to be i ale—P.C. Whiting gave corroborative evidence, and the Bench fined defendant 40s. and costs.—Ellis Brown, James Burrows, Thomas Allen, and James Hayes were charged with aiding and abetting Peter Boardman to commit an offence against the Licensing Act during prohibited hours.—The Bench fined them ss. and costs each. STRIKE OF COLLIERS.—A strike affecting upwards of two hundred hands connected with Messrs. Evans and Co.'s Golborne colliery commenced on Wednesday morning owing to a change in the rates for getting coal, both round and small. On Monday Messrs. Evans' representative, Mr. Glover, intimated to the hands that a change in this depart- ment would take place on Wednesday morning, the firm having decided to have the round coal separated from the small, or burgy, the price to be paid for the former being is. 2d. per ton and for the latter 10d. per ton. Meetings of the men were held to consider the effect this change would have upon their earnings. Having considered the matter, they stated that owing to the shall being in greater portion than the round coal the prices offered .ave..db.i be against them, and they could not therefore accept .tie change in its present form. The protracted strike of last winter is still fresh in the memory of the inhabitants, many of whom suffered in consequence, and it is hoped that an amicable settlement will shortly be arrived at, and thus prevent what might prove a serious loss and inconvenience to both employers and employed.

The annual meeting of the Provincial Grand. Lodge of West Lancaehire was held on Wednesday in the Winter Gardens, Blackpool, under the presidency of the Earl of Lathom, F.G.M. Nearlo 1,000 Freemasons were present, probably the largest gathering ever held in the diviaion. Large sums were voted in charity, and several schemes were inaugurated with a view of putting the West Lancashire province on a proper footing with regard to the general masonic charities.

Witness rushed into the house, and at the door by which the kitchen is entered he found the deceased lad. The gas was lighted and he saw the blood was flowing from his head. The servant was standing near the lad and said something to him about either stopping, or wiping off the blood from the youth. She was not holding anything in her hand. She appeared very much alarmed. He rushed into the place with the object of seeing if he could be of any assistance to the youth by carrying him to a surgeon, but on perceiving that he was shot in the head, he saw the uselessness of any help he could render and ran off for a doctor and a policeman. He did not tell the deceased young woman where he was going. He took off his coat in order that he might run the faster, there being some books in the pockets, and on .neet- ins, Dr. Brown and a policeman he sent them to the house. —By Juryman: Were the lad and the girl on good terms? Yes.—What sort of a disposition had this girl? Was she lively ? She was not a lively girl; some days she would not speak to me for a whole day.—Was the lad steady? Yes •, he was a very intelligent boy. I had him as a scholar in the Sunday school when he was young.—ls Mn. Row- lands related to you? She is my aunt, sir. I was really fond of this boy. [Witness appeared considerably affected whilst giving his evidence.] Samuel Overton, of 10, Milton-street, said he was labourer at Messrs. Gossage's. About twenty minutes to seven o'clock on Saturday evening he heard a report, some- thing like a pistol going off. Immediately after the servant girl ran out and said that a lad in their house bad shot him- self. At this time the witness Ethall came down the entry, gave witness's wife his coat, and ran off, saying he was going for a doctor. He went into the house with the young woman Pendleton, and asked how theaccident had happened. She told him that the lad had been playing with the pistol, and it went off and shot him. He told her he must ran out and fetch someone else in. He did not mention the police. At the same time he saw her take the revolver off the dresser. The body of the boy was lying by the side of the dreeser. She then said she would show him how the poor' lad took hold of the revolver. He ran out of the house without waiting to see anything further. When he had got to the back door of the house he heard the report of the pistol. He went as far as the entry and then turned back into the house, when he saw the young woman lying upon the kitchen floor, with her head towards the front doer. She did not speak or take any notice of him. He did not see the pistol. Soon afterwards Dr. Brown entered, and he told him bow the act had been done. The two deceased were alive when the doctor came, but they died immediately afterwards. .He had never heard of any difficulty or quarrelling between the two deceased, or that there was a revolver in the house. The police came immediately afterwards.—By the Inspector: The revolver was in the middle of the dresser when he ob- served it, and the barrel was pointing to the back door, which is a considerable distance from the t oy.—By jury- man: Was the revolver where he was likely to have dropped it? No, sin—Supposing that he was standing where his feet were, would it not be near his hand ? It would be close; but still, in the position in which he was lying, it would be impossible for him to put the revolver down.—The Coroner: Why? Witness: Because it looked to me that he had fallen I "outside."--The Coroner: But then it would fall. lam not 'supposing that he laid it down. Could not it fall? Not 'there, sir.—ln answer to another juryman, witness said the revolver would naturally have fallen upon the floor.—By a juryman: Had the boy his hand up, as if he had been 'warding off a blow? No; his hands were "outside." P.C. He told Mr. Birchall that as he was not going up home at once he would rather not have it in his pocket. Mr. Birchall replied that he would send for the firearm in order that he might see it. The lad was told to go for it, and then in the short space of two minutes the youth Ather- ton came back saying that the messenger had shot himself. He went to ehe house at once, and Mr. Birchall ran before him. When witness got there the young woman and the boy were on the floor. Dr. Brown said, "There is life in the girl, but the boy is quite dead. Let us lift her on to the sofa," and they did so. The revolver was lying on the floor, about six or nine inches from the servant's left hand. There were two charges in the firearm, and another couple had been let off. Dr. O'Keeffe, in reply to the Coroner, said that Dr. Brown had not attended as lie was only representing Dr. McDonnell, who was out of town on the Saturday. Witness got to the place immediately after the accident, —at about ten minutes past seven. He found both deceased dead from gun shot wounds in the head. There was not very much loss of blood, comparatively speaking.. He examined the young woman first, and found the tongue terribly lacerated, and the cervical vertebrm dislocated. The boy had a wound on the left side of the nose, about half an inch from the tip. The size of the wound was such as might have been caused by a bullet like that new produced, which fitted the revolver belonging to Mr. Birchall. On putting his hand into the lad's mouth he found one of the cervical vertebrre fractured. He was of opinion that the wounds had been caused by placing tele muzzle of the revolver in the mouths of deceased. The bullets had not gone to the brain in either case. He could only theorise upon the cause of death, as what he had seen did not enable him to come to any definite conclusion. The jury returned the following 'verdicts :—(No. 1.) "That Janes Hague, being a boy of the age of 13, on the Bth day of October, was accidentally killed by a pistol shot wound then inflicted on the said deceased, as they believe, by misadventure, by Harriet Pendleton, and that he came to his death by the said misadventure, and not otherwise." (No, 2.) " That Harriet Pendleton, on the Bth October, died from a pistol shot then received by the deceased, and, as they believe, by her own hand, she firing the said pistol in the excitement produced, as they also believe, having im- mediately before, by misadventure and in ignorance of the same being loaded, shot a certain boy with a pistol she was bringing down stairs, for him to take to his employer." This terminated the enquiry.

The body of the young woman Pendleton was removed from Widnes on Tuesday evening at a comparatively late hour, to Hale, where her mother lives, for interment on the following day. Probably the removal being made so late in the day accounts for the fact that there was no demon- stration of any kind. The funeral of tie youth James Hague took place on Thursday afternoon, and was attended by several thousands of spectators. Most of the shops along the line of route were closed at a mark of sympathy. About a quarter-past three o'clock the sad cortege, headed by a drum and fife band of which Hague had been a member,played the "Dead March," in " Saul, ' started from the house in Wellington- street. The next in the solemn procession were the parents and a number of friends of the lad, who seems to have been very popular; and then came the coffin, which was very appropriately carved by four boys who had been the com- panions of the unfortunate little fellow, and it was covered by several wreaths of immortelles. The route to the grave- yard of the Parish Church, where the interment took place, was lined with spectators, and vast numbers followed the mourners. A multitude of people surrounded the gates of the unpretentious little church, and all the efforts of policemen present were needed to preserve that decorousness of demeanour which ought always to be associated with so solemn an event as committing a fellow mortal to the dark house and the long sleep. Some short time elapsed before the coffin and its bearers could enter the churchyard, but this ob- ject was at last effected. The eager crowd made for the edifice, and would have immediately filled every nook and corner of it, had not restrictions been placed upon their admission. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes, seized the opportunity of saying a few solemn words to those present, no doubt in the hope that some would lay them to heart. He said : "As there are a large number of persons in the church who seldom come on other o 3casions, I may ask you to take part solemnly in the service; and remember that though he whose death brings us together has been sud- denly cut off, what is his fate to-day may be ours to mor- row ! Therefore, whether many here be drawn together from curiosity, from a morbid feeling, or from respect to the deceased, or respect to his friends, if we lay this service and event to heart, under God's blessing, the sad occurrence will not be without its silver lining." The reverend gentleman then read the usual service. None but the friends of the deceased and the members of the band were allowed to ap- proach the grave. After the conclusion of the solemn rites the vast concourse quietly dispersed.

div.head: ANOTHER TRAGEDY AT WIDNES,
div.p: ANOTHER TRAGEDY AT WIDNES,

TWO PEOPLE KILLED WITH A REVOLVER. During the last few years the town of Widnes has obtained e sad pre-eminence on account of the murders and crimes of violence which have taken place within its borders. It is a somewhat strange fact that all these tragedies have been enveloped in a veil of mystery which the efforts of the litnspector of Police have entirely failed to unravel. The murder of the unfortunate watchman at Messrs. Snape's chemical works was alleged to have been the act of some members of a secret society, but, in reality, the public know nothing of who committed this crime, which still is hidden in the darkest mystery. Then came the Tracey tragedy, in which, though two men suffered the full penalty of the law, the conviction was obtained on circumstantial evidence alone, and every one who has paid any attention to the literature of crime knows full well that evidence of this particular character alone has more than once sent to the scaffold many a man who soul was like Eugene Aram's school chil- dren, "untouched by sin." These two terrible crimes remind one of Poe's graphic tale of "The murder in the Rue Morgue," which, it will be remembered by the readers of that writer's "Tales of Mystery and Imagination," was surrounded by circumstances which clearly pointed to a cer- ,tain individual as the murderer, though the guilty one was .a monkey of a large species. Another mysterious affair has this week to be recorded, in ewhich a young woman and an errand lad lost their lives. The details, which are as follows, are of a very sad descrip- tion:—The names of the unfortunate victims are a young woman named Harriet Pendleton, who had been employed by Mts. Rowlands, of Milton-street, as a domestic servant, for a short time; and James Hague, aged 13, the son of a labourer, and engaged as an errand boy by Mr. James Birchall, draper, who has two establishments in the town, the principal being in Waterloo-road. The last named gentleman lodges with Mrs. Rowlands, and on Saturday night P.C. Stott, a worthy officer in the Widnes force, who is about teetry his fortune under the Southern Cross, called upon him for the purpose of paying an account. Probably the young police officer had proved a good customer, bet whether from this reason or sheer good nature, Mr. Birchall told him he would present him with a revolver which was at Ilia lodgings. He sent the lad Hague for it, telling bim whereabouts it was in his bedroom, wrapped in paper. This was about twenty minutes to seven, and, on his way to the house, the youth met a companion named James Atherton, and acked him to go with him. He did so, and he had only been standing by the yard door a very few minutes when he saw a tall person, who, it is supposed, was the domestic ser- vant Pendleton; go upstairs, and immediately afterwards he heard the report of a firearm being discharged. Atherton waited a few seconds in anxious suspense, and then the back door of the house was thrown open and the young woman Pendleton rushed out, looking very pale, and requested him to fetch Mr. Birchall, as there had been an accident. Atherton agreed to do so, but before going looked in at the kitchen door, and saw the lad Hague lying motionless upon the floor, and bleeding from the mouth. He did not wait to ask the servant a question as to the manner in which the sad affair had happened, and it is much to be regretted that he did not do so, as light would then have been thrown upon a case which is open to all manner of curious surmises. Atherton hal no sooner gone, than a young man named Ethall, wko is employed as a weigh clerk at one of the works in the town, and lodges at Rowlands', entered the dwelling, and was thunderstruck to seethe lad lying upon the floor, his young life-blood ebbing fast away, whilst the servant, who ap- peared to be labouring, under the greatest excitement, en- treated him to get something for the purpose of rubbing the youth's mouth. Atherton ran off for a doctor; and no sooner had he left than a neighbour named Overton, who had been alarmed by the dircharge of the revolver, went into Rowlands' and asked the servant what had happened. She took up the firearm from the dresser,and remarking that the boy had shot himself, said she would show him how he did it. He, however, apparently considering the state of the errand lad extremely critical, did not wait for the proffered explanation, but ran off for assistance. He had, however, scarcely got more than a few yards when he heard another shot, and full of foreboding, he entered the kitchen, where he found Pendleton lying upon the floor, with blood stream- ing from her mouth, and the revolver lying by her side. Mr. Brown, who was acting as tocum tenens to Dr. McDon- nell, was passing near the house, and, hearing what had happened, he ran ia. He found that both the victims of the strange tragedy were alive, but they only lived a very few minutes, and neither of them was able to utter a word. The police were rapidly on the scene, and, on taking possession of the revolver, they found that two of the four chambers which it contained, had been discharged. Dr. O'Keeffe was afterwards instructed by the Inspector of Police to examine the bodies' and the result of his investigations was that the bullets had not in either case penetrated the brain, but death had resulted from injury to the cervical vertebrre. We need hardly say that the sad tragedy caused much ex- citement in the town. The young woman, Pendleton, had only so late as the previous Thursday visited her mother at Hale to tell her of her approaching marriage, which was to take place within a week. At the inquest, Mr. Driffield, the county coroner, made some strong remarks to the effect that he considered Mr. Birchall morally, though not criminally, responsible for the deaths, owing to the fact that he bad allowed the revolver to lie about in his bedroom, and not uttered a word of caution to the errand boy when he sent him for it. Some of the jury appeared to think otherwise. Mr. Birchall seemed much affected by his position.

div.head: HARVEST THANKSGIVINGS.
div.p: HARVEST THANKSGIVINGS.

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The annual harvest festival in connection with the above church was held on Thursday evening, and was well attended. The service was read by the vicar, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, and the lessons by the Rev. T. Louch, curate, the sermon being preached by the Rev. .1. Wright- Williams, of Widnes, who took for his text Psalm ciii, 2, "Bless the Lord, Oh my soul, and forget not all his benefits." The old fashioned structure had been very neatly decorated with fruits, flowers, ferns, cerials, and vegetables, and the chancel presented a most attractive appearance. Much labour had been spent upon the pulpit which was exquisitely embellished, and showed that the decorators were possessed of much artistic ability. Great pains had been taken with the reading and prayer desks, and the ornamention through- out was greatly admired by the congregation.

CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE. Harvest thanksgiving services were held in Christ Church Padgate, on Sunday morning and evening last. The sacred edifice • had been most tastefully decorated. The window . . . . .

ledges were ornamented with plants, fruit, berries, and flowers. On the altar were placed baskets of grai 03 and, vases of choice flowers. In the centre was a handsome floral cross, the work of the Vicar. The pulpit was fringed with oats, and bordered with ivy leaves, while in the centre was a large and handsome bouquet. Rich clusters of grapes hung from the gas brackets, and the altar rails, font, and gas brackets were neatly decorated, and looked very pretty. The decorations had been carried out by the following:— Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Doming, the Misses Crawford, Miss Samson, the Misses Wrightson, of Paddington, and the Misses Turner, assisted by Mr. George Wrlliams. The morning preacher was the vicar, the Rev. W. H. Wil- liams, who took for his text Luke ii, 3, "Give .us day by day our daily bread." He said many of them had, no doubt, read with much interest the inaugural address of the Presi- dent of the British Association delivered at York a short time since. They were amazed as they read the statements of the wonderful developments and the mighty strides that had been made in the scientific word during the last 50 years. But if the reading of the address gave them plea- sure on the one hand it was a souses of pain on the other, since no mention or any allusion was made to Goers existence, His Providence, His goodn-ss or His omnipotenFe. He seemed to have no place, and to t ,Ite no part in the vast field of this Universe. What the scientific assembly had not the power or reason to fully expl tin, or sufficient capa- city to elucidate they put down as an hypothesis, a supposi- tion —a something not proved but a something to be taken for granted in order to draw a cone Ilion for the sake of an argument. Whatever force there n lat be in such a conclu- sion, or in such method of reasoni is, he did not think it would lessen their belief in God's xistence, or in any de- gree militate against His revealed tirord. That Word had stood the most intense crucial test . f the scientific mind in all ages of the world since it definer led from its heaven-born court, and it would stand, since no earthly hnman science would ever be able to undermine it; plain simple declarations. Referring to the untiring exertions which had been made in agriculture and which of late had been so badly requited, he said if there was a class of men who deserved especial praise and sympathy, a class whose patience had been sorely tried, and who had yet evinced remarkable courage, it was the English farmer. The suffering from agricultural depression had cast a deep shadow of gloom over the country, but thus far, if they read rightly, the adverse seasons had not impared the fertility of the soil and the feeding qualities-of the pasture land. This was an age of progress. The Eng- lish farmer must swim with the tide; he must strive to batter his condition, and adopt those scientific principles which were being more and more brought into requisition. They had nobly batted with depression, and the rain and the storm. They must still battle them with the same heroism, ! fortitude and patience, and they. would yet reap their reward. To patient waiting the prize was sure. In conclusion he re- marked that the collections that day were to be appropriated to the Chancel Fund. The cost of beautifying the house of God had been estimated at £O5O, and he was glad to an- nounce that they had about one-half of that slim already in the bank. The sermon in the evening was preached by the Rev. W. Quekett, rector of Warrington, from the words of Jeremiah "'rho harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved," and he alluded, in the course of his remarks to the different kinds of harvest,'making special referenceto the joy it gave parents to zee their children grow up to be useful members of society. The collections for the day amounted to £8 12s. ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.

Considering the unfavourahle state of the weather there was a good congregation at the harvest thanksgiving service held in St. Barnabas' church, Lovely-lane, on Wed- nesday evening. The pretty little church had been rendered unusually attractive by the effective decorations, which, although on a limited scale, had been executed with great taste, and the artistic floral combinatiedis produced by the forty ladies and gentlemen the congregation who had undertaken the e -7:ee'ilishment of the edifice, were greatly adT..;eu. The font was almost hidden from view by a Variety of ferns, studded with white dahlias, with which it was bedecked. Around the pulpit were arranged borders of oats, the effect of which was greatly heightened by the artistic disposition of dahlias, and liliumss ; while on the top was a border of ivy leaves, relieved with fuschias. The reading desk was fringed with oats, and bordered with geranium leaves neatly ornamented with liliass, geraniums, and fusehias. The" pedestal was entwined with oats and geraniums, and at the foot was a choice assortment of fruits. Borders of ivy leaves and dahlias were placed on the choir stalls; and the altar rails were decorated with a fringe of oats, bordered with ivy and geranium leaves, and set off with chrysanthiumms, dahlias, and fuschias. • Above the altar were the following words in yellow ornamental capitals on a red g•ound :—"They joy before Thee according to the joy in harvest." Below this was a handsome cross composed of fetus and.liliams. On the altar was a splendid bunch of grapes, and other fruits, and on either side were vases of roses and geraniums, and sheaves of wheat. A variety of plants were arranged in the chancel; and miniature sheaves of wheat were placed on the window ledges, amid splendid collections of dahlias. On the whole the decorations re- flected the greatest credit upon the ladies and gentlemen by whom they were executed. The sermon was preached by the Rey. F. Wainwright, of Altrincham, from bt. Matthew, vi. 2:3. "Behold the fowls of the air ; for they sow not, neither do not reap, nor gather into barm. ; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not better than they ?" After pointing out the superiority of man over the dumb creatures, the preacher remarked that in the text man was rebuked because he did not rise to a higher point, and cheered because he saw God had such love for the lower creatures how much must He have for him. How often, he said, people were asking just now what would be the end of their troubles. How often they were asking was there any way of escape in connection with the harvest. For example it was only a few weeks ago people were saying "lam afraid there will be no harvest ; it will all be ruined ; the country will be impoverished; trade will he destroyed." And in many houses people were saying "if this harvest fails we are undone There wr:e plenty of cases in which people had really prepared to give up their last hope when they saw the rain descending in torrents, and believed the Providence of God had forsaken them. They could not trust God. gut they had been rebuked since then, for they found the dark prophecies had not been realised, the harvest had not been altogether lost, the corn had not all sprouted, trade had not qn ite come to a stand still, and the nation was not yet quite utterly ruined. If the birds could be so happy in their trust how happy man's confidence should be.

, CHRIST CHURCH LATCHFORD. Thanksgiving services for the ingathering of the harvest were held at this church on Wednesday. During the day Holy Communion, Matins and Litany, and a children's service were held. Then followed the evening service, which was well attended, the following clergy being present Rev. Canon Greenall, Grappenhall ; Rev. G. H. Spooner, Rev. W Slater, St. James's, Latchford; the vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, and the curate, the Rev. James Prescott. The pretty church with its floral adornment looked doubly handsome, and those ladies of the congregation who had taken part in the decorations, are to be congratulated on the tastefnl and beautiful display. The font, at the west end of the church, with its drapery of the delicate maiden hair, moss and other green leaves, intermingled with the almost pure white of the Bikini, the jessamine and the dahlia, had a quiet, subdued, but most pleasant kind cf beauty. The whiteness of the flowers seemed the purer, by contrast with the dark green of the leaves which surrounded them. Above the font, and at the apex of a cone of what appeared ropes of leaves and ferns, was a small cross formed of liliums, the effect being most pleasing. Behind was the west window decorated with ferns, leaves, cerials, and many bright coloured flowers. The other windows were also nicely adorned in the same manner, and entwining each gas standard, was a garland of flowers, leaves, and wheat, plenti- fnlly, but tastefully, sprinkled with geraniums, coloured dahlias, wild red berries, and occasionally a group of pears. The pulpit was much admired. A border of leaves and red berries, with a fringe of cereals went round the top. The panels were covered with a white woollen substance, and in the centre of each was placed a flower or cluster of flowers, with a spray of maiden hair and other ferns. The boquets stood out in bold relief from the white ground, and the effect was beautiful. A boquet of lilium with a graceful spray of ferns appeared as if a work in Las relief, with this difference, that it was real, and far more beautiful than any imitation. Each panel had its distinctive marks of beauty, and with the garlands of leaves and flowers which surrounded its base, the pulpit was indeed pretty. The next thing that attracted the attention was the reading desk, which, for a width of about eight inches round the top, was covered with mosses and ferns. In the centre a pretty cross made of cauliflower was fixed, on the right a bunch of tomatoes, and on the left a large sunflower. Beneath was suspended a bunch of luscious purple grapes. The lower part of the desk was draped with ferns, green leaves, roses, dahlias, B:c., and as a whole was a good specimen of the decorative art. On the communion table was a beautiful cross covered with mosses and ferns, with a large variety of pretty white flowers. The communion rails and choir stalls were also adorned, and the entrance to the transcept was, wreathed with leaves and wild berries. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Mr. Spooner, who took for his text the latter part of the 56th verse of the 12th chapter of the Book of Exodus :—" What mean ye by this service." He said one characteristic of Christianity was its universality and comprehensiveness; for it could adapt itself to men and to all circumstances belonging to all nations. Man was said to be possessed of three parts— body, mind, and spirit. Christianity told us that our body was a "temple of God's holy spirit ;" that our mind was a talent to be exercised upon God's revelation in nature and in His Holy Book; that our spirit, if there was to be true religion, must be in union with the spirit of Christ. It was a Levitical law that the people should be furnished with the reason for each ceremony, and if it was necessary in those early ages it was certainly necessary in the nineteenth century ; for they were constantly asked why they took this form of Christianity, and why that form. With regard to the harvest festival there were three forms in which it could be considered—the harvest miracle, the harvest mercy, and the harvest responsibility. Had they not seen how a seed after being in the earth a short time appeared to have lost all vitality, and thought it was perfectly corrupt and use- lefs ; then by the aid of the microscope seen the tender germ of life which had begun to show itself. That was the mira- cle. "First the blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear." It was some times said that the time for miracles bad passed away. But miracles were being repeatedly per- formed in nature which were not noticed. It was a miracle that they were permitted to gather there to celebrate the goodness of God for the past harvest. With regard to the harvest mercy. They had read a good deal in the news- papers about the disastrous crops in Lancashire and the Midland Counties, but in the parish over which he presided the harvest had been a most bountiful one. Supposing their district had not been blessed by God, bad they to have no harvest celebration? Shortly there would be grain in abundance poured into our ports from America, and in their thanksgiving service they were not simply to think of the harvest in their own parish, in Cheshire or in England, but of all the world. Our responeibililies were to show our thankfulness to God for His In Lay kindaesses by living more holy, more sanctified lives, to show in our relation to others that we were not living in faith, but trying to leave that circle where God had placed us better for our influence.— A collection was made on behalf of the Chester Diocesan Association.

div.head: FARN WORTH.
div.p: FARN WORTH.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at Farnworth Parish Church on Sunday, morning and evening. The ser- vice was read by the Rev. S. A. Spooner, and the preacher was the Rev. J. S. Eagar. Mr. Eagar, in the course of his sermon alluded to the heavy rains by which the ruin of the harvest had been threatened, and to the prayers for fair weather, which in almost every church had been offered up to the Most High. In the evening the service was read by the Rev. G. Holloway, vicar of Farnworth, and Mr. Eagar again occupied the pulpit. There were collections at both services on behalf of the Curates' Fund. That in the morn- ing realised £3 103.

div.head: ST. AMBROSE'S, WIDNES.
div.p: ST. AMBROSE'S, WIDNES.

Thanksgiving services at this place of worship were con- tinued on Sunday. In the morning the sermon was preached by the Rev. G. Holloway, vicar of Farnworth, who took his text from Psalm civ., 28. The offertory, which was on be- half of the Curates' Fund, amounted to £1 19s. 7d. In the evening the sermon was preached by the Rev. S. A. Spooner, who took as his text Psalm lxvii., 5, G. In the course of his remarks the reverend gentleman alluded to the gratitude and thankfulness which men, individually and collectively, owed to God. To the members of that congregation the new church in which they worshipped ought to be an object for thanksgiving. • The offertory at the evening service amounted to £2 9s. 4d.

div.head: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

Much labour had been bestowed on the decoration of the interior of this church, and the effect of the elaborate or- namentation must have been pleasing to the large congre-. gation which assembled there on Thursday evening to thank the Giver of all for the fruits of the harvest. Entering by the south door the visitor was exhorted by a conspicuous motto to " Enter into His courts with praise." The font next would call for an admiring glance. It was surmounted by a pyramid of flowzrs, arranged most artistically, and is quite a new feature in the church embellishment. The pillars were treated uniformly with fringes of wheat depend- ing from evergreens. The altar rails had received deft at- tention, and the pulpit and choir stalls were adorned with flowers. Upon the altar table were some choice fruit and flowers, while at the foot were arranged some rare hothouse I plants. Tastefully chosen flowers ornamented the rood- screen, W hich was surmounted -by two beautiful white crosses. In the centre aisle there was a minature haystack, placed there by Mr. Wm. Baker, of llocksayage, mud this was an object greatly dmirecl. There were also two small wheat stacks near the altar, placed there by Mr. Wm. Stokes, of Prospect Farm. Many of the neighbouring farmers supplied grain, Sm., for decorative purposes; and a hamper of flowers was given by Mr. Thomas Acton, of Henley Wood. Mrs. Jones, of Holly Bank, lent some. plants ; and the whole decorations were carried out under the superin- tendence of Lady Brooke. The sermon was preached by the I Rev. T. Pym Williamson, of Tbelwall.

div.head: ST. CHAD'S, OVER.
div.p: ST. CHAD'S, OVER.

The annual harvest thanksgiving at St. Chad's was com- memorated on Thursday, when a tea for those from a dis- tance was partaken of by about 200, in the; Darnhall school, and later in the evening the venerable pile of St. Chad's was crowded by worshippers and sight-seers. It was very taste- fully decorated with corn, fruits, ferns, flowers, and moss by the ladies of the congregation. The sermon was delivered by the Rev. J. Ti. Cooper, M.A., rural dean of Middlewich and rector of Tarporley. The clergy who assisted the Rev. G. W. Ninis, the vicar, were the Rev. E. Nixon, M.A., in- cumbent of Christ Church. Winsford, and the Rev. J. Richards, M.A., of Minshull.

TERRE= CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. —The opening concert of the season was given in the Club Roam, Stocks- lane, on Friday evening, and, being in every way a decided success, auaurs well for the course of entertainments which is to be continued through the winter. The singers were Miss White, of Liverpool, and Miss Richardson, of War- rington; Messrs. Booth, Hargreaves, Reddish, and Wood- ward, and the audience greeted each and all with well merited applause. The humorous element was contributed by Miss Larry Manogue and Fred Highlev, who for some twenty minutes simply kept the company in a roar. THE APPLICATION FOR AN ADVANCE IN COLLIERS' WAGES.—On Monday afternoon, a largely-attended meeting of representatives from the principal colliery districts in the county was held at the Miners' Hali,Wigan, for the purpose of receiving the reply of the masters to the applicath n recently made by the men for an advance of 15 per cent. on their present rate of wages. The replies sent in from indi- vidual employers were very voluminous and wee on the whole regarded as of a satisfactory character. The masters generally allowed that during the past month there had been a slight improvement in trade principally in house coal, but this, it was stated, could be attributed mainly to the effect of the rumour in the manufacturing districts that. coals were about to be increased in price. However, should the improvement continue and show signs of permanency, they suggested that the end of the present month would be a more opportune time for making the application for an advance, and intimated that in all probability an increase might then be granted. After a full discussion of the matter the following resolution was unanimously agreed to by the meeting and ordered to be forwarded to the masters: —"Gentlemen,—We very much regret that you are not yet prepared to give us an advance of 15 per cent.;- but as you seem to think the end of the present month a more oppor- • tune time we hereby agree to extend our presenti notice to • the end of the present month, at which time, f our advance ' be not given, we shall hold ourselves at liberty to take such steps as we may deem advisable to secure the same." The notice originally given expired on Wednesday.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.— In connection with the Science and Art Department, Kensington, and City and Guilds of London Institute. —Session 1881-82.—The eighth Session has now commenced. SYLLABUS : Mondays : Inorganic Chemistry, 6-30 to 8-0 p.m.; Alkali Manufacture, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Tuesdays: Art —Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 p m.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art—Freehand Drawing, 6-30 to 8-0 p.m.; Building Construction and Draw- ing, 8-0 to 9-0 p.m. Fridays: Sound, Light, and Heat, 7-0 to 8-0 p.m.; Animal Physiology, 8-0 to 9-0 pm. The Technologi- cal Class (Alkali Manufacture) will include the manufacture of Sulphuric Acid, Sulphate of Soda. Soda Ash, Caustic Soda, Soda Crystals, and Bleaching Powder. Candiddtrs eligible for the Technological Class (Alkali Manufacture) must be actually employed in Chemical or other allied works, and they must have passed, or pass during the coming session, In two of the following-named subjects :—Machine Construction, Building Construction, Theoretical Mechanics, Applied Mechanics, Acdustics, Light and Heat, and Inorganic Chemistry. Fee, 3s. per class, payable in advance. No class will commence unless a sufficient number of students join. Those who intend to join these classes must do so before the end of October. JOSEPH MORRISON, Hon. Sec. Widnes, September 22nd, 1881.
